To gain a more comprehensive understanding of these changes on a global scale, Damioli’s study analysed a large micro-level database from PATSTAT, covering 23,915 applicants holding at least one AI-related patent between 2000 and 2016. Using text-mining techniques to identify patent families with AI-relevant keywords in titles or abstracts, the study revealed a rapid expansion of AI innovation: comparing the periods 2000–2005 and 2011–2016, the number of AI innovators grew by 338%, AI patent families increased by 276%, non-AI patent families rose by 15%, and the ratio of AI to non-AI patents surged by 227%. Interestingly, however, the average number of AI patents per innovator decreased by 25%, suggesting broader participation but more focused patenting activity per entity. In terms of sectoral distribution, from 2000 to 2016 around 38% of AI patents originated from core ICT industries, with 27% in ICT manufacturing (computers, electronics, optical products, electrical equipment) and 11% in ICT services (publishing, audiovisual and broadcasting, telecommunications, IT, and other information services). Other important contributors included machinery manufacturing (13%), transport equipment (9%), and scientific R&D (10%). Notably, service industries played an increasingly prominent role, accounting for 39% of all AI patents, compared to just 15% of non-AI patents filed by the same innovators, highlighting the growing diffusion of AI beyond traditional IT sectors (Damioli et al., [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR15 "Damioli, G., Van Roy, V., Vertesy, D., & Vivarelli, M. (2025). Is artificial intelligence leading to a new technological paradigm? Structural Change and Economic Dynamics, 72, 347–359. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.strueco.2024.12.006
                  
                ")).

These developments suggest that AI is becoming a key tool for generating and accelerating innovation across the economy, reinforcing its role as an “enabling technology”. Thanks to its expanding application and ability to improve data-driven decision-making, AI is increasingly positioning itself as the foundation of a new technological regime, either within the existing IT paradigm or as a fundamental transformation of it.

The use of AI in predicting employee attrition illustrates a tangible, positive impact of AI on the labour market. A recent European study applied advanced machine learning methods to a unique cross-national survey covering 9,296 employees from 30 countries. The researchers compared both interpretable models, such as logistic regression, and state-of-the-art black-box models, including LightGBM (Light Gradient Boosting Machine), to predict employees’ intention to leave their organizations within three months. Using robust evaluation procedures, including repeated 10-fold cross-validation and the Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUC-PR) to account for imbalanced data, the study found that LightGBM and logistic regression were the top-performing models, achieving predictive performance more than twice the baseline (0.225). The analysis further identified the most influential factors driving turnover intention, including Sustainable Employability, Employership, Attendance Stability, Motivation, and Vitality. Causal analysis using structural causal models and partial dependence plots confirmed that improvements in these areas, particularly in employee motivation, are likely to reduce turnover. This approach enables organizations to anticipate attrition, plan staffing more effectively, and implement targeted interventions, highlighting how AI can support workforce stability while providing actionable insights for HR policies (Lazzari et al., [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR29 "Lazzari, M., Alvarez, J. M., & Ruggieri, S. (2022). Predicting and explaining employee turnover intention. International Journal of Data Science and Analytics, 14(3), 279–292. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s41060-022-00329-w
                  
                ")).

Some authors suggest that with the coming of advanced artificial intelligence, especially “General AI”, there is not only a change in existing professions, but also the creation of entirely new job market offers and forms of work. With the ability to combine previously separate domains (e.g., healthcare and data science), new professions and fields are created. These changes cannot be explained simply by the automation of routine activities, but reflect a deeper transformation in innovation strategies, organisational learning, and the ability of companies to redefine the problem and solutions. This transformation of work reality emphasises interdisciplinary thinking, creativity, and the ability to navigate uncertain environments, redefining the concept of qualifications and competences in the labour market. Building on this idea, (Giacomoni, [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR19 "Giacomoni, G. (2022). Towards a general framework for innovation shaped with AI to create and transform market offerings. European Management Review, 19(1), 107–122. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/emre.12492
                  
                ")) proposes a conceptual framework showing how AI can actively shape the innovation process itself. According to this framework, AI is not merely a tool for automating tasks, but a catalyst for _creating and transforming market offerings_, especially in complex sectors such as biotechnology and pharmaceuticals. By integrating AI into early-stage decision-making and organizational learning, firms can explore previously uncharted solution spaces, hybridize knowledge from distinct domains, and adapt more flexibly to changing market conditions. This suggests that the arrival of General AI may accelerate the generation of novel products, services, and professional roles, supporting the notion that AI-driven innovation is closely intertwined with the evolution of work and the labor market.

## 2 Aim and methods

This research was created in response to the need to understand the dynamic changes that the increasing implementation of artificial intelligence is bringing to the field of work and human resource management. Given the rapid speed of technological development and the diverse approaches to AI adoption in different sectors and types of organizations, it is essential to create a comprehensive overview of current knowledge.

This study aims to identify key trends in employment, skills requirements, and HR practices through a thematic analysis of published research from the last five years, while assessing institutional and industry differences in approaches to digital transformation. This overview provides not only a basis for the research itself but also contributes to the formulation of strategies on how AI can be implemented equitably and sustainably. A comprehensive approach that connects the technological, organisational, institutional, and social dimensions will make it possible to identify the key factors that determine whether AI will promote inclusive work transformation or, moreover, reinforce existing inequalities.

This study uses a qualitative approach based on thematic analysis of secondary data. The starting point is a set of academic studies and empirical research published between 2020 and 2025 that focus on the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on the labour market, the transformation of job roles, skills requirements, and changes in Human Resource (HR) management. Web of Science was used as the main scientific database, which provides access to peer-reviewed and high-quality scientific resources.

We searched the Web of Science (WoS) database for scientific papers focusing on AI, Artificial intelligence, Machine Learning, Natural Language Processing, HR, Human Resources, Labour/Labor Market, Digital Transformation and Economic issues. Although there are other databases, out priority was to filter out only those papers with the highest impact in the area under study (therefore articles published on conferences or by the publisher MDPI were purposely excluded from the results – low reputation (Beall list). In this way, we gradually entered requests for all of the above keyword combinations. Analysis of scientific papers with PRISMA standard

Publications were further analyzed based on relevance, subject focus, and type of study. After a further round of selection, the sample was reduced to about only 100 articles, and 44 of these were identified as the most relevant for detailed analysis.

The initial search strategy yielded more than 3,000 publications related broadly to artificial intelligence (AI). However, a substantial share of these studies addressed AI from a purely technical, computational, or engineering perspective without explicit relevance to labour market outcomes, employment structures, or human resource management. Given the interdisciplinary nature of AI research, an additional thematic delimitation step was therefore required to systematically identify studies situated at the intersection of AI and labour market analysis.

To achieve this, we employed VOSviewer (Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#Fig3)), a bibliometric visualisation tool, to conduct a co-occurrence analysis of keywords based on titles, abstracts, and author keywords. This approach allowed us to map the conceptual structure of the AI-related literature and to distinguish clusters focusing on labour market, employment, skills, human resources, and organisational change from those centred on algorithmic development or technical optimisation.

Analysis of scientific papers with VOSviewer

The co-occurrence network was constructed using VOSviewer based on keyword extraction from titles, abstracts, and author keywords. A minimum occurrence threshold of five was applied to reduce noise in the network. The full counting method was used for co-occurrence calculation, and association strength normalization was applied for link weighting. The clustering structure was generated using the default VOSviewer modularity-based clustering algorithm.

Specifically, keywords such as _labour market_, _employment_, _jobs_, _skills_, _human resources_, _wages_, and _workplace_ were used as focal points in the co-occurrence network. Publications located within or closely connected to these thematic clusters were retained for further screening, while studies positioned exclusively within technical AI clusters were excluded. This bibliometric filtering step substantially reduced the dataset to a thematically coherent subset of publications with direct relevance to the research problem.

Following this visual and thematic delimitation, the remaining publications were subjected to manual screening based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria and assessed using a modified PRISMA 2020 framework. This two-step process—combining bibliometric mapping with qualitative screening—ensured that the final sample captured the most relevant scholarly contributions addressing the impact of AI on labour market dynamics rather than AI development in general.

As we can see, at first glance it may seem that the issue of AI’s impact on the labour market has been extensively studied and analysed. However, this is not the case; in fact, there are very few scholarly research papers that have addressed this issue. This research aims to understand the recent impact of AI (analysed through analysis using WoS and PRISMA 2020 standard) on different aspects of the implementation of AI in the labour market and identify the primary challenges that limit its broader adoption.

The implementation of AI in HR management represents one of the strongest positive significant transformations of the current labour market. Despite the obvious benefits of AI, such as decision support, turnover prediction, or optimization of HR processes, its implementation raises serious questions about employment equity, disproportional distribution of benefits, gender and skill inequalities, and different approaches to employee retraining and participation. An important factor influencing the impact of AI is the institutional environment and the ability of organisations to involve employees in co-creating technological change.

Despite the abundance of scholarly literature and scientific papers, both in journals and at conferences, on the economic and technological aspects of AI, a comprehensive overview of how AI adoption affects job seekers, workers themselves, and interpersonal employment relationships, as well as skill dynamics across sectors, is lacking. Most existing studies rely on the rationale of technological progress, while overlooking the social, participatory, and institutional dimensions of AI implementation. This study responds to this gap by examining how AI adoption works from an interdisciplinary perspective, with an emphasis on technological, organizational, and human aspects.

### 2.1 Research problem

_How does the implementation of AI influence job structures_,_skill requirements_,_and equity in employment across sectors and organisations with different levels of technological maturity and institutional capacity?_

The proposed research aims to explore how the impacts of implementing AI in HR vary between sectors and different types of organisations, with a focus on changes in employment, skills requirements and perceptions of fairness. The research will be based on a holistic approach that includes technological, organisational, institutional, and social aspects of AI implementation. This framework will identify the key factors that determine whether AI contributes to an inclusive transformation of the working environment or, on the other hand, leads to an increase in existing inequalities.

Based on the research problem, we set the research questions. Each of the proposed research questions addresses a critical aspect of how artificial intelligence (AI) transforms the labour market. Together, they provide a comprehensive lens for analysing the structural, organisational, and human-level implications of AI adoption.

RQ1: How are skill requirements evolving as a result of AI adoption in different sectors?

This question aims to identify the specific changes in the demand for skills driven by AI, such as the increasing importance of technical, data-analytical, and soft skills, and the obsolescence of certain routine competencies. Understanding these dynamics is essential for designing responsive training programmes, shaping educational curricula, and supporting workforce adaptability.

### Contribution RQ1

Offers insights for policymakers and educational institutions to anticipate future skill needs and align learning pathways accordingly.

RQ2: To what extent does AI contribute to employment polarisation between high- and low-skilled workers?

This question explores whether AI accelerates the divergence in employment opportunities and earnings between highly skilled and low-skilled workers. It addresses the concern that AI may disproportionately benefit those already in advantaged labour market positions, thereby reinforcing existing inequalities.

### Contribution RQ2

Provides empirical evidence to inform equity-oriented labour market policies and contributes to the theoretical discourse on skill-biased technological change.

RQ3: How does the institutional environment affect the implementation and outcomes of AI in the workplace?

This question investigates the role of institutions—such as trade unions, legal frameworks, and participatory decision-making structures—in mediating the effects of AI. The institutional context can either amplify or mitigate the risks of job displacement, inequality, and algorithmic control.

### Contribution RQ3

Highlights the importance of social governance and participatory practices, offering guidance for inclusive digital transformation strategies.

RQ4: What strategies are companies using to address skill gaps and facilitate reskilling in the context of AI?

This question examines how organisations respond to AI-induced skill shortages—whether through investment in employee training, hiring strategies, or partnerships with educational providers. It sheds light on organisational readiness and capacity to adapt to technological change.

### Contribution RQ4

Informs human resource development practices and fosters understanding of effective approaches to reskilling and workforce sustainability.

RQ5: To what extent does AI implementation result in job displacement versus the creation of new roles?

This question assesses the balance between automation-driven job loss and the emergence of new positions requiring novel competencies. It aims to clarify the extent to which AI disrupts employment or facilitates occupational transformation and innovation.

### Contribution RQ5

Supports a more nuanced view of “technological unemployment” and provides data for forecasting future employment trends in the context of digital transformation.

### 2.2 Analytical propositions guiding the thematic synthesis

Based on the research problem and research questions, this study formulates a set of analytical propositions that serve as organising devices for the thematic synthesis of the reviewed literature. These propositions are not hypotheses in the confirmatory sense, nor are they empirically tested within this study. Instead, they provide a structured lens through which convergence, divergence, and contextual variation across existing studies can be systematically examined. This approach is consistent with qualitative and integrative literature review methodologies, where propositions are used to guide interpretation rather than to validate causal claims.

*   _Rationale_: Employee participation and voice have long been recognised as central mechanisms shaping employee perceptions during periods of organisational and technological change trust (Doellgast, [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR17 "Doellgast, V. Recent contributions in the context of AI adoption highlight participation as a potential moderator of employee responses, including perceived job insecurity and acceptance of algorithmic management (Gómez Gandía et al., [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR20 "Gómez Gandía, J. ## 3 Literature review

In the literature review, we describe various approaches that are currently implemented as AI elements in the labour market. Artificial intelligence (AI) is a broad field that encompasses different computational approaches designed to perform tasks requiring human-like intelligence, such as learning, reasoning, or decision-making. Within AI, machine learning (ML) has become the most influential subfield, as it allows algorithms to improve their performance through exposure to data rather than explicit programming. Building on ML, a number of specialised application areas have emerged that are particularly relevant to the labour market and human resource management, such as Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Recommender Systems (RS). These methods can be very effective as an initial filter when submitting applications / CVs of applicants to larger companies, or for quickly determining the correctness of code for programmers.

### 3.1 Machine learning

For example, a study in China applied deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to predict mineralization potential in gold deposits, illustrating how ML can manage complex, high-dimensional datasets and make accurate predictions in uncertain environments. The dataset included 43 features per spatial unit, comprising 39 geochemical elements (such as Ag, Au, Pb, Zn) and 4 geological features (faults and stratigraphic layers), with data density of 4 samples/km². The data were split into training and testing areas at an 8:2 ratio to evaluate model performance. The DRL agent treated each data point as a state and interacted with the environment to predict high or low mineralization potential. The model used ε-greedy policy and replay memory, with neural networks having three hidden layers (256, 64, 16 units). During training, the agent gradually learned to distinguish between known deposits and unlabeled areas. In the testing area, approximately 48.94% of the mineral potential areas identified by DRL with optimal parameters (_n_ = 0.8, _p_ = 0.2) contained around 80% of known gold deposits, while about 60% of these predicted areas covered 100% of known deposits, demonstrating strong predictive power. This example highlights that ML models, when properly designed, can leverage both labeled and unlabeled data to predict complex outcomes, even in dynamic or poorly understood systems. Similarly, in the labour market, predictive models trained on employee datasets (e.g., demographics, performance metrics, tenure) can forecast turnover probabilities, optimise staffing plans, and identify employees at risk of leaving, thereby improving workforce stability. The success metrics in these studies—such as the proportion of correctly identified deposits—are analogous to measures like prediction accuracy, recall, or precision in HR analytics, showing the tangible impact of AI-driven predictions. (Shi et al., [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR38 "Shi, Z., Zuo, R., & Zhou, B. (2023). Deep Reinforcement Learning for Mineral Prospectivity Mapping. Mathematical Geosciences, 55(6), 773–797. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s11004-023-10059-9
                  
                ")). ML thus provides the methodological foundation on which more specialised applications, such as NLP or RS, can be built. Machine learning thus provides the foundation for specialised applications such as NLP or recommender systems. In health data, models like random forests, SVMs, and neural networks are evaluated using metrics such as AUC, F₁-score, and recall. High AUC values (closer to 1.0) indicate strong predictive ability, while 0.5 corresponds to random performance. These metrics allow ML to handle high-dimensional datasets like EHRs or genomic data and quantify predictive performance objectively. (Cho et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR13 "Cho, H., She, J., De Marchi, D., El-Zaatari, H., Barnes, E. L., Kahkoska, A. R., Kosorok, M. R., & Virkud, A. V. (2024). Machine Learning and Health Science Research: Tutorial. Journal of Medical Internet Research, 26, e50890. 
                  https://doi.org/10.2196/50890
                  
                ")).

### 3.2 Natural Language Processing

Natural Language Processing (NLP) applies ML algorithms to textual and spoken data to understand, classify, or generate human language. Key HR applications include CV screening, employee feedback analysis, and sentiment monitoring. Modern NLP relies on pre-trained deep learning models, especially BERT and GPT variants, which achieve over 90% accuracy on benchmark tasks like sentiment analysis (IMDB: 50,000 reviews) and question answering (SQuAD-1.1: 100,000 questions; SQuAD-2.0: 150,000 questions including unanswerable ones). These models use large unlabeled corpora for pre-training and fine-tuning on target datasets, exploiting architectures such as transformers with self-attention, which outperform classical ML methods and RNNs. For instance, GPT-2 (1.5B parameters) and GPT-3 (175B parameters) generate human-like text and enable zero- and few-shot learning. Despite their high performance, challenges remain in computational cost, interpretability, and reproducibility, as only 26% of recent papers report multiple fine-tuning runs, and 80% lack complete model selection procedures (Lauriola et al., [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR28 "Lauriola, I., Lavelli, A., & Aiolli, F. (2022). An introduction to Deep Learning in Natural Language Processing: Models, techniques, and tools. Neurocomputing, 470, 443–456. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2021.05.103
                  
                ")). Beyond traditional NLP tasks, these techniques have also been successfully applied to predictive optimization problems, where a study evaluated four vectorization and seven regression techniques to forecast application performance. Using NLP to analyze the input code, the framework predicts the optimal optimization sequence with a minimum performance drop of 0.5% and an average drop of 18% compared to the actual best sequence, demonstrating the ability of NLP-driven methods to identify highly accurate, task-specific solutions and highlighting their practical relevance for HR and other domain-specific applications (Ahmed et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR1 "Ahmed, H., Fahim Ul Haque, M., Raza Khan, H., Nadeem, G., Arshad, K., Assaleh, K., & Cesar Santos, P. (2024). Selecting the Best Compiler Optimization by Adopting Natural Language Processing. Ieee Access : Practical Innovations, Open Solutions, 12, 121700–121711. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2024.3451516
                  
                ")).

### 3.3 Recommender Systems

Recommender Systems (RS) represent another major application area that builds directly on ML techniques. Unlike NLP, which focuses on language, RS use data on user preferences and behaviour to generate personalised recommendations. In the HR context, this includes suggesting suitable candidates for a vacancy, recommending training opportunities, or mapping career development paths. Experimental studies on movie recommendation datasets, such as MovieLens 100k and IMDB, demonstrate that combining PCA feature extraction, K-means clustering, and collaborative filtering yields highly accurate recommendations. For instance, clustering movies into six groups based on genre and incorporating user demographic attributes enabled the system to predict relevant items efficiently, achieving strong precision, recall, and F-measure scores while reducing runtime. These results highlight how RS can leverage ML techniques to generate targeted, high-quality recommendations, showing potential for analogous applications in HR decision-making (Yassine et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR46 "Yassine, A., Mohamed, L., & Al Achhab, M. (2021). Intelligent recommender system based on unsupervised machine learning and demographic attributes. Simulation Modelling Practice and Theory, 107, 102198. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.simpat.2020.102198
                  
                ")). Modern RS combine collaborative filtering with content-based and hybrid approaches, often supported by deep learning. Although RS are technically an application of ML rather than a distinct conceptual field, they illustrate how AI can be operationalised in human resource management to improve decision-making and employee development.

### 3.4 AI in relation to the labour market

This section synthesises the reviewed studies thematically to highlight shared patterns and divergences in the literature, rather than presenting isolated study-by-study summaries. The findings are grouped into interconnected sub-themes reflecting key labour market dynamics associated with AI adoption. Empirical research using quantitative surveys with 420 responses (210 from business leaders, 210 from employees) shows statistically significant differences in the perception of automation across four areas: Business Processes, Technology and Tools, Skills and Professional Development, and Motivation and Engagement. For example, regarding workflow simplification (A1), business leaders rated it positively with a mean of 4.19 (SD = 0.394), while employees rated it 4.03 (SD = 0.167, t(210) = 5487, _p_< 0.05, d = 0.54). Similarly, in Technology and Tools, business leaders saw higher benefits in tools efficiency (B1, M = 3.66, SD = 0.476) compared to employees (M = 3.20, SD = 0.401, t(210) = 10.647, _p_< 0.05, d = 1.04). Differences were also notable in Skills and Professional Development, with work-life balance (C3) rated much lower by employees (M = 2.26, SD = 0.441) than by business leaders (M = 2.99, SD = 0.138, t(210) = 22.861, _p_< 0.05, d = 2.23). Across Motivation and Engagement, large differences were observed in creativity (D1, d = 0.93), career planning (D2, d = 0.82), and skill obsolescence (D5, d = 0.8). These results illustrate that while management emphasises efficiency and operational gains, employees are more concerned about job security, skill requirements, and personal development. Such divergent perspectives underline that AI adoption is not solely a technical process but also a socio-organisational one. Sustainable implementation, therefore requires participatory approaches, transparent communication, and targeted investment in competence development to align organisational objectives with employee needs and support long-term workforce sustainability (Gómez Gandía et al., [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR20 "Gómez Gandía, J. This is an open-access review article published in the journal "Management & Marketing" (Volume 21, article number 2, 2026) titled "The impact of AI on the labour market," authored by Michaela Doubková and Martin Magdin, published April 17, 2026. The article has 10k accesses and 2 citations.

**Research Overview:**
The study explores how AI impacts the labour market, focusing on changes in job roles, skill requirements, and human resource (HR) practices. Unlike previous surveys that focused primarily on technological aspects, this research systematically integrates technological, organisational, and institutional perspectives. Key findings from a literature review (2020–2025) show that AI adoption is associated with rising demand for technical and interdisciplinary skills, restructuring of work roles, and widening wage gaps between AI-skilled and non-AI-skilled workers. Importantly, many jobs are not eliminated but transformed, as AI frequently functions in augmentation rather than pure substitution mode.

**Methodology:**
- Qualitative approach using thematic analysis of secondary data from Web of Science (2020-2025)
- Initial search yielded more than 3,000 records; filtered to approximately 100 articles, with 44 identified as most relevant
- Used modified PRISMA 2020 standard and VOSviewer bibliometric analysis for thematic filtering
- Excluded conference papers and MDPI publications due to perceived low reputation

**Research Questions:**
Five research questions address: (1) evolving skill requirements, (2) employment polarisation between high- and low-skilled workers, (3) institutional environment effects, (4) company reskilling strategies, and (5) job displacement versus job creation.

**Key Examples and Findings:**
- Deutsche Telekom deployed ~400 RPA bots with ALMATO (starting 2015), automating 40+ processes across 30 applications by 2016 (handling ~320,000 transactions/month); expanded to 1,500+ "Frontend Assistants" by 2018 supporting 4 million monthly transactions
- Damioli et al. (2025) study of 23,915 patent applicants (2000-2016) found AI innovators grew 338%, AI patent families increased 276%, non-AI patents rose 15%, and AI-to-non-AI patent ratio surged 227% between 2000-2005 and 2011-2016
- Service industries accounted for 39% of AI patents vs. only 15% of non-AI patents
- Lazzari et al. (2022) study on employee attrition prediction used machine learning on 9,296 employees from 30 countries, finding LightGBM and logistic regression achieved predictive performance more than twice the baseline (0.225), with key factors including Sustainable Employability, Employership, Attendance Stability, Motivation, and Vitality

**AI Technical Applications Discussed:**
- Machine Learning (ML): including deep reinforcement learning, predictive modeling for HR analytics
- Natural Language Processing (NLP): CV screening, employee feedback analysis, sentiment monitoring; BERT and GPT variants achieve over 90% accuracy on benchmark tasks
- Recommender Systems (RS): candidate matching, training recommendations, career development mapping

**Perception Gap Findings:**
A survey of 420 respondents (210 business leaders, 210 employees) found statistically significant differences in automation perceptions across Business Processes, Technology and Tools, Skills and Professional Development, and Motivation and Engagement—with employees showing much lower ratings on work-life balance (M=2.26 vs. 2.99) and expressing more concern about job security and skill obsolescence.

**Conclusion:**
The future of work in the AI era will be determined less by technology itself than by how organisations, institutions, and policies govern its implementation. Sustainable AI implementation requires participatory approaches, transparent communication, and targeted investment in competence development.

## Abstract

The impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on employment has attracted widespread attention, but the literature has generally viewed AI as a continuation of automation, arguing that technology will result in wage polarization. However, existing literature overlooks the unique aspects of AI technology. This study proposes new theoretical mechanisms and AI measure method to estimate the impacts of AI on wage dynamics and inequality. Based on an empirical study of data from listed companies in China from 2014 to 2022, we find that AI applications raise wages through three mechanisms: productivity improvement, crowding out low-wage routine jobs, and creating high-wage creative and social jobs. While executive pay does not increase because of AI applications, the pay for regular employees increases through job restructuring. Ultimately, AI applications narrow wage inequality between executives and regular employees. This study provides a new quantitative evaluation method for assessing AI progress. It also reveals the unique mechanisms of AI on firms' wage distribution, which differs from that of traditional technologies. These findings deepen our understanding of the complex relationship between AI development and wage changes.

## Introduction

The effects of artificial intelligence (AI) on employment have attracted considerable attention. The new generation of AI technology relies on deep learning algorithms and big data to accomplish specific tasks rather than traditional rule-setting and logical reasoning. Considering that AI can handle many unconventional tasks and extend or replace human brain functions, the issue of “machine for human” has once again aroused widespread concern. Numerous studies predict that AI will have a major impact on the labor market (Acemoglu et al., 2022). Although AI is essentially an automation technology, the new generation of AI technology based on big data and deep learning is significantly different from traditional automation technology. Therefore, the impact of AI technology on the labor market is also markedly different. Traditional automation technologies, such as industrial robots, primarily replace manual labor, whereas the new generation of AI technology replaces both manual and mental labor (Raj & Seamans, 2019). Currently, AI has replaced some jobs in the service industry (Huang & Rust, 2018), such as bank tellers and corporate customer service representatives. With improvements in machine learning algorithms, AI is beginning to perform tasks that require human-specific abilities, such as intuition and emotion, which could have a disruptive impact on future employment (Gruetzemacher et al., 2020). However, relevant empirical research is still lacking because of the difficulty in measuring the level of AI application (Raj & Seamans, 2019). In particular, the differences in how AI and traditional automation technologies affect wage inequality require further study.

The impact of AI on wages is a complex topic that depends on different economies and occupational fields (Cramarenco et al., 2023). According to the International Monetary Fund, AI could affect the wages of approximately 40% of jobs globally, rising to 60% in developed economies and about 26% in low-income countries. AI applications can perform critical tasks required for many jobs, placing workers at a bargaining disadvantage, or causing job loss. The European Central Bank has noted that, at least for now, AI is more likely to affect wages than employment, and that rapid advances in AI could exacerbate income and wealth inequality. Workers with skills that enable them to use AI may see their productivity and wages increase, whereas those who do not may see their wages decrease. The introduction of AI will increase labor productivity; however, smart investments will weaken labor employment and further reduce labor demand and wages. Therefore, the effect of AI on wages and distribution may be of greater concern than its effect on employment.

Although many studies predict that AI technologies will significantly impact the labor market, relevant empirical evidence is lacking (Raj & Seamans, 2019). Existing literature generally views AI as a continuation of automation policies (Autor, 2015). AI applications increase the demand for high-skilled labor and substitute for low-skilled labor, leading to a gap in wage and employment opportunities, resulting in wage polarization (Babina et al., 2024; Cramarenco et al., 2023; Fossen et al., 2022; Jia et al., 2024; Pereira et al., 2023). However, existing research faces two challenges. The first challenge is to accurately measure the progress of AI technology. Existing literature often uses robotics or AI job recruitment data as proxy variables for AI technology applications. However, industrial robotics is only one application area of AI. Moreover, in addition to recruiting AI-related positions, companies may introduce AI technology through service outsourcing, purchasing equipment (software), and other means. Therefore, the existing proxies cannot accurately reflect the progress of AI applications in companies. Second, the existing research has generally concluded that AI will increase the need for high-skilled jobs and reduce the number of low-skilled jobs, which in turn will result in wage polarization. However, in the context of AI, the high- and low-skill labor division needs to be redefined. Some perceived high-skill positions, such as programming and writing, can now be performed using AI systems such as ChatGPT. Conversely, some low-skill positions, such as nursing, cannot be easily replaced by AI. Therefore, it may not be reasonable to examine AI-induced wage polarization from traditional high- and low-skill dimensions.

This study uses new theories and empirical data to explore the unique impact of AI on wages and the wage gap. First, this study highlights differences between AI and human labor across dimensions of routine, creativity, and sociality, and then proposes a theoretical hypothesis on how AI influences wage levels and gaps. Unlike traditional perspectives based on skill levels, this new theory captures unique mechanisms of AI on the labor market. Second, in the empirical study, we employ a text mining method to construct a new firm-level AI index. This method fully utilizes the unstructured text information disclosed by listed companies, offering a novel approach for accurately measuring firm's AI application.

The empirical analysis in this paper uses data from listed companies in China. As one of the countries with the most widespread AI application, China provides valuable insights for understanding AI's impact on the labor market with important global implications. Our findings indicate that AI applications have increased overall wages, while narrowing the wage gap between executives and regular employees. This shift is primarily due to AI displacing routine jobs, such as those in production, administration and finance, and creating more creative and social jobs, such as researching and selling. In other words, a change in employment structure is a key driver of wage growth and the reduction of wage inequality. These findings demonstrate that the impact of AI on the wage distribution differs significantly from that of traditional automation and other technologies. Our research clarifies the complex relationship between technological development and wage distribution and provides new insights into how technological progress affects the economy.

This is a research article published in the International Review of Economics & Finance (Volume 96, Part C, November 2024, Article 103739) by Elsevier, authored by Yongqiu Wu, Zhiwei Lin, Qingcui Zhang, and Wei Wang (corresponding author), all affiliated with Chongqing University, China. The study is titled "Artificial intelligence, wage dynamics, and inequality: Empirical evidence from Chinese listed firms" (DOI: 10.1016/j.iref.2024.103739).

PURPOSE: The study examines the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on wage dynamics and inequality in Chinese listed companies, challenging the traditional view that AI simply continues automation and leads to wage polarization. The authors argue that existing literature overlooks the unique aspects of AI technology compared to traditional automation, and that the high/low-skill division needs redefinition in the AI context (e.g., some high-skill jobs like programming can now be done by AI, while some low-skill jobs like nursing cannot).

METHODOLOGY: 
- Sample: Chinese listed companies from 2014 to 2022
- Data sources: Wind database for financial data and annual reports; China Research data for employee information
- Novel approach: Text mining method to construct a firm-level AI index using unstructured text information disclosed by listed companies (addressing the measurement challenge since existing proxies like robotics or AI job recruitment data are inadequate)
- Empirical method: Two-way fixed effects (FEs) model
- The study highlights differences between AI and human labor across dimensions of routine, creativity, and sociality

KEY FINDINGS:
1. AI applications raise wages through three mechanisms: (a) productivity improvement, (b) crowding out low-wage routine jobs, and (c) creating high-wage creative and social jobs
2. Executive pay does not increase due to AI applications, but pay for regular employees increases through job restructuring
3. AI applications NARROW wage inequality between executives and regular employees
4. AI displaces routine jobs (production, administration, finance) and creates creative and social jobs (researching, selling)
5. Employment structure change is a key driver of wage growth and reduction of wage inequality
6. Baseline regression: AI applications coefficient is 0.030, significant at the 1% level

CONTEXT: The IMF notes AI could affect wages of approximately 40% of jobs globally (60% in developed economies, ~26% in low-income countries). The European Central Bank has noted AI is more likely to affect wages than employment and could exacerbate inequality.

CONCLUSION: The impact of AI on wage distribution differs significantly from traditional automation technologies. The study provides a new quantitative evaluation method for assessing AI progress and deepens understanding of the relationship between AI development and wage changes.

FUNDING: Supported by the National Social Science Fund of China (23AGL034). The authors declare no conflicts of interest. The article has been cited by 19 works and has 17 citation indexes, 56 Mendeley readers, and 1 news mention.

Ultimately, AI applications narrow wage inequality between executives and regular employees."

# **The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Employment and Wage Inequality**

## Authors

* Syed Muhammad Haris Shah   Department of Economics Aitchison College, A levels Mall Road lahore Pakistan

## DOI:

 <https://doi.org/10.63075/n955m318>

## Abstract

**Introduction:** Artificial Intelligence (AI) is playing an increasingly prominent role in technological progress, impacting not only the structure of jobs but also wages and the labor market across the globe. Despite its promise for increased productivity, efficiency, and innovation, there are concerns about the implications of AI on job security and income inequality. The purpose of this study was to assess the employment implications and wage gaps across various industries and skill sets following the adoption of AI. It also explored how AI use relates to job insecurity, salary increases, and upskilling. While AI is increasingly being incorporated into business operations, there is a lack of evidence on the concurrent effects of AI on employment and wage inequality, especially across occupational groups. **Methods:** The cross-sectional survey was carried out with 350 respondents across a number of industries, such as Information Technology, Manufacturing, Healthcare, Finance, Education, and Customer Service. Data were gathered from the structured questionnaire and analyzed using descriptive statistics, Chi-square testing, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), and multiple linear regression techniques. **Results:** The findings showed that 72.6% of the respondents stated that their companies were currently using AI. Almost half of those who answered (48.9%) believed that AI would create new job prospects, while 24.6% were worried about job loss. There were substantial differences between skill categories in terms of wage growth (high-skilled workers had higher wage growth than low-skilled workers, p < 0.001, 8.7% vs. 2.8%). There was a statistically significant relationship between the adoption of AI and concerns about job displacement (χ² = 12.84, p = 0.002). In addition, there were significant correlations between wage growth and the adoption level of AI (β = 0.38, p < 0.001) and worker skill level (β = 0.42, p < 0.001), as well as participation in AI-related training programs (β = 0.21, p = 0.008). **Conclusion:** The results indicate that AI is significantly shaping today's job market, generating new job opportunities and also playing a significant role in the emergence of skill-based wage gaps. While the economic value of AI integration seems to be larger for more skilled workers, AI workforce training and reskilling programs could be key to mitigating negative labor market effects on vulnerable populations. The results underscore the importance of employment policies and capacity development initiatives based on evidence to drive inclusive and sustainable labor market development in the era of growing AI adoption.

[AI, tech, & the economy](https://equitablegrowth.org/issue/ai-tech-economy/)[Labor](https://equitablegrowth.org/issue/labor/)

#### AUTHORS:

### Key takeaways:

* The impacts of AI are difficult to measure. Work, workers, and the labor market are not a monolith, and AI is developing rapidly, which may change its impact over time.
* Across the research, the range of current estimates imply that the overall impact of AI on the labor market will come from the balance of potential benefits and harms felt across tasks, skills, occupations, people, places, and time.
* Research findings on AI and the labor market offer valuable information about AI within specific contexts. Equitable Growth’s new database of AI research allows for an easier synthesis of relevant literature and makes reading and understanding AI research more accessible. Those using our database can sort by several topics and subtopics.
* **What this means for growth:** Technological change through AI could have substantial economic impacts, but without deliberate policy interventions, workers might not share in those gains.

Artificial intelligence will have a largely unpredictable but potentially profound effect on the labor market. Individuals have speculated how AI will affect the workforce since its earliest developments. But public attention has skyrocketed since late 2022, when the proliferation of chatbots made forms of AI highly accessible to workers and firms. As AI capabilities are further advanced by developers and increasingly adopted by firms and growing segments of the public, speculation on AI’s ultimate impact on work, workers, and the labor market abound.

Headlines often paint extreme and dissonant pictures of AI’s future impact. In 2023, [a report by Goldman Sachs](https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/articles/generative-ai-could-raise-global-gdp-by-7-percent.html) predicted that AI would have widespread business applications that would complement jobs and industries, leading to 7 percent growth in Gross Domestic Product over a 10-year period. Dario Amodei, CEO of the AI company Anthropic, [suggested in October 2024](https://darioamodei.com/essay/machines-of-loving-grace#3-economic-development-and-poverty) that AI may generate significant economic growth in developing nations but later warned of “unusually painful” market disruptions in [January 2026](https://www.darioamodei.com/essay/the-adolescence-of-technology#4-player-piano).

[Navigating the research on the impacts of AI on work, workers, and the labor market](https://equitablegrowth.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Navigating-the-research-on-the-impacts-of-AI-on-work-workers-and-the-labor-market.pdf)[Download](https://equitablegrowth.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Navigating-the-research-on-the-impacts-of-AI-on-work-workers-and-the-labor-market.pdf)

Workers themselves echo the conflicting feelings of optimism and dread expressed by industry leaders. In 2025, [a survey on worker sentiment by the Pew Research Center](https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2025/02/25/u-s-workers-are-more-worried-than-hopeful-about-future-ai-use-in-the-workplace/) found that while 52 percent of workers answered “yes” when asked whether they feel worried about AI’s future in the workplace, only 36 percent answered “yes” to feeling hopeful about it.

There is little agreement among experts over how AI will impact the labor market. AI capabilities and applications are still emerging, so it is unsurprising that the research on their effects is also still in process. AI has myriad potential uses and thus there are myriad hypotheses about the potential effects AI may have. Academic researchers have hypothesized several ways the technology may influence the labor market. They largely anticipate changes that will be equally capable of helping the economy as hurting it.

One prevalent concern about AI is that it will perform jobs currently done by humans, causing large amounts of labor displacement. But researchers also anticipate that new AI-centric jobs will be created. Similarly, some researchers hypothesize that workers who lack the expertise needed for a job will be able to use AI to work in occupations previously inaccessible to them. Others worry that AI devalues expertise, lowering the returns to education for workers who have invested years into their training.

Given the myriad and often conflicting potential impacts of AI’s distribution across the labor market, there are many open questions about how this emerging technology will change the nature of work or the economy. Countless questions still need to be studied. How are the impacts of AI concentrated, especially by industry or occupation? Are certain demographics of workers more at risk? Will there be enough work available? Who shares in the productivity gains from AI? How gradually or suddenly will these changes be felt?

Broadly, though, most questions pertaining to AI and the labor market can be broken down into three fundamental questions:

* Which workers are the most vulnerable to the potential negative impacts of AI?
* Who is likely to benefit the most from AI?
* What will be the aggregate effect of AI on work, workers, and the labor market?

This issue brief and the companion database of research papers seek to make reading and understanding AI research easier and more accessible. These resources are meant to help readers understand key terms and frameworks in AI research, discover relevant AI literature,read abbreviated summaries of insightful papers, and feel better-equipped to think critically about this emerging field.

Much like its subject matter, current research examining the influence of AI on work, workers, and the labor market is wide-ranging, uncertain, and conflicting. This is due in part to a wide range of definitions, data sources, frameworks, and motives for the research. Parsing through the literature to determine how to think about AI and the workforce—much less come to any conclusions—can feel daunting. The resources catalogued in this issue brief are not meant to tell readers what to think about AI or AI research but rather how to navigate the evidence.

Readers new to this topic should start here for a broad overview before browsing the database. Let’s begin with some basic definitions.

#### What is AI?

![](https://equitablegrowth.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/ai-lit-review-chapter.jpg)

The term “artificial intelligence” broadly refers to the use of computational systems to learn, reason, perceive, make decisions, and solve problems—functions otherwise associated with human intelligence. “Narrow” or “weak” AI operates solely within its training domain and is the only type of AI currently available. Narrow AI encompasses applications from recommendation engines to autonomous vehicles and from speech to image recognition.

At the time of writing, artificial general intelligence, or AGI, and superintelligence—or technologies that would learn, reason, and perform tasks as well as or better than humans—remain unrealized. When we refer to AI in these resources, we refer to narrow forms of AI.

 Artificial intelligence can be further (and more usefully) classified based on the technology underpinning its function and capabilities. Machine learning is a subfield of AI and allows systems to learn from data without being explicitly programmed with rules. Via machine learning, AI models can recognize patterns, predict outcomes, and can be retrained to improve their accuracy. A deeper subfield is known as deep learning, which analyzes complex patterns in large datasets and powers generative AI and large language models.

Generative AI produces content, often in response to prompts. The generative AI service DALL-E, for example, creates images based on user requests and specifications. Large language models, or LLMs, are generative AI tools that process and generate human language. OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude are examples of text-based generative AI, as is Gemini (from Alphabet Inc.’s Google unit) and Copilot (from Microsoft Corp.). They all utilize large language modeling. The interface for these services is sometimes called a chatbot, but the term chatbot also includes much simpler technologies.

Large language models represent a significant leap in AI systems’ ability to process unstructured language at scale, facilitating natural language interaction between humans and machines. Anyone with an internet-enabled device can use large language models, creating wide access for use in the workplace and at home.

Because large language models are widely available, many headlines, public debates, and academic papers focus on this technology’s effect on the labor market, particularly since the release of ChatGPT in November 2022. But generative AI is far from the only type of artificial intelligence that may change how work is performed.

#### Our approach to navigating the research on AI

![](https://equitablegrowth.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/ai-lit-review-chapter.jpg)

For this study, we limit our scope to research that discusses how a type of AI technology may affect the nature, productivity, or distribution of work.At present, we do not include research into how AI may be used for worker surveillance or how AI might affect competition between firms. For a wider discussion on the potential impacts of AI, please see [Equitable Growth’s AI and Technology resources.](https://equitablegrowth.org/issue/ai-tech-economy/)

This project casts a wide net on the kinds of AI included in the database but stops short of robotics, computer vision, and other physical AI systems. We include research at both the microeconomic and macroeconomic levels. At the micro level, AI may impact specific components of certain occupations for a subset of workers. Additionally (or alternatively), AI might change how firms grow and structure their workforces. But these influences may also be felt at the national or global level if economies contract or expand with fluctuating employment and productivity levels.

### How are experts studying the impact of AI on the labor market?

#### Frameworks for thinking about AI and labor

At the time of writing, one framework for studying AI has emerged as a popular theory: the Task-Biased Technological Change framework, hereafter referred to as the task-based framework. This theory begins with the idea that jobs can be broken down into the tasks people perform in the course of their jobs. Receptionists, for example, might be abstracted into the tasks they perform, such as greeting customers, transcribing, proofreading, and other administrative duties. According to the task-based framework, technology does not replace (or complement) workers themselves, but rather, it impacts the individual tasks they perform. Grammar software may entirely perform proofreading tasks, and voice-to-text software may improve speed and accuracy in transcription, for example, but neither type of AI helps or replaces the task of greeting and interacting with guests.

The task-based framework is popular in AI and labor research. Researchers use the framework to estimate which parts of a job AI could influence or transform, whether that occupation could experience consequential shifts in supply or demand, and how the labor market could change as a result. But there are some drawbacks to this framework. In particular, the task-based framework does not capture the more holistic elements of an occupation. There are likely spillover effects between tasks, for instance, that cannot be accounted for within the task-based framework. Another major disadvantage is that, so far, the task-based framework can only produce estimates. Estimates should be treated with caution; they offer informed projections about what might happen but cannot replace analyses of what is actually happening.

The task-based framework is not the only way to assess how labor is impacted by advances in AI technology. Other methods include (but are not limited to) measurements of how many firms have adopted AI technology, the use of an AI program as a treatment in a controlled experiment, or qualitative discussions with experts and impacted populations.

Academic papers in Equitable Growth’s database can be filtered by types of framework and other characteristics. For a full list and explanation of filters, please see our [AI research database](http://ec2-3-233-85-18.compute-1.amazonaws.com/AI_database/AI_database.html).

#### Data sources for measuring the prevalence of AI in the labor market

Once researchers decide how to conceptually think about AI and labor, they need a way to measure its presence. Researchers can derive information about work, workers, and the labor market from publicly available government data. U.S. Census Bureau data, such as the American Community Survey, quantify workers and their characteristics, while other Census sources, such as the Annual Business Survey, provide insights into firm behaviors.

Below, we discuss other commonly used data sources.

#### The Occupational Information Network, or O\*NET

One dataset from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics is especially popular among studies that utilize a task-based framework is the Occupational Information Network, or O\*NET. This is a public dataset that breaks down approximately 1,000 occupations to the abilities, skills, and actions needed to perform them. Crucially, the dataset links a series of unique tasks to each occupation and provides metrics on how frequently they are performed in the course of work.

These tasks can be aggregated to several levels of work activities, which are shared between occupations. For instance, a bartender’s task to create drink recipes and a bioinformatic scientist’s task to develop data models and databases both fall under the O\*NET work activity “Thinking Creatively.” Researchers often study how AI could be used during an O\*NET task, which allows them to examine how the technology might interact with a particular occupation or activity. (See Figure 1.)

**Figure 1**

O\*NET has become a common dataset to study AI and labor due to its compatibility with the task-based framework, its public availability, and the ease with which it can be linked to other Census Bureau data. But [some researchers](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1900949116) point out that the dataset includes assumptions on how jobs are broken down into their tasks and is not fully updated every year, making it a less-than-ideal option, given AI’s rapid development.

#### Other AI data sources

Researchers also use other creative data sources relevant to the field of labor and AI. Some research studies compile resumes or job opportunities posted by firms to study changes in job posting language. Others track how workers are highlighting AI-based experience in their resumes. Researchers can use these types of information to track when and how AI is described as a desired skill within the labor market, estimate rates of AI adoption by firms, and associate other worker characteristics with the technology.

Alternatively, some researchers construct proprietary datasets, conduct field surveys, or source qualitative input from focus groups and use other methods of data collection. The firms developing AI technologies also are a common source of private data, such as data from [Microsoft’s Copilot](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.07935) and [Anthropic’s Claude](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.04761). Researchers may draw from these data sources when public alternatives do not exist.

Private data sources have limitations. In the case of the two sources above, for example, a major limitation is that the data only capture the use of a specific large language model by voluntary users. In other words, they capture the patterns of a small subset of people using one service for personal and/or professional use and therefore cannot be used to extrapolate larger trends about AI writ large. A study that employs ChatGPT usage data, for example, can show how users might ask ChatGPT accounting-related questions but cannot draw conclusions about how the work of accountants might be impacted by AI more generally.

Furthermore, when private datasets are not publicly available, study findings cannot be externally replicated. Importantly, private data sources typically describe fee-for-service products and thus may be imbued with different motives than public sources, such as U.S. Census Bureau data.

Academia, advocates, and policymakers are calling for the federal government to collect detailed, real-time, impartial data on AI and its economic impacts. At the time of writing, a few congressional bills have been introduced that would require government statistical agencies to begin scoping such data collection, but no concrete action has been taken yet. Until such data are available, students of AI must judiciously engage with the existing literature and limited empirical evidence of AI’s overall impact.

### How are experts estimating the effects of AI on the labor market?

AI has the potential to affect work and workers in different ways, depending on the worker’s occupation, industry, and demographic characteristics. Worker interactions with AI may replace some occupations, augment others, or simply change how jobs are performed.

The potential for AI to automate, augment, or simply interact with a task, job, or industry is typically referred to as AI exposure. The definition of exposure varies and can change depending on a study’s author, data source, or methods. But, in broad terms, AI exposure can be thought of as the potential for AI to interact with a task, worker, occupation, firm, industry, or region.

While many researchers tailor their interpretation of AI exposure to their specific study, a few common measures of exposure are beginning to emerge. Stanford University economist Michael Webb developed an [early example of a popular approach](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3482150). This method can be used to   estimate exposure to tasks for several types of technologies, including AI. Webb constructs this dataset by matching patent language to similar O\*NET tasks and estimating how new technology might overlap with current human tasks. The occupations with the highest number of tasks that relate to AI’s capabilities (as described by its patent language) are predicted to be the most exposed to AI automation. Occupations are then ranked by their exposure percentiles. Webb, for instance, estimates that computer programmers have more AI-automatable tasks than 94 percent of sampled occupations and thus assigns them a score of 94. His paper only considers how exposed tasks might be automated, not augmented.

Economists Edward Felten at Princeton University and Manav Raj and Robert Seamans at NYU Stern School of Business provide [another approach](https://sms.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/smj.3286) to estimating AI exposure, linking a list of AI capabilities to O\*NET data. Where Webb’s exposure measure focuses on tasks, Felten, Raj, and Seamans look at abilities. The authors match AI capabilities to O\*NET abilities and then use this relatedness to estimate AI exposure by occupation. The authors’ AI occupational exposure scores are relative. The exposure score for computer programmers, for example, is 1.272, while the exposure score for manicurists and pedicurists is 0.034. The authors interpret the difference in scores to mean that the human abilities needed to program computers overlap with AI capabilities far more than they do for nail care. Notably, these scores do not assess whether an occupation can be supported or replaced by AI.

Later approaches, such as one by Open AI’s Tyna Eloundou, Sam Manning, and Pamela Mishkin, alongside Daniel Rock at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School, [narrows the scope of estimated exposure to a specific type of AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.10130)—in this case, large language models. The authors consider either an O\*NET task or detailed work activity as “exposed” if the time a human would take to complete it is reduced by 50 percent or more when performed by an large language model or LLM-powered system. They offer a small range of calculated scores per occupation, which represent the lower to upper bound of possible AI exposure. The four authors, for example, estimate at least 90 percent of computer programming tasks can be directly automated or augmented by large language models, giving computer programmers an estimated exposure score of 0.9.

AI company Anthropic’s Kunal Handa and others provide their [own measurements](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.04761) for use of Anthropic’s chatbot, Claude, by linking queries made to Claude with O\*NET tasks. In this case, task exposure is calculated as the proportion of user conversations with Claude that concern a certain task. Because each O\*NET task is unique to an occupation, individual task-exposure scores are grouped by profession and added together, creating an aggregated occupational exposure score. (The authors caveat that the data include questions asked to Claude for personal use.) The authors calculate the exposure score for computer programmers to be 0.061, which estimates that 6.1 percent of all queries made to Claude can be associated with tasks performed by computer programmers. Estimates include both automation and augmentation in the aggregated occupational exposure score.

The list of exposure measurement methods in Table 2 below illustrates the variety of methods used to define and estimate AI’s impact on different occupations. Existing exposure measures are estimates, rather than empirical evidence of where and how AI is changing work. Morgan Frank at the University of Pittsburgh and Yong-Yuel Ahn and Esteban Moro at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, for example, find that [no single exposure estimate is fully accurate](https://academic.oup.com/pnasnexus/article/4/4/pgaf107/8104152), at least when it comes to predicting AI job losses. They conclude that while existing AI exposure scores still have limited predictive power individually, they may each identify a separate pathway through which AI could impact the labor market and that the predictive power of these metrics may come from their combined use.

Researchers are increasingly combining approaches to estimating AI exposure. Anthropic’s latest effort to measure [“observed exposure,”](https://www.anthropic.com/research/labor-market-impacts) for example, leverages their own usage data with those estimated by Eloundou and her co-authors. The strengths and weaknesses of any exposure estimate, including data sources, should be considered when evaluating how and where to apply a study’s insights. (See Table 2.)

#### What are some common themes across the literature on AI and work, workers, and the labor market?

![](https://equitablegrowth.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/ai-lit-review-chapter.jpg)

As mentioned earlier (and regularly in media headlines), predictions about AI’s effect on the labor market range in both their level of certainty and the types of changes that could occur. At least for now, research mostly finds that AI’s effect on the labor market is much more complicated than what both the [“doomsayers” and the “optimists”](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1900949116?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=21506599862&gbraid=0AAAAAqiPmCwf6Ls11ZOxoc8nmk314ZlnC&gclid=Cj0KCQjwmunNBhDbARIsAOndKpmCCVNI9YuHWQT2nxXexZBzczlEISiqSYnLmqt0NdEwSV7wn-S-cdUaAnOdEALw_wcB) assert. In fact, few scientific papers make predictions about how, or even if, AI will change labor.

### The impacts of AI are difficult to measure

There are many reasons why definitive, scientifically backed statements about the impact of AI on the labor market are so far largely unavailable. First and most obviously, AI is a new technology. While researchers have been theorizing about how AI may change the labor market, the long-term effects of technology shocks are typically felt over the course of several decades.

Furthermore, AI is evolving quickly, and the research process can take significant time. OpenAI’s release of ChatGPT in November 2022 was a significant step forward in AI commercial accessibility and use. Studies published as recently as 2023 may lack data on how the proliferation of large language models such as ChatGPT might be impacting work and workers.

Even studies that include generative AI have to navigate difficult macroeconomic distortions. Because all studies of generative AI have taken place after 2022, it is incredibly challenging to isolate its effects from contemporary phenomena. The rise of remote work, increased outsourcing and contracting, high interest rates, and other labor market disruptions have likely impacted labor at the same time as generative AI, making it difficult to separate the effects of one from the other.

A second complication is that AI might not just reshape or displace jobs but also is likely create them. A pillar of general purpose technologies, which many consider AI to be, is that they spur innovation, giving rise to new occupations that complement their new capacities. Just one case in point: Individuals studying how electricity affected the labor market shortly after its invention were not able to fully predict the rise of the energy sector and could only quantify the obsolescence of the lamp lighter. It is impossible to design forward-looking studies that wholly and accurately predict how future sectors and occupations might change work.

### Work, workers, and the labor market are not a monolith

The effects of AI on work, workers, and the labor market are not likely to be uniform. Employment outcomes are heterogeneous by gender, race, age, and education—and so too may be the effects of AI. Inequalities already present in the economy could be exacerbated or mitigated, depending on where, when, and how AI disrupts or restructures the workforce.

### AI is developing rapidly, which may change its impact

The complications inherent to measuring the current impact of AI on the labor market (much less predicting its future effects) may be one source of conflicting narratives and may be why, even in empirical research, findings are not consistent.

Take, for example, [the findings](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4475923) of Tania Babina at the University of Maryland (formerly at Columbia Business School) and her co-authors. Their working paper finds that nontech firms that invest in AI technology hire more junior workers while reducing middle-management and senior roles. The authors credit such flattening of workforce hierarchies to the predictive qualities of AI, which empower junior workers to make more decisions and decrease their need for supervision.

In contrast, José Azar, Mireia Gine, and Javier Sanz-Espín at the University of Navarra [find](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5842084) that for the firms they studied, as firm exposure to generative AI rose, the share of junior positions shrank, and mid-level positions increased by a comparable amount. The authors theorize that as AI replaces the tasks that junior workers traditionally perform, less-experienced employees are pushed up the organizational ladder. Consequently, the supply for mid-level positions swells with less-credentialed workers, and wages for mid-level roles decrease.

Similarly, in 2025, Harvard University’s Seyed Mahdi Hosseini Maasoum and Guy Lichtinger [find similar reductions](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5425555) in junior employment, relative to their senior counterparts, in firms that adopted generative AI. They theorize, however, that the restructuring was not the result of automated junior roles, but rather the anticipatory slowed hiring of firms that expected such work to be performed by generative AI in the near future.

Such inconsistent findings underscore the influence that timing and data have on this emerging field of research. Babina and her co-authors note, for example, that their data covers 2010–2018 and thus only examines firms’ use of AI before the popularization of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT. Conversely, Azar, Gine, and Sanz-Espín and Hosseini and Lichtinger specifically examine firms’ structures following ChatGPT’s release and exclusively examine firms’ adoption of generative AI. These conflicting results demonstrate the rapid pace at which AI technology develops. Its adoption and impact on the labor market could be equally as dynamic.

Another explanation for incongruous findings is how each study defines AI investments, use, and exposure. While Babina and her co-authors track firm-level AI investments by the composition of employees’ AI-related skills, Azar, Gine, and Sanz-Espín use the data provided by Open AI’s Eloundou and co-authors to create an occupational exposure index that describes the feasibility of substituting the generative AI large language model GPT-4 for specific work activities. These exposure metrics are not wholly comparable and may contribute to the diverging results. Hosseini and Lichtinger also draw on Eloundou and co-authors’ exposure metrics, and though they use a different primary measure than Azar, Gine, and Sanz-Espin, they derive similar results.

#### The overall effect of AI on labor might be the sum of potential contradictions

![](https://equitablegrowth.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/ai-lit-review-chapter.jpg)

At the time of writing, most academic papers, if they make predictions at all, propose that the overall effect of AI on work, workers, or the labor market will be a matter of balance. A few examples of such proposals include:

* The effect of automation on workers may rest partially on [how many of their tasks](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5466890) can be automated and their individual skillsets. A moderate amount of automation might lead to higher wages, but two workers in the same job could have different outcomes.
* AI could facilitate a [rebuilding of the U.S. middle class](https://www.nber.org/papers/w32140) if deployed in ways that democratize expertise, [but those same lowered barriers to entry could reduce wages even as they expand employment opportunities.](https://www.nber.org/papers/w33941)
* Technological change through [AI could have substantial economic impacts, but without deliberate policy intervention, workers might not share in those gains.](https://www.nber.org/papers/w34854)

When viewed as a whole, the research currently estimates that the overall impact of AI on the labor market will be a combination of potential benefits and harms felt across tasks, skills, occupations, people, places, and time.How such impacts will be ultimately be felt across the labor market, and on what time scale, cannot be fully predicted. But existing research provides a valuable foundation and highlights where our understanding still needs to grow as AI evolves and integrates into the economy.
