**Kamer Daron Acemoğlu**[[a]](#cite_note-2) (born September 3, 1967) is a [Turkish-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish-American "Turkish-American") economist of [Armenian descent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenians_in_Turkey "Armenians in Turkey") who has taught at the [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology") since 1993, where he is currently the [Elizabeth and James Killian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Rhyne_Killian "James Rhyne Killian") Professor of Economics, and was named an [Institute Professor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Institute_Professors_at_the_Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "List of Institute Professors at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology") at MIT in 2019.[[2]](#cite_note-MIT-CV-3) His primary research fields include political economy, development economics, and labor economics. He received the [John Bates Clark Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bates_Clark_Medal "John Bates Clark Medal") in 2005, and the [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") in 2024.[[2]](#cite_note-MIT-CV-3)[[3]](#cite_note-4)

Acemoglu ranked third, behind [Paul Krugman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Krugman "Paul Krugman") and [Greg Mankiw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Mankiw "Greg Mankiw"), in the list of "Favorite Living Economists Under Age 60" in a 2011 survey among American economists. In 2015, he was named the most cited economist of the past 10 years per [Research Papers in Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_Papers_in_Economics "Research Papers in Economics") (RePEc) data. According to the [Open Syllabus Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Syllabus_Project "Open Syllabus Project"), Acemoglu is the third most frequently cited author on college [syllabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syllabus "Syllabus") for economics courses after Mankiw and Krugman.[[4]](#cite_note-5)

In 2024, Acemoglu, [Simon Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Johnson_(economist) "Simon Johnson (economist)"), and [James A. Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_A._Robinson "James A. Robinson") were awarded the [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") for their [comparative studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-cultural_studies "Cross-cultural studies") in prosperity between states and empires.[[5]](#cite_note-6) He is regarded as a centrist with a focus on institutions, poverty and econometrics.

## Early and personal life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daron_Acemoglu&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early and personal life")]

Kamer Daron Acemoğlu[[6]](#cite_note-7)[[7]](#cite_note-bl.uk-8)[[b]](#cite_note-11) was born in [Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul") to [Armenian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenians "Armenians") parents on September 3, 1967.[[10]](#cite_note-mit_cv-12)[[11]](#cite_note-13)[[12]](#cite_note-hurriyetdailynews2015-14) His father, Kevork Acemoglu (1938–1988), was a commercial lawyer and lecturer at [Istanbul University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_University "Istanbul University"). His mother, Irma Acemoglu (d. 1991), was a poet and the principal of [Aramyan Uncuyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aramyan_Uncuyan?action=edit&redlink=1 "Aramyan Uncuyan (page does not exist)") [[tr](https://tr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aramyan%20Uncuyan%20Ermeni%20İlk%20ve%20Ortaokulu "tr:Aramyan Uncuyan Ermeni İlk ve Ortaokulu"); [hy](https://hy.wikipedia.org/wiki/Արամյան-Ունճյան%20վարժարան "hy:Արամյան-Ունճյան վարժարան")], an Armenian elementary school in [Kadıköy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kadıköy "Kadıköy"),[[13]](#cite_note-15)[[14]](#cite_note-armenianweekly-16)[[15]](#cite_note-boston_2005-17) which he attended, before graduating from [Galatasaray High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galatasaray_High_School "Galatasaray High School") in 1986.[[16]](#cite_note-18)[[17]](#cite_note-azatutyun-19)[[18]](#cite_note-20) He became interested in politics and economics as a teenager.[[15]](#cite_note-boston_2005-17)

He was educated at the [University of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_York "University of York"), where he received a [BA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") in economics in 1989, and at the [London School of Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics") (LSE), where he received an [MSc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") in econometrics and mathematical economics in 1990, and a [PhD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Philosophy "Doctor of Philosophy") in economics in 1992.[[19]](#cite_note-mit.edu-21) His doctoral thesis was titled *Essays in Microfoundations of Macroeconomics: Contracts and Economic Performance*.[[10]](#cite_note-mit_cv-12)[[7]](#cite_note-bl.uk-8) His [doctoral advisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctoral_advisor "Doctoral advisor") was [Kevin W. S. Roberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_W._S._Roberts "Kevin W. S. Roberts").[[20]](#cite_note-genealogy-22) [James Malcomson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_M._Malcomson "James M. Malcomson"), one of his doctoral examiners at the LSE, said that even the weakest three of the seven chapters of his thesis were "more than sufficient for the award of a PhD."[[21]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShimer2007191-23) [Arnold Kling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Kling "Arnold Kling") called him a [wunderkind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wunderkind "Wunderkind") due to the fact that he received his PhD by the time he was 25.[[22]](#cite_note-24)

Acemoglu is a [naturalized US citizen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizenship_of_the_United_States "Citizenship of the United States").[[23]](#cite_note-frontiersofknowledgeawards-25) He is fluent in English and [Turkish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_language "Turkish language"),[[24]](#cite_note-26) and speaks some [Armenian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_language "Armenian language").[[25]](#cite_note-VoA2018-27) He is married to [Asuman "Asu" Ozdağlar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asuman_Özdağlar "Asuman Özdağlar"), a professor of electrical engineering and computer science at MIT,[[15]](#cite_note-boston_2005-17)[[26]](#cite_note-28) who is the daughter of [İsmail Özdağlar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/İsmail_Özdağlar "İsmail Özdağlar"), a former Turkish government minister. Together, they have authored several articles.[[27]](#cite_note-29)[[28]](#cite_note-30) As of 2015[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daron_Acemoglu&action=edit), they live in [Newton, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton,_Massachusetts "Newton, Massachusetts"), with their two sons, Arda and Aras.[[29]](#cite_note-31)

## Academic career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daron_Acemoglu&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Academic career")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Daron_Acemoglu.jpg/250px-Daron_Acemoglu.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Daron_Acemoglu.jpg)

Acemoglu in 2009

 [![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Daron_Acemoglu2020.jpg/250px-Daron_Acemoglu2020.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Daron_Acemoglu2020.jpg)

Acemoglu in his office, January 2020

Acemoglu was a [lecturer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lecturer "Lecturer") in economics at the London School of Economics from 1992 to 1993.[[2]](#cite_note-MIT-CV-3) He was appointed an [assistant professor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assistant_professor "Assistant professor") at MIT in 1993, where he became the [Pentti Kouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentti_Kouri "Pentti Kouri") Associate Professor of Economics in 1997, and was [tenured](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_tenure "Academic tenure") in 1998.[[2]](#cite_note-MIT-CV-3)[[30]](#cite_note-imf-32) He became a [full professor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professor_(highest_academic_rank) "Professor (highest academic rank)") at MIT in 2000, and served as the [Charles P. Kindleberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_P._Kindleberger "Charles P. Kindleberger") Professor of Applied Economics there from 2004 to 2010.[[2]](#cite_note-MIT-CV-3)[[31]](#cite_note-Mallard-33) In 2010, Acemoglu was appointed the [Elizabeth and James Killian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Rhyne_Killian "James Rhyne Killian") Professor of Economics at MIT.[[10]](#cite_note-mit_cv-12) In July 2019, he was named an [Institute Professor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Institute_Professors_at_the_Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "List of Institute Professors at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology"), the highest faculty honor at MIT.[[32]](#cite_note-InstProf-34)

As of 2019[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daron_Acemoglu&action=edit), he has mentored over 60 PhD students.[[32]](#cite_note-InstProf-34) Among his doctoral students are [Ufuk Akçiġit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ufuk_Akcigit "Ufuk Akcigit"), [Robert Shimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Shimer "Robert Shimer"), [Mark Aguiar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Aguiar "Mark Aguiar"), [Pol Antràs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pol_Antràs "Pol Antràs"), and [Gabriel Carroll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Carroll "Gabriel Carroll").[[20]](#cite_note-genealogy-22) In 2014, he made $841,380, making him one of the top earners at MIT.[[33]](#cite_note-35)

Acemoglu is a research associate at the [National Bureau of Economic Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Bureau_of_Economic_Research "National Bureau of Economic Research") (NBER), and was elected a [Fellow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fellows_of_the_Econometric_Society "List of fellows of the Econometric Society") of the [Econometric Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Econometric_Society "Econometric Society") in 2005.[[19]](#cite_note-mit.edu-21)[[2]](#cite_note-MIT-CV-3)[[34]](#cite_note-36) He was elected to the [American Academy of Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Academy_of_Arts_and_Sciences "American Academy of Arts and Sciences") in 2006, and to the [National Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Academy_of_Sciences "National Academy of Sciences") in 2014.[[35]](#cite_note-37)[[36]](#cite_note-38) He is also a Senior Fellow at the [Canadian Institute for Advanced Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Institute_for_Advanced_Research "Canadian Institute for Advanced Research"), and a member of several other learned societies.[[19]](#cite_note-mit.edu-21)[[37]](#cite_note-39)[[38]](#cite_note-40) He edited *[Econometrica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Econometrica "Econometrica")*, an academic journal published by the [Econometric Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Econometric_Society "Econometric Society"), from 2011 to 2015.[[39]](#cite_note-41)

Acemoglu has authored hundreds of academic papers.[[40]](#cite_note-scholar.google-42) He noted that most of his research has been "motivated by trying to understand the sources of poverty."[[23]](#cite_note-frontiersofknowledgeawards-25) His research includes a wide range of topics, including [political economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_economy "Political economy"), [human capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_capital "Human capital") theory, [growth theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Growth_theory "Growth theory"), [economic development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_development "Economic development"), innovation, [labor economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_economics "Labor economics"),[[19]](#cite_note-mit.edu-21)[[41]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShimer2007199–200-43) income and wage inequality, and [network economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_economics "Network economics"), among others.[[42]](#cite_note-44) He noted in 2011 that most his research of the past 15 years concerned with what can be broadly called political economy.[[43]](#cite_note-Clement-45) He has made contribution to the labor economics field.[[23]](#cite_note-frontiersofknowledgeawards-25)

Acemoglu has extensively collaborated with [James A. Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_A._Robinson_(economist) "James A. Robinson (economist)"), a British political scientist and his peer at the [London School of Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics").[[30]](#cite_note-imf-32) Acemoglu has described it as a "very productive relationship." They have worked together on many articles and books, most of which are on the subject of growth and economic development.[[23]](#cite_note-frontiersofknowledgeawards-25) The two have also extensively collaborated with economist [Simon Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Johnson_(economist) "Simon Johnson (economist)").[[44]](#cite_note-JohnsonNYTimes12-46)

## Research and publications

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daron_Acemoglu&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Research and publications")]

Acemoglu is considered a follower of [new institutional economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_institutional_economics "New institutional economics").[[45]](#cite_note-47)[[46]](#cite_note-48)[[47]](#cite_note-49) His influences include [Joel Mokyr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel_Mokyr "Joel Mokyr"), [Kenneth Sokoloff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Sokoloff "Kenneth Sokoloff"),[[48]](#cite_note-Mokyr&Sokoloff-50) [Douglass North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglass_North "Douglass North"),[[49]](#cite_note-51) [Seymour Martin Lipset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seymour_Martin_Lipset "Seymour Martin Lipset"),[[50]](#cite_note-Dewan-52) and [Barrington Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrington_Moore "Barrington Moore").[[50]](#cite_note-Dewan-52)

### Books

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daron_Acemoglu&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Books")]

#### *Economic Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy*

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daron_Acemoglu&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Economic Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy")]

Published by [Cambridge University Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_University_Press "Cambridge University Press") in 2006, *Economic Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy* by Acemoglu and [Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_A._Robinson_(economist) "James A. Robinson (economist)") analyzes the creation and consolidation of democratic societies. They argue that "democracy consolidates when elites do not have a strong incentive to overthrow it. These processes depend on (1) the strength of civil society, (2) the structure of political institutions, (3) the nature of political and economic crises, (4) the level of economic inequality, (5) the structure of the economy, and (6) the form and extent of globalization."[[51]](#cite_note-53) The book's title is derived from *[Social Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Origins_of_Dictatorship_and_Democracy "Social Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy")*, a 1966 book by [Barrington Moore Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrington_Moore_Jr. "Barrington Moore Jr.")[[52]](#cite_note-Acemoglu_Page_38-54)

[Romain Wacziarg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romain_Wacziarg "Romain Wacziarg") praised the book and argued that its substantive contribution is the theoretical fusion of the Marxist [dialectical materialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dialectical_materialism "Dialectical materialism") ("institutional change results from distributional struggles between two distinct social groups, a rich ruling class and a poor majority, each of whose interests are shaped primarily by economic forces") and the ideas of [Barry Weingast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Weingast "Barry Weingast") and [Douglass North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglass_North "Douglass North"), who argued that "institutional reform can be a way for the elite to credibly commit to future policies by delegating their enactment to interests that will not wish to reverse them."[[53]](#cite_note-55) [William Easterly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Easterly "William Easterly") called it "one of the most important contributions to the literature on the economics of democracy in a long time." [Edward Glaeser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Glaeser "Edward Glaeser") described it as "enormously significant" work and a "great contribution to the field."[[54]](#cite_note-56)

#### *Why Nations Fail*

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daron_Acemoglu&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Why Nations Fail")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/%22Why_Nations_Fail%22_by_Daron_Acemoglu_and_James_Robinson.jpg/120px-%22Why_Nations_Fail%22_by_Daron_Acemoglu_and_James_Robinson.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:)

*Why Nations Fail* was included in the Shortlist of the 2012 *[Financial Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Times "Financial Times")* [Business Book of the Year Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Times_and_McKinsey_Business_Book_of_the_Year_Award "Financial Times and McKinsey Business Book of the Year Award").

In their 2012 book, *[Why Nations Fail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Why_Nations_Fail "Why Nations Fail")*, Acemoglu and Robinson argue that economic growth at the forefront of technology requires political stability, which the [Mayan civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayan_civilization "Mayan civilization") (to name only one) did not have,[[55]](#cite_note-57) and [creative destruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_destruction "Creative destruction"). The latter cannot occur without institutional restraints on the granting of monopoly and oligopoly rights. They say that the [Industrial Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution") began in [Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain "Great Britain"), because the English [Bill of Rights 1689](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_of_Rights_1689 "Bill of Rights 1689") created such restraints.

Acemoglu and Robinson insist that "development differences across countries are exclusively due to differences in political and economic institutions, and reject other theories that attribute some of the differences to culture, weather, geography or lack of knowledge about the best policies and practices."[[56]](#cite_note-Radelet-58) For example, "Soviet Russia generated rapid growth as it caught up rapidly with some of the advanced technologies in the world [but] was running out of steam by the 1970s" because of a lack of creative destruction.[[57]](#cite_note-59)

The book was written for a general audience.[[56]](#cite_note-Radelet-58) It was widely discussed by political analysts and commentators.[[58]](#cite_note-60)[[59]](#cite_note-Friedman-61)[[60]](#cite_note-62)[[61]](#cite_note-63) Warren Bass wrote of it in *[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post "The Washington Post")*: "bracing, garrulous, wildly ambitious and ultimately hopeful. It may, in fact, be a bit of a masterpiece."[[62]](#cite_note-64)

[Clive Crook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Crook "Clive Crook") wrote in *[Bloomberg News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomberg_News "Bloomberg News")* that the book deserves most of the "lavish praise" it received.[[63]](#cite_note-65) In his review in *[Foreign Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Affairs "Foreign Affairs")* [Jeffrey Sachs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_Sachs "Jeffrey Sachs") criticized Acemoglu and Robinson for systematically ignoring factors such as domestic politics, geopolitics, technological discoveries, and natural resources. He also argued that the book's appeal was based on readers' desire to hear that "Western democracy pays off not only politically but also economically."[[64]](#cite_note-66) [Bill Gates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Gates "Bill Gates") called the book a "major disappointment" and characterized the authors' analysis as "vague and simplistic."[[65]](#cite_note-67) Ryan Avent, an editor at *[The Economist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Economist "The Economist")*, responded that "Acemoglu and Robinson might not be entirely right about why nations succeed or fail. But at least they're engaged with the right problem."[[66]](#cite_note-68)

#### *The Narrow Corridor*

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daron_Acemoglu&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: The Narrow Corridor")]

In *The Narrow Corridor. States, Societies, and the Fate of Liberty* (2019), Acemoglu and Robinson argue that a free society is attained when the power of the state and of society evolved in rough balance.[[67]](#cite_note-69) The book introduces the concept of the "red queen effect," which suggests that liberty is maintained only when both the state and society continually evolve to keep each other in check.

#### *Power and Progress*

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daron_Acemoglu&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Power and Progress")]

Published in 2023, *Power and Progress: Our Thousand-Year Struggle Over Technology and Prosperity* is a book by Acemoglu and [Simon Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Johnson_(economist) "Simon Johnson (economist)") on the historical development of technology and the social and political consequences of technology.[[68]](#cite_note-70) The book addresses three questions, on the relationship between new machines and production techniques and wages, on the way in which technology could be harnessed for social goods, and on the reason for the enthusiasm around artificial intelligence.

*Power and Progress* argues that technologies do not automatically yield social goods, their benefits going to a narrow elite. It offers a rather critical view of [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") (AI), stressing its largely negative impact on jobs and wages and on democracy.

Acemoglu and Johnson also provide a vision of how new technologies could be harnessed for social good. They see the [Progressive Era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_Era "Progressive Era") as offering a model. They also discuss a list of policy proposals for the redirection of technology that includes: (1) market incentives, (2) the break up of [big tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Tech "Big Tech"), (3) [tax reform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_reform "Tax reform"), (4) investing in workers, (5) privacy protection and data ownership, and (6) a digital advertising tax.[[69]](#cite_note-71)

### Papers

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daron_Acemoglu&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Papers")]

#### Social programs and policies

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daron_Acemoglu&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Social programs and policies")]

In a 2001 article, Acemoglu argued that the [minimum wage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_wage "Minimum wage") and [unemployment benefits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unemployment_benefits "Unemployment benefits") "shift the composition of employment toward high-wage jobs. Because the composition of jobs in the [laissez-faire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laissez-faire "Laissez-faire") equilibrium is inefficiently biased toward low-wage jobs, these labor market regulations increase average labor productivity and may improve welfare."[[70]](#cite_note-72) Furthermore, he has argued that "minimum wages can increase training of affected workers, by inducing firms to train their unskilled employees."[[71]](#cite_note-73)

#### Democracy and economy

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daron_Acemoglu&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Democracy and economy")]

Acemoglu *et al.* found that "[democracy has a significant and robust positive effect on GDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy_and_economic_growth "Democracy and economic growth")" and suggested that "[democratizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratization "Democratization") increase GDP per capita by about 20% in the long run."[[72]](#cite_note-74) In another paper, Acemoglu *et al.* found that "there is a significant and robust effect of democracy on tax revenues as a fraction of GDP, but no robust impact on inequality.".[[73]](#cite_note-75) The authors argue that democratic institutions contribute to economic growth by expanding education, improving public capacity, and encouraging investment.

#### Social democracy and unions

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daron_Acemoglu&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Social democracy and unions")]

Acemoglu and [Philippe Aghion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippe_Aghion "Philippe Aghion") argued in 2001 that although deunionization in the US and UK since the 1980s is not the "underlying cause of the increase in inequality", it "amplifies the direct effect of skill-biased technical change by removing the wage compression imposed by unions."[[74]](#cite_note-76)

According to Acemoglu and Robinson, unions historically had a significant role in creating democracy, especially in western Europe, and in maintaining a balance of political power between established business interests and political elites.[[75]](#cite_note-77)

#### Nordic model

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daron_Acemoglu&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Nordic model")]

In a 2012 paper titled "Can't We All Be More Like Scandinavians?", co-written with Robinson and Verdier, he suggests that "it may be precisely the more 'cutthroat' American society that makes possible the more 'cuddly' Scandinavian societies based on a comprehensive social safety net, the welfare state and more limited inequality." They concluded that "all countries may want to be like the 'Scandinavians' with a more extensive safety net and a more egalitarian structure," however, if the United States shifted from being a "cutthroat [capitalism] leader", the economic growth of the entire world would be reduced.[[76]](#cite_note-Like_Scandinavians-78) He argued against the US adopting the Nordic model in a 2015 op-ed for *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")*. He again argued: "If the US increased taxation to Denmark levels, it would reduce rewards for entrepreneurship, with negative consequences for growth and prosperity." He praised the Scandinavian experience in [poverty reduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poverty_reduction "Poverty reduction"), creation of a [level playing field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Level_playing_field "Level playing field") for its citizens, and higher [social mobility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_mobility "Social mobility").[[77]](#cite_note-79) This was critiqued by [Lane Kenworthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Kenworthy "Lane Kenworthy"), who argues that, empirically, the US's economic growth preceded the divergence in 'cutthroat' and 'cuddly' policies, and there is no relationship between inequality and innovation for developed countries.[[78]](#cite_note-Lane_Kenworthy_2012-80)

#### Colonialism

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daron_Acemoglu&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Colonialism")]

"[The Colonial Origins of Comparative Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_origins_of_comparative_development "Colonial origins of comparative development")", co-written by Acemoglu, Robinson, and [Simon Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Johnson_(economist) "Simon Johnson (economist)") in 2001, is by far his most cited work.[[40]](#cite_note-scholar.google-42) Graham Mallard described it as an "excellent example of his work: an influential paper that has led to much debate."[[31]](#cite_note-Mallard-33) They argue that Europeans set up extractive institutions in colonies where they did not settle, unlike in places where they did settle and that these institutions have persisted. They estimated that "differences in institutions explain approximately three-quarters of the [income per capita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Income_per_capita "Income per capita") differences across former colonies."[[79]](#cite_note-81)[[80]](#cite_note-82) Historical experience dominated by extractive institutions in these countries has created a [vicious circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicious_circle "Vicious circle"), which was exacerbated by European colonization.[[81]](#cite_note-freakonomics12-83)

#### A critique of modernization theory

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daron_Acemoglu&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: A critique of modernization theory")]

Daron Acemoglu and [James A. Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_A._Robinson "James A. Robinson"), in their article "Income and Democracy" (2008) show that even though there is a strong cross-country correlation between income and democracy, once one controls for country fixed effects and removes the association between income per capita and various measures of democracy, there is "no causal effect of income on democracy."[[82]](#cite_note-84) In "Non-Modernization" (2022), they further argue that [modernization theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernization_theory "Modernization theory") cannot account for various paths of political development "because it posits a link between economics and politics that is not conditional on institutions and culture and that presumes a definite endpoint—for example, an 'end of history'."[[83]](#cite_note-85)

#### Automation and labor markets

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daron_Acemoglu&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Automation and labor markets")]

Beginning in the late 2010s, Acemoglu expanded his research to focus on the economic effects of automation and artificial intelligence on labor markets. In collaboration with Pascual Restrepo, he examined how industrial robots affected employment and wages in the United States. Their study "Robots and Jobs: Evidence from U.S. Labor Markets" (2020) found that regions with greater exposure to industrial robots experienced larger declines in employment and modest reductions in wages, suggesting that the economic benefits of automation were not evenly distributed.[[84]](#cite_note-86) Acemoglu and Restrepo extended this analysis in "Tasks, Automation, and the Rise in U.S. Wage Inequality" (2022), arguing that automation has contributed to rising wage inequality in the United States by replacing many middle-skill tasks while increasing demand for higher-skill labor.[[85]](#cite_note-87) This body of research has influenced broader discussions on the future of work, emphasizing that technological change does not automatically benefit workers and can lead to unequal outcomes if incentives favor labor-replacing technologies. Acemoglu has argued that policy and institutional frameworks play an important role in determining whether new technologies complement human labor or substitute for it.

## Views

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daron_Acemoglu&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Views")]

Journalists and economists have described Acemoglu as a [centrist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centrist "Centrist").[[c]](#cite_note-91) *Why Nations Fail* was well received by both liberal and conservative economists.[[89]](#cite_note-92) Acemoglu's and Robinson's long-time collaborator Simon Johnson suggests that their "point is not just about how things may become awful when the government goes off track (a right-leaning point). They are also more deeply concerned about how powerful people fight to grab control of the state and otherwise compete to exert influence over the rest of society (a left-leaning perspective)."[[44]](#cite_note-JohnsonNYTimes12-46)

Acemoglu has praised the successes of the [Progressive Era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_Era "Progressive Era"), and argued in favor of its replication.[[90]](#cite_note-93) He argues that the [market economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_economy "Market economy") is the only system that creates prosperity, and believes in finding an appropriate balance between "incentivizing creativity, hard work and risk-taking and creating the essential [public services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_service "Public service"), [social safety nets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_safety_net "Social safety net") and [equality of opportunity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_opportunity "Equal opportunity")."[[91]](#cite_note-cnn_soc-94) For Acemoglu, markets work only with regulations and [predictable laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_certainty "Legal certainty") and that all [markets are regulated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulated_market "Regulated market") to some extent; it is only a matter of degree.[[30]](#cite_note-imf-32) He suggests that free markets are not unregulated markets.[[92]](#cite_note-hoover2009-95)

### Wall Street

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daron_Acemoglu&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Wall Street")]

In September 2008, Acemoglu signed a petition condemning the [Bush administration's bailout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_Economic_Stabilization_Act_of_2008 "Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of 2008") plan for the US financial system.[[93]](#cite_note-96) As the main cause of the [2008 financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis"), he stated that policy makers were "lured by ideological notions derived from [Ayn Rand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayn_Rand "Ayn Rand")'s novels rather than economic theory" and opined: "In hindsight, we should not be surprised that unregulated profit-seeking individuals have taken risks from which they benefit and others lose."[[92]](#cite_note-hoover2009-95) In an early analysis of the [Great Recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Recession "Great Recession"), Acemoglu wrote: "When channeled into [profit-maximizing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profit_maximization "Profit maximization"), competitive, and innovative behavior under the auspices of sound laws and regulations, greed can act as the engine of innovation and economic growth. But when unchecked by the appropriate institutions and regulations, it will degenerate into [rent-seeking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rent-seeking "Rent-seeking"), corruption, and crime."[[30]](#cite_note-imf-32) He ar

This is a Wikipedia article about Daron Acemoglu (born Kamer Daron Acemoğlu, September 3, 1967, in Istanbul, Turkey), a Turkish-American economist of Armenian descent. He is the Elizabeth and James Killian Professor of Economics at MIT, where he has taught since 1993, and was named an MIT Institute Professor in 2019 (the university's highest faculty honor). He received the John Bates Clark Medal in 2005 and the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 2024 (shared with Simon Johnson and James A. Robinson) for their comparative studies on prosperity between states and empires. He is regarded as a centrist focused on institutions, poverty, and econometrics.

**Early Life & Education:** Acemoglu was born to Armenian parents in Istanbul. His father Kevork was a commercial lawyer/lecturer at Istanbul University; his mother Irma was a poet and school principal. He attended Aramyan Uncuyan Armenian school and graduated from Galatasaray High School in 1986. He earned a BA in economics from the University of York (1989), and an MSc (1990) and PhD (1992) from the London School of Economics. His thesis was "Essays in Microfoundations of Macroeconomics: Contracts and Economic Performance," supervised by Kevin W. S. Roberts. He is married to Asu Ozdağlar, an MIT professor and daughter of a former Turkish minister; they have two sons and live in Newton, Massachusetts.

**Academic Career:** He was a lecturer at LSE (1992-1993), then joined MIT as assistant professor (1993), became tenured (1998), full professor (2000), Kindleberger Professor (2004-2010), Killian Professor (2010), and Institute Professor (2019). He has mentored over 60 PhD students (including Ufuk Akcigit, Robert Shimer, Mark Aguiar, Pol Antràs, Gabriel Carroll, Melissa Dell, Benjamin Jones). He is a research associate at NBER, Fellow of the Econometric Society (2005), American Academy of Arts and Sciences (2006), National Academy of Sciences (2014), and edited Econometrica (2011-2015). He is the most-cited economist of the past decade per RePEc data (2015) and third most-cited author on economics syllabi after Mankiw and Krugman.

**Major Books:**
- *Economic Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy* (2006, with Robinson) — analyzes democratic consolidation, arguing democracy consolidates when elites lack incentive to overthrow it.
- *Why Nations Fail* (2012, with Robinson) — argues development differences across countries are exclusively due to differences in political and economic institutions, rejecting culture/geography theories; was an FT Business Book of the Year shortlistee; praised by many but criticized by Jeffrey Sachs and Bill Gates (who called it "vague and simplistic").
- *The Narrow Corridor* (2019, with Robinson) — argues liberty exists when state and society power are in balance, introducing the "red queen effect."
- *Power and Progress* (2023, with Simon Johnson) — critical view of AI's impact on jobs, wages, and democracy; proposes redirecting technology via market incentives, breaking up big tech, tax reform, worker investment, privacy/data ownership, and a digital advertising tax.

**Key Research/Papers:**
- His most cited work, "The Colonial Origins of Comparative Development" (2001, with Johnson and Robinson), argues extractive institutions in colonies persist and explain ~3/4 of income per capita differences across former colonies.
- Found democracy has a robust positive effect on GDP (~20% increase in long run) and on tax revenues but not inequality.
- Critiqued modernization theory ("Income and Democracy," 2008), finding no causal effect of income on democracy once controlling for fixed effects.
- Research with Pascual Restrepo (2020-2022) on robots/automation found industrial robots reduced employment and wages in exposed US regions and contributed to rising wage inequality by replacing middle-skill tasks.
- Argued minimum wage and unemployment benefits can shift employment composition toward high-wage jobs and improve welfare.
- In the Nordic model debate, argued US's "cutthroat" capitalism enables Scandinavian "cuddly" welfare states, and the US adopting Denmark-level taxation would reduce entrepreneurial rewards.

**Views:** Described as centrist. He argues market economy is the only system creating prosperity, but markets require regulations and predictable laws; praised the Progressive Era as a model. He condemned the 2008 Bush administration bailout, blaming policymakers "lured by ideological notions derived from Ayn Rand's novels," and stated unchecked greed degenerates into rent-seeking and corruption. He and Robinson argued unions historically helped create democracy in western Europe.
args.key_excerpts: "democracy consolidates when elites do not have a strong incentive to overthrow it. These processes depend on (1) the strength of civil society, (2) the structure of political institutions, (3) the nature of political and economic crises, (4) the level of economic inequality, (5) the structure of the economy, and (6) the form and extent of globalization.", "development differences across countries are exclusively due to differences in political and economic institutions, and reject other theories that attribute some of the differences to culture, weather, geography or lack of knowledge about the best policies and practices.", "differences in institutions explain approximately three-quarters of the income per capita differences across former colonies.", "When channeled into profit-maximizing, competitive, and innovative behavior under the auspices of sound laws and regulations, greed can act as the engine of innovation and economic growth. But when unchecked by the appropriate institutions and regulations, it will degenerate into rent-seeking, corruption, and crime.", "If the US increased taxation to Denmark levels, it would reduce rewards for entrepreneurship, with negative consequences for growth and prosperity."

## Abstract

We analyze for the first time the economic contributions of modern industrial robots, which are flexible, versatile, and autonomous machines. We use novel panel data on robot adoption within industries in seventeen countries from 1993 to 2007 and new instrumental variables that rely on robots’ comparative advantage in specific tasks. Our findings suggest that increased robot use contributed approximately 0.36 percentage points to annual labor productivity growth, while at the same time raising total factor productivity and lowering output prices. Our estimates also suggest that robots did not significantly reduce total employment, although they did reduce low-skilled workers’ employment share.

This is a Semantic Scholar page for the paper "Robots at Work" by Georg Graetz and Guy Michaels, published in the Review of Economics and Statistics (2015, Volume 100, pages 753-768; DOI: 10.1162/rest_a_00754). The paper provides one of the first economic analyses of modern industrial robots—flexible, versatile, and autonomous machines. Using novel panel data on robot adoption within industries across 17 countries from 1993 to 2007, and new instrumental variables based on robots' comparative advantage in specific tasks, the authors find that increased robot use contributed approximately 0.36 percentage points to annual labor productivity growth. The paper has 1,531 citations.

Key citing works highlighted include: "The rise of robots and the fall of routine jobs" (de Vries, Gentile, Miroudot, Wacker, 2020, Labour Economics); "The rise of robots in the German labour market" (Dauth, Findeisen, Südekum, Woessner, 2017); "Robots and Jobs: Evidence from US Labor Markets" (Acemoglu & Restrepo, 2020, Journal of Political Economy, 3,862 citations); "Robots worldwide: The impact of automation on employment and trade" (Carbonero, Ernst, Weber, 2018); "Robots at work: recent evidence with new data" (Almeida, Highly Influenced); "You have been terminated: robots, work, and taxation" (Akar, Casalone, Zagler, 2023); "Robots and Non-Participation in the US" (Lerch, 2022); "Robots, skill demand and manufacturing in US regional labour markets" (Leigh, Kraft, Lee, 2019); "The Adjustment of Labor Markets to Robots" (Dauth, Findeisen, Suedekum, Woessner, 2021, Journal of the European Economic Association, 429 citations); and "Who is Replaced by Robots?" (Damelang & Otto, 2023, Work and Occupations).

The paper also lists 61 references, including foundational works such as Acemoglu & Restrepo's "The Race between Machine and Man" (2017); Feng & Graetz's "Rise of the Machines" (2015); Doms, Dunne & Troske's "Workers, Wages, and Technology" (1997); Autor, Katz & Krueger's "Computing Inequality" (1997); Autor's "Why Are There Still So Many Jobs?" You are tasked with summarizing the raw content of a webpage retrieved from a web search. Your goal is to create a summary that preserves the most important information from the original web page. This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information. Here is the raw content of the webpage: [Economic Opportunity](https://tcf.org/topics/economy-jobs/)[Manufacturing](https://tcf.org/topics/economy-jobs/manufacturing/) How Robots Are Beginning to Affect Workers and Their Wages Report [Manufacturing](https://tcf.org/topics/economy-jobs/manufacturing/) # How Robots Are Beginning to Affect Workers and Their Wages * [Download (EN) (EN)](https://production-tcf.imgix.net/app/uploads/2019/10/22171153/Robots_Final.pdf) ## Executive Summary Much has been written about the rise of robots and the potential impacts of automation on the economy. Yet most analysis tends to be prospective in nature, and estimates of future impacts on employment vary widely, with some studies predicting that as many as 50 percent of all workers are at risk of losing their jobs to automation. Even less is understood about the actual impacts of robots on jobs, wages, and workers today. While more recent studies have begun to measure these effects, the results here, too, are mixed. This report analyzes the impact of robots in the years following the Great Recession, from 2009 to 2017—a period of significant, steady job growth and economic recovery, as well as one in which the use of robots in the U.S. workplace more than doubled. The report’s findings, summarized below, offer new insights that can help inform ongoing debates about the future of work and the impact of automation. The first takeaway is that robots are, indeed, coming—but there is little evidence (yet) that robotic growth is leading to widespread job displacement, as some have predicted. That said, there are winners and losers with automation. While robots may have negligible effects on national employment as a whole, certain industries and regions are more impacted by robotic growth, and particular groups of workers disproportionately suffer the negative effects of this growth. It is also the case that job losses from robotization may have little impact on total employment, as displaced workers find other jobs (especially in a strong economy with low unemployment), even if at lower pay. Lastly, we find that the economic boom of the past decade has effectively “masked” some of the impacts that robots have had on workers. It’s not that robots weren’t displacing jobs—it’s that the overall economic expansion was large enough to offset some of these job losses. ## Key Findings ### 1. Trends in Robot Growth We constructed a measure of the use of robots—commonly referred to as “robot intensity”—to estimate trends in robot exposure across more than 250 metropolitan areas and over time, finding that: * During the Great Recession, robot intensity plummeted. But since 2009, **robot intensity has sharply increased** nationwide. * States in the Midwest (the East North Central, or ENC, census division)—**Michigan, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, and Wisconsin**—consistently have the highest robot intensities, typically at least twice the intensity of all other regions. * Midwest (ENC) states also experienced **the sharpest growth in robots** since 2009. * Robot intensity in **manufacturing industries** greatly exceeds the national average: + Since 2009, the number of manufacturing robots has more than doubled—from 0.813 per thousand workers to 1.974 per thousand workers. * **Highly unionized states** have much lower robot intensities than states with low rates of unionization. ### 2. Impact of Robots Varies across Workers We assess the impact of robot intensity on the employment and earnings outcomes of non-college educated men and women, finding that: * The adoption of robots since the Great Recession has been accompanied by **employment gains for some groups** of workers, and appears **not to have** **affected other groups.** + Positive impact on: young, less-educated men and less-educated adult women. + No impact on: young, less-educated women and less-educated adult men. * The adoption of robots since the Great Recession has been accompanied by wage **increases for some groups** of workers, and appears **not to have adversely affected other groups.** + Positive impact on: young, less-educated women and less-educated minority men and women. + No significant impact on: less-educated adult men and women. * Yet, robotization has **adversely affected other types of workers** at the national level—for example, in manufacturing industries. Our findings suggest that, at the current stage and pace of robot growth, and with the right economic conditions in place, some workers without a college degree may benefit from robotization. This is perhaps due to robots stimulating demand for goods, creating new markets, and spurring wage growth. ### 3. Impacts of Robots in the Rust Belt Given that the Midwest has the greatest concentration of robots and the fastest robot growth (and thus is most likely to show the effects of robots), we focus in on the ENC region and examine the effects of robots on employment and wages by race/ethnicity, gender, age, and industry, finding that: * In Midwest manufacturing industries, robots have **sizably decreased employment** for some groups of workers (**young, less-educated men and women**). + Estimated impact: for an increase of one robot per thousand workers, the employment-to-population ratio falls by an estimated 3.5 percentage points. * In Midwest manufacturing industries, robots have **sizably decreased wages** for some groups of workers (**young, less-educated men and women**). + Estimated impact: an increase of one robot per thousand workers is associated with a 4.0 percent to 5.0 percent decline in wages. * The biggest negative impact of robots was on **young, less-educated black men and women**—groups that already have lower wages and employment rates, on average. args.summary:
This report from The Century Foundation analyzes the impact of industrial robots on workers and wages in the United States during the period following the Great Recession (2009–2017), a time when robot use in the U.S. workplace more than doubled.

## Key Findings

**1. Robot Growth Trends:**
- Robot intensity (robots per thousand workers) plummeted during the Great Recession but sharply increased after 2009.
- Midwest states (Michigan, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Wisconsin — the East North Central/ENC census division) consistently have the highest robot intensities, typically at least twice that of all other regions.
- Manufacturing robot intensity more than doubled from 2009, rising from 0.813 to 1.974 robots per thousand workers.
- Highly unionized states have much lower robot intensities than states with low unionization rates.
- Top ten metro areas for robot intensity include Los Angeles, Chicago, Houston, Phoenix, Detroit, Milwaukee, Philadelphia, San Jose, Indianapolis, and Cleveland.

**2. National-Level Impacts Vary by Worker Group:**
- Positive employment impact on young less-educated men and less-educated adult women; no impact on young less-educated women and less-educated adult men.
- Positive wage impact on young less-educated women and less-educated minority men and women; no significant impact on less-educated adult men and women.
- At the national level, some workers may benefit from robotization through increased demand for goods, new markets, and wage growth.

**3. Rust Belt (ENC) Impacts:**
- In Midwest manufacturing, robots have sizably decreased employment for young, less-educated men and women: an increase of one robot per thousand workers reduces the employment-to-population ratio by 3.5 percentage points.
- Wages for these same workers fall by 4.0–5.0 percent per additional robot per thousand workers.
- The biggest negative impact fell on young, less-educated Black men and women — groups already facing lower wages and employment rates.

**4. The "Masking" Effect of the Economic Boom:**
- With robots and economic recovery: employment-to-population ratio for young, less-educated ENC workers rose from roughly 34% to 45.5%.
- With robots but no recovery: the ratio would have fallen from 34% to approximately 30%.
- This demonstrates that the post-2009 economic expansion offset robot-driven job displacement; absent the boom, robots would have displaced far more jobs, particularly for minority young workers.

## Methodology and Context
The authors constructed robot intensity measures for 262 metropolitan statistical areas using International Federation of Robotics (IFR) data and Current Population Survey Outgoing Rotation Group (CPS-ORG) micro-data, focusing on non-college-educated African American, Latinx, and white men and women aged 16-24 (youth) and 25-64 (adults). The study builds on prior research by Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo (MIT/Boston University) and by Georg Graetz and Guy Michaels, which found robot-driven job displacement and wage effects. The report notes that robot intensity differences do not explain racial employment gaps. Key caveats include that robots also contribute to productivity and competitiveness, potentially saving some jobs by allowing U.S. firms to compete with low-wage nations. The report concludes with recommendations for public-private partnerships, workforce training, and support for displaced workers, especially young minority and women workers in manufacturing communities.
args.key_excerpts: "The first takeaway is that robots are, indeed, coming—but there is little evidence (yet) that robotic growth is leading to widespread job displacement, as some have predicted. That said, there are winners and losers with automation."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an NBER working paper (No. 24196, January 2018) by Daron Acemoglu (MIT) and Pascual Restrepo (Boston University) titled "Artificial Intelligence, Automation and Work," prepared for the Economics of Artificial Intelligence volume. The paper develops a task-based framework for studying how automation and AI affect the demand for labor, wages, and employment.

KEY ARGUMENTS AND FRAMEWORK:
The authors argue the current debate around AI and automation presents a "false dichotomy" between alarmist claims (that AI will end human work) and benign claims (that technology always increases labor demand). Their task-based framework conceptualizes production as a range of tasks, some automatable by capital and some requiring labor.

CORE CONCEPTS:
1. DISPLACEMENT EFFECT: Automation replaces workers in tasks they previously performed, reducing labor demand, wages, and employment. This is the central mechanism, absent from standard factor-augmenting production function approaches (F(AL,BK)).

2. COUNTERVAILING FORCES:
   - Productivity effect: Cheaper automated production expands the economy and increases labor demand in non-automated tasks. Examples cited include ATMs increasing bank teller employment (Bessen, 2016) and the cotton gin increasing slave labor demand in the US South.
   - Capital accumulation: Automation raises capital intensity, triggering capital accumulation that boosts labor demand.
   - Deepening of automation (intensive margin): Improvements to machinery in already-automated tasks create productivity effects without displacement (e.g., CNC machines replacing punched-card controlled machines).

3. NEW TASKS (REINSTATEMENT EFFECT): The most powerful countervailing force—creation of new labor-intensive tasks where labor has comparative advantage. Historical examples: new factory, engineering, and managerial jobs absorbing workers displaced from textiles and agriculture in the 19th-20th centuries. Acemoglu and Restrepo (2016) document that new tasks explain about half of US employment growth from 1980-2010. AI itself may create new jobs like "trainers," "explainers," and "sustainers" (Accenture, 2017).

KEY FINDINGS:
- Automation necessarily makes production more capital-intensive and increases output per worker more than wages, reducing labor's share in national income.
- The displacement effect causes a decoupling of wages from output per worker.
- "So-so" automation technologies (just productive enough to be adopted but not generating strong productivity effects) pose the greatest danger to labor.

CONSTRAINTS ON ADJUSTMENT:
1. Mismatch between skills and technology requirements slows adjustment and reduces productivity gains (historical examples: mass schooling in 19th-century Britain, the US "high school movement" in the early 20th century).
2. EXCESSIVE AUTOMATION: Automation may proceed faster than socially desirable due to (a) US tax code biases subsidizing capital relative to labor, and (b) labor market frictions pushing equilibrium wages above the social opportunity cost of labor. This could help explain the productivity slowdown.
3. Missing productivity growth: US labor productivity growth fell from 2.7% annually (1947-1973) to 1.5% (1974-1994), rebounded to 2.8% (1995-2004), then fell to 1.3% (2005-2015). Excessive focus on automation may crowd out investment in other productivity-enhancing technologies, including new task creation.

MODEL STRUCTURE:
The paper outlines a formal task-based model where aggregate output combines tasks x ∈ [N-1,N] via Cobb-Douglas aggregator. Tasks x ∈ [0,I] are technologically automated (can use labor or machines), while others must use labor. Labor has comparative advantage in higher-indexed tasks. Four types of technological change are distinguished: labor-augmenting, automation (extensive margin, parameter I), deepening of automation (intensive margin), and creation of new tasks.

HISTORICAL CONTEXT:
The paper cites the Luddite movement and Captain Swing riots as rational responses to genuine displacement fears. It discusses the "Engel's pause" (Allen, 2009)—an 80-year period from the Industrial Revolution's start to the mid-19th century when British wages stagnated and the labor share fell despite ongoing technological progress—as evidence that adjustment to automation can be slow and painful. The authors also contrast the current applied AI (deep learning, big data methods for prediction, pattern recognition) with the earlier "cybernetics" ambitions of human-level AI (Herbert Simon, Marvin Minsky), arguing current AI's limited scope means it cannot automate complex reasoning, judgment, empathy, and abstract problem-solving.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the Richard T. Ely Lecture by David H. Autor, published in AEA Papers and Proceedings 2019, examining the paradox of falling real wages for less-educated workers in the US alongside rising wage inequality over four decades. 

**Key Thesis:** Autor argues that occupational polarization—the concentration of employment in high-education/high-wage and low-education/low-wage occupations at the expense of middle-skill jobs—has been disproportionately concentrated in urban labor markets, and this geographic dimension has profoundly contributed to the decline of non-college wages.

**Historical Wage Trends (1963–2017):** The progression of inequality divides into three epochs: (i) 1963–1972 with robust, even wage growth; (ii) 1973–1979 stagnation following the first oil shock; and (iii) 1980 forward with secularly rising inequality. Among high school dropouts, graduates, and those with some college, real weekly earnings of full-time male workers in 2018 were 10–20 log points below 1980 levels. Women with high school or lower education earned less than 1980 counterparts for a 15+ year period between 1981 and 1997.

**Educational Attainment Changes:** The share of labor hours from workers with high school or lower education fell from 75% in 1963 to under 40% in 2017, while bachelor's+ degree holders rose from under 15% to over 35%.

**Occupational Polarization:** US employment in 1970 was roughly evenly split among low-skill (31.4%), middle-skill (38.4%), and high-skill (30.2%) occupations. By 2016, middle-skill employment fell to 23.3%, high-skill rose to 46.2%, and low-skill fell slightly to 30.6%. Among non-college workers, middle-skill employment fell by 14 percentage points (43% to 29%) from 1980, with only a slight increase in high-skill (15.4% to 16.8%), meaning most displaced middle-skill workers moved into low-skill work. Autor describes this as a "broadly deskilling" process for non-college workers.

**Calibration Exercise:** A counterfactual analysis holding wage structure at 1978 levels while allowing occupational reallocation found that occupational change alone cannot explain most between-group wage inequality—the observed wage series had five times the range of the counterfactual. Autor notes this provides a "loose lower bound" because it ignores general equilibrium effects on wages across occupations.

**Geographic Polarization:** The paper's key contribution shows polarization was disproportionately urban. In 1970, non-college workers in the densest commuting zones (CZs) were ~25 percentage points more likely to work in middle-skill occupations than those in low-density CZs. This gradient sharply eroded and reversed by 2015. The urban-non-urban gap in high-skill work grew from 5 to 15 percentage points between 1970 and 2015. The decline of middle-skill work was driven by (i) decline of manufacturing production work due to automation and trade pressure and (ii) office computing hollowing out clerical/administrative ranks. Both trends hit cities hardest.

**Immigration:** Polarization was equally pronounced among foreign-born and native-born non-college workers, ruling out simple supply-side immigration explanations.

**Three Mechanisms Linking Polarization to Falling Non-College Wages:** (1) Shunting non-college workers from middle-skill career occupations rewarding specialized skills into low-education occupations requiring generic skills; (2) disproportionately depressing middle-wage employment in urban labor markets, attenuating the urban non-college wage premium; and (3) creating excess supply of less-educated workers depressing non-college wages across all occupations and areas.
</summary>

URL: https://equitablegrowth.org/research-paper/navigating-the-research-on-the-impacts-of-ai-on-work-workers-and-the-labor-market

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research issue brief from the Washington Center for Equitable Growth (published May 21, 2026, authored by Chiara Chanoi) that navigates the research on AI's impacts on work, workers, and the labor market. It serves as a guide to understanding the complex, uncertain, and often conflicting academic literature on AI and labor, and introduces a companion database of AI research papers.

Key points:
- The impacts of AI are difficult to measure because work is not a monolith, AI is developing rapidly, and studies published as recently as 2023 may lack data on ChatGPT's proliferation (released November 2022). Researchers also struggle to isolate AI effects from concurrent phenomena like remote work, outsourcing, and high interest rates.
- Current research suggests the overall impact of AI will be a balance of potential benefits and harms across tasks, skills, occupations, people, places, and time. Contradictory findings exist—for example, Babina et al. (data 2010-2018) find AI flattens hierarchies by hiring more junior workers, while Azar, Gine, and Sanz-Espín (post-ChatGPT) find junior positions shrank as AI replaced junior tasks.
- The brief defines key concepts: narrow AI (only currently available type), machine learning, deep learning, generative AI, and large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Copilot.
- The popular Task-Biased Technological Change (task-based) framework breaks jobs into tasks and examines how AI impacts individual tasks, though it only produces estimates with limitations.
- O*NET (Occupational Information Network) from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics is the most popular dataset, breaking down ~1,000 occupations into tasks, though critics note it includes assumptions and isn't fully updated yearly.
- AI exposure measurement methods are discussed: Michael Webb (Stanford) matches patent language to O*NET tasks; Felten, Raj, and Seamans match AI capabilities to O*NET abilities; Eloundou, Manning, Mishkin, and Rock (OpenAI/Wharton) focus on LLM-specific exposure; Anthropic's Kunal Handa et al. measure Claude usage linked to O*NET tasks. Morgan Frank et al. find no single exposure estimate is fully accurate for predicting job losses, but combined use may improve predictive power.
- Key statistics cited: Goldman Sachs (2023) predicted AI could add 7% to global GDP over 10 years; Pew Research Center (2025) found 52% of workers worried about AI's workplace future vs. 36% hopeful; Webb estimates computer programmers have more AI-automatable tasks than 94% of occupations; Eloundou et al. estimate at least 90% of computer programming tasks can be automated/augmented by LLMs.
- A Pew survey found more workers worried than hopeful about AI in the workplace (52% vs 36%).
- Research on job displacement shows little evidence so far of large net job displacements—Bonney et al. (Census Bureau) find firms using AI replace tasks but not overall employment; Hampole et al. find AI substitutes at task level but is offset by productivity gains.
- The database allows filtering by sector (academia, industry, government, other), type of study (empirical, summary statistics, theory, literature reviews), type of data (government, O*NET, resumes/job postings, private), level of study (tasks through global), and other topics (generative AI, LLMs, job displacement, automation, augmentation, inequality, policy implications, etc.).
- Three fundamental research questions frame the field: Which workers are most vulnerable to AI's negative impacts? Who benefits most? What is the aggregate effect?
- Conclusion: Technological change through AI could have substantial economic impacts, but without deliberate policy interventions, workers might not share in those gains. Calls for federal government collection of detailed, real-time, impartial data on AI's economic impacts.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Across the research, the range of current estimates imply that the overall impact of AI on the labor market will come from the balance of potential benefits and harms felt across tasks, skills, occupations, people, places, and time."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Organizational Structure for AI-First Operations: Beyond Traditional Hierarchies ---
URL: https://www.innovativehumancapital.com/article/organizational-structure-for-ai-first-operations-beyond-traditional-hierarchies

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an academic article from the Human Capital Leadership Review (HCL Review), authored by Jonathan H. Westover, PhD, published October 26, 2025, titled "Organizational Structure for AI-First Operations: Beyond Traditional Hierarchies" (eISSN 2693-9452, doi.org/10.70175/hclreview.2020.27.1.2, Vol. 27, Issue 1).

The article examines how AI-first operations—where AI systems execute primary workflows rather than merely supporting human tasks—necessitate new organizational forms blending human oversight with algorithmic autonomy. It draws on research across technology, financial services, healthcare, and logistics sectors.

Key arguments and content:
- Traditional hierarchies built for human decision-making prove inadequate when algorithms assume core operational roles. AI-first operations are defined by three characteristics: algorithmic decision-making authority over primary workflows, continuous learning/adaptation, and human involvement structured around boundary-setting and exception handling rather than direct supervision (Davenport & Ronanki, 2018).
- AI-first operations have penetrated financial services (customer service routing), logistics (real-time routing), and healthcare (diagnostics), driven by cloud computing, machine learning advances, competitive pressure, and pandemic-compressed digital transformation.
- Structural adaptation often lags operational deployment, creating "structural drag" where new technologies operate within outdated organizational forms.

Evidence-based organizational responses identified:
1. Platform-based structural models: modular, reconfigurable teams (pods/squads) organized around data flows and algorithmic processes, replacing functional silos. Examples: Spotify's autonomous squads for content recommendation, cross-functional AI product teams, shared services platforms, marketplace models, federated governance.
2. Algorithmic governance and oversight roles: model risk management teams, ethics/fairness review boards, human-in-the-loop exception handlers, algorithmic auditors. Example: JPMorgan Chase's centralized Model Risk and Development team with multilayered oversight.
3. Hybrid team configurations and role evolution: augmentation models, relay models, collaboration models, AI trainer/supervisor roles. Example: Stitch Fix's hybrid human-AI styling model where stylist feedback trains algorithms.
4. Dynamic authority and decision rights frameworks: confidence-based escalation, risk-tiered decision frameworks, learning-phase authorities, context-triggered oversight. Example: Capital One's dynamic decision rights in credit underwriting.
5. Data stewardship and algorithmic transparency structures: Chief Data Officer roles, data product management, algorithmic explainability specialists, data ethics review. Example: Cleveland Clinic's Analytics and Data Institute with AI Ethics Committee.

Long-term adaptive capacity requires: continuous learning and improvement systems (feedback loops, dedicated improvement teams with implementation authority), distributed leadership models with coordination mechanisms (synchronization forums, shared dashboards, escalation paths), and preservation of human agency and organizational purpose through cultural investment.

Performance findings: structurally adapted AI-first organizations show faster decision cycles, improved resource utilization, adaptability, and quality improvements, while poorly managed transitions correlate with employee anxiety, decreased job satisfaction, and turnover. The article concludes that organizational design must evolve as fundamentally as the technologies reshaping operations.

References cited: Bughin et al. (2017), Davenport & Ronanki (2018), Faraj et al. (2018), Fountaine et al. (2019), Parker et al. (2016), Raisch & Krakowski (2021), Redman (2018), Wilson & Daugherty (2018).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The resulting organizational challenge is not simply technological but fundamentally structural—how do we design organizations where authority, accountability, and coordination flow through both human hierarchies and algorithmic networks simultaneously?"
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Organizational Structure and Artificial Intelligence. Modeling the Intraorganizational Response to the AI Contingency ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/0718-1876/16/6/129

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed open-access academic article published in the Journal of Theoretical and Applied Electronic Commerce Research (JTAER) in 2021 (Volume 16, Issue 6, pages 2341-2364). The paper, titled "Organizational Structure and Artificial Intelligence. Modeling the Intraorganizational Response to the AI Contingency," is authored by Ihor Rudko (Eurokleis srl, Rome), Aysan Bashirpour Bonab (University of Cassino), and Francesco Bellini (Sapienza University of Rome). The article was submitted on August 5, 2021, revised August 30, 2021, accepted September 7, 2021, and published September 13, 2021. It belongs to the special issue "Digital Resilience and Economic Intelligence in the Post-Pandemic Era" with DOI 10.3390/jtaer16060129.

The paper addresses how artificial intelligence influences organizational structure, emphasizing the role of human agency in AI-driven organizational changes. It is described as the first study to investigate the interplay between AI and organizational structure broken down by individual micro and meso components. The research used contingency theory frameworks and multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) applied to an online survey conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Key research questions addressed: (RQ1) plausible influences of AI on single organizational variables at micro and meso levels; (RQ2) how employees vary in their explicit attitudes toward AI-driven organizational changes; (RQ3) best strategies to implement AI-driven changes given potential organizational inertia and resistance.

The study hypothesized best organizational fits to the AI contingency, drawing from IT literature where AI-specific research was limited. The analysis identified four types of jobholders based on attitudes toward hypothesized organizational changes: skeptics, doubtful skeptics, optimists, and doubtful optimists (the latter consisting primarily of emerging adults). Findings showed that attitudes varied along two dimensions: affect (positive/negative) and intensity (strength). Doubtful optimists were identified as the most critical social group, able to set organizational trends and positively influence skeptics and doubtful skeptics. The main practical implication is that promoters of AI-driven organizational changes should design their communication efforts around emerging adults.

The literature review covers multiple organizational variables: job variety and job richness (micro-level), span of control (meso horizontal axis), decentralization and chain of command (meso vertical axis), and coordination mechanisms including standardization, formalization, and incentives. Key findings include that AI is expected to reduce job scope but increase job enrichment; decentralization is the leading organizational trend facilitated by IT; AI may become the ultimate substitute for hierarchy, flattening organizational structures; and organic structures are more suitable in dynamic environments (drawing on Burns and Stalker's contingency theories and Bauman's concept of 'liquid modernity').

Keywords: artificial intelligence, contingency theories, organizational structure, explicit attitudes, cultural intermediaries, organizational change.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Our findings showed doubtful optimists to be the most important group, able to set organizational trends and positively influence skeptics and doubtful skeptics. Accordingly, promoters of AI-driven organizational changes are advised to design their communication efforts around emerging adults."

--- SOURCE 4: The role of AI in changing company structures and dynamics | Databricks Blog ---
URL: https://www.databricks.com/blog/role-ai-changing-company-structures-and-dynamics

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post (by Dael Williamson and Fabian Lanz, published in the Data Strategy category) examines how generative AI is fundamentally reshaping organizational structures and dynamics. The authors identify three main focus areas for AI's impact on operating models:

**Workforce**: The post argues that middle management stands to gain the most from reinvention in the AI age. As individual contributors gain AI tools that increase their scope and efficiency, self-organizing corporate structures become more viable. The concept of a "Management Index (MI)" is introduced — the ratio of management to individual contributors — which AI could allow companies to lower sustainably (more individual contributors per manager). Examples cited include Bayer AG cutting nearly half of its management and executive positions in 2024 under its "Dynamic Shared Ownership" model, and X (formerly Twitter) supporting a growing user base despite radical headcount reduction. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy mandated that each organization increase the ratio of individual contributors to managers by at least 15% by end of Q1 2025 to flatten organizations and decrease bureaucracy. The post references Hackman's Authority Matrix (1986) to explain the shift from Management toward self-designing and self-governing teams, noting that Spotify and Stripe attempted this a decade ago but struggled — with AI now serving as the catalyst.

**Processes**: The post introduces a "Process Complexity Index (PCI)" where task complexity is rated on a logarithmic 1-5 scale (analogous to the Richter scale). AI's role is to reduce the number of tasks and/or reduce individual task complexity. Administrative processes (forms, sheets, approvals) are well-suited for AI incorporation, and combining AI-enhanced process automation with flatter structures could dramatically reduce bureaucracy. Process mining is highlighted as critical for identifying bottlenecks and making implicit processes explicit. The post notes a shift toward chaining multiple specialized AI agents (Agentic AI) rather than ever-larger monolithic models, with companies like Orby already developing this functionality. A side effect noted is that individual contributors will need to develop management skills (delegation, scoping, budget allocation) to effectively guide AI systems.

**Operations**: AI's role is to facilitate decision-making by streamlining people-process interactions. AIOps (AI for IT operations) was the obvious first choice due to IT's deterministic nature, but GenAI's LLMs and multimodal frameworks now open the door to AI decision support in qualitative domains like PeopleOps, HROps, and Embedded Finance. Operations extend beyond internal scope to out/near-sourcing, offshoring, partnerships, and supply chain coordination, where compound AI systems can enhance processes requiring extensive system coordination.

**Conclusions**: The authors emphasize there is no one-size-fits-all approach, but companies should focus on three areas: (1) re-thinking organizational structures to let AI augment workforce focus on high-value objectives, (2) AI-driven process augmentation shifting from individual use cases to end-to-end processes, and (3) operating better with less by reducing levers/processes for more effective resource use and timely decision-making. The post concludes with a promotional mention of the Databricks Data + AI Platform.
</summary>

"Having fewer managers will remove layers and flatten organizations…. If we do this work well, it will increase our teammates' ability to move fast, clarify and invigorate their sense of ownership, drive decision-making closer to the front lines where it most impacts customers (and the business), decrease bureaucracy, and strengthen our organizations' ability to make customers' lives better and easier every day." — Andy Jassy, Amazon CEO (Fortune, September 2024)

The article examines the relationship between AI technologies and human workers, particularly focusing on blue-collar and non-office workers.

Key findings from the article include:

- The article recommends a phased approach to AI implementation when AI complements human expertise, allowing workers to build foundational experience first.
- AI can both positively (reducing stress, improving job satisfaction) and negatively (reducing social interaction, potentially causing burnout and turnover) affect worker well-being, suggesting a human-centered approach to AI integration.
