## Abstract

To achieve [organizational innovation](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/organisational-innovation) in a competitive environment, firms need to focus on their human [artificial intelligence](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/computer-science/artificial-intelligence) (AI) skills. Applying a dynamic capability view and using survey [data collected](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/computer-science/collected-data) from Chinese firms, we find that technical AI skills and managerial AI skills have positive impacts on [organizational innovation](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/organisational-innovation), and that managerial AI skills have a more important impact on organizational innovation than technical AI skills. Moreover, digital organizational culture plays a positive moderating role in the relationship between human AI skills and organizational innovation. This study contributes to the literature on AI-driven innovation by theoretically and empirically clarifying the importance of human AI skills and digital organizational culture.

## Keywords

Human AI skill

; 

Organizational innovation

; 

Digital organizational culture

## Introduction

Globalization and changing technology have created a competitive business environment, prompting companies to constantly innovate (Kotsopoulos et al., 2022, Marcello et al., 2023). Innovation brings many strategic advantages to firms, such as increasing productivity, developing unique and difficult-to-imitate product features, strengthening special organizational capabilities, and triggering new and necessary strategic reconfigurations (Bahoo et al., 2023, Mariani et al., 2023). To date, there has been little dispute over whether innovation can affect the long-term survival, growth, and competitive advantages of companies (Joshi et al., 2010, Oke, Walumbwa, & Myers, 2012). The rapid development of technological innovation, information system synchronization and industrialization make it inevitable for firms to adopt AI technology. Despite this growth and ever-increasing investments in AI technologies, including natural language processing, machine/deep learning, computer vision, robotics, as well as techniques like (genetic) algorithms, swarm intelligence, speech synthesis systems, and expert systems, many firms are still unable to identify the potential business value of AI (Broekhuizen et al., 2023). Petrescu et al. (2022) found that 37% of companies incorporated AI into products and processes and less than 15% used AI-based capabilities in their work, especially in the first few years when many AI initiatives fail, and companies invested in AI (sometimes less than 50%) rarely reported significant business gains. Companies are increasingly realizing that it is only by combining digital technologies with appropriate human skills that it is possible to meet innovation challenges and thereby improve their competitive advantage (Ciarli et al., 2021).

By combing through a large number of scattered literature, it is found that more and more scholars are concerned that firms should pay attention to the cultivation of appropriate human skills in the organization when adopting AI technology (Ciarli et al., 2021, Fuller et al., 2022, Tekic and Fuller, 2023). For example, Tekic and Fuller (2023) argue that in order to achieve AI-driven innovation in an organization, it is necessary to consider and develop appropriate talent in innovation teams who have good knowledge of AI technologies and the ability to anticipate the demand for AI potential and the availability of more data. AI-enhanced human capabilities enable human-centered decision making, sensing opportunities in the environment, and anticipating changes, thereby enhancing an organization’s ability to innovate (Fuller et al., 2022). AI impacts innovation management by complementing human decision making through increasing rationality and creativity in decision making (Pietronudo et al., 2022). In knowledge-intensive industries, skills are a fundamental component that firms must invest in to accumulate and transform capabilities to meet innovation challenges (Pedraza Rodriguez et al., 2023). Broekhuizen et al. (2023) argue that organizations developing new skills to adapt to evolving digital technologies is an important step in fostering innovation.

Although previous studies have focused on the importance of human skills in the process of technology application, there is still a lack of research on the specific types of human skills that organizations need to cultivate to adapt to the application process of AI technology to promote organizational innovation. Previous research has mostly focused on the relationships between human skills and organizational outcomes (e.g., organizational performance) in traditional information technology (IT) (Mamonov & Peterson, 2021) and big data analytics contexts (Gupta et al., 2020, Mikalef and Krogstie, 2020, Patrick et al., 2020). Combining the research of Gupta et al. (2020) on analyzing human skills in the traditional big data analysis environment and Mikalef and Gupta (2021) on the classification analysis of AI capabilities, we put forward the concept of human AI skills, which refers to the ability of human beings in processing and applying AI technologies. They include technical AI skills and managerial AI skills. Technical AI skills refer to the ability of humans to develop, implement and maintain AI technologies, including the understanding and application of machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, computer vision and other related technologies. It requires skills such as data analysis, algorithm design, and programming to be able to develop and optimize AI models and apply them to solve real-world problem (Gupta et al., 2020, Patrick et al., 2020, Tekic and Fuller, 2023). Managerial AI skills refer to the ability of humans to organize and manage AI projects and teams. This includes skills in strategic planning, resource management, risk assessment and project execution (Chowdhury et al., 2022, Mikalef and Gupta, 2021). These skills can provide companies with new impetus to innovate, redesign and optimize business processes and resources (Chowdhury et al., 2022). Therefore, more empirical research is urgently needed to identify and investigate the relationship between human AI skills and organizational innovation.

Furthermore, many firms fail in digital innovation because they do not have an organizational culture that can adapt to the corresponding digital environment (Martinez Caro et al., 2020). Digital organizational culture refers to the values, beliefs and behavior patterns held within an organization in the digital era to adapt to and promote digital transformation (Grover et al., 2022, Martinez Caro et al., 2020). It is a culture that is closely aligned with technology, data, and innovation to promote flexibility, agility, and creativity in organizations in the digital environment (Martinez Caro et al., 2020). Digital organizational culture encourages employees to actively try new technologies and methods, and promotes innovation and experimentation (Haffar et al., 2023, Martinez Caro et al., 2020). Moreover, digital organizational culture focuses on the collection, analysis, and utilization of data, so that employees are motivated to use data to support decisions and actions, and use data as a basis for improvement and optimization (Grover et al., 2022). Digital organizational culture adapt to a rapidly changing digital environment by encouraging collaboration and knowledge sharing among employees, as well as emphasizing the importance of learning and continuous development (Grover et al., 2022). Previous literature on the boundary conditions of the formation of organizational innovation has primarily focused on innovation orientation (Farzaneh et al., 2022), competitive and institutional environment (Krammer, 2022), organizational resistance (Naveed et al., 2022),and technological turbulence (Jin et al., 2022), while neglecting the moderating effect of digital organizational culture.

Therefore, there is a limited understanding of the effects of human AI skills on organizational innovation and the moderating role of digital organizational culture in such a relationship. This presents an uncharted and less explored environment in which organizations will need to develop human AI skills and the corresponding cultural climate to facilitate the formation of organizational innovation. Given the limited concepts, experiences, and background development in this field, this study aims to bridge such gaps in the literature on AI-enabled innovation. This leads us to the following research questions motivating our current study: _(1) How do human AI skills affect organizational innovation? Specifically, how do technical AI skills and managerial AI skills relate to organizational innovation? (2) How does a digital organizational culture influence the relationship between human AI skills and organizational innovation?_

To address these research questions, we developed a theoretical model based on dynamic capability view to determine the impact of human AI skills on organizational innovation and to understand the moderating role of digital organizational culture in this relationship. This study makes three important contributions to the literature. First, our work contributes to understanding the importance of human AI skills: This study highlights the importance of human AI skills in the digital age by exploring the impact of AI skills on organizational innovation, and it provides a theoretical basis for how organizations can effectively apply and develop human AI skills. Second, we reveal the moderating effect of digital organizational culture on the influence of human AI skills on organizational innovation. This has theoretical implications for understanding the role and importance of organizational culture in digital transformation. Third, our research contributes to a better understanding of the current state of AI-based innovation management, its implications for future innovation practices, and adds perspectives that organizations can focus on as they face the innovation challenges of the AI era.

This is a research article published in the Journal of Business Research (September 2024, Volume 182, Article 114786) by Meng An (Ph.D. Student, South China Agricultural University), Jiabao Lin (Full Professor, South China Agricultural University), and Xin (Robert) Luo (Full Professor, University of New Mexico). The study examines the impact of human AI skills on organizational innovation, with digital organizational culture as a moderating factor.

Key findings:
- The study applies a dynamic capability view and uses survey data collected from Chinese firms.
- Both technical AI skills (ability to develop, implement, and maintain AI technologies including machine learning, deep learning, NLP, computer vision) and managerial AI skills (ability to organize and manage AI projects and teams, including strategic planning, resource management, risk assessment) have positive impacts on organizational innovation.
- Managerial AI skills have a MORE important impact on organizational innovation than technical AI skills.
- Digital organizational culture (values, beliefs, and behavior patterns held within an organization in the digital era to adapt to and promote digital transformation) plays a positive moderating role in the relationship between human AI skills and organizational innovation.
- Response surface analysis shows organizational innovation increases along a perfect balance between technical and managerial AI skills.

Background context: The study notes that 37% of companies incorporated AI into products and processes and less than 15% used AI-based capabilities in their work, with many AI initiatives failing and firms rarely reporting significant business gains. The research addresses two questions: (1) How do human AI skills affect organizational innovation? (2) How does digital organizational culture influence this relationship?

The research was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (72371105, 71873047) and the Guangdong Basic and Applied Basic Research Foundation (2023A1515011263). Measurements used a seven-point Likert scale, with measures adapted from Mikalef and Gupta (2021) for AI skills, Martinez Caro et al. (2020) for digital organizational culture. The article has been cited by 69 subsequent works, including studies on GenAI adoption, AI and enterprise total factor productivity, and AI knowledge's role in disruptive innovation and circular economy.

# The EFMD business magazine

# Embracing AI to Unleash Growth and Innovation: An Opportunity for Corporate Learning?

* [Martin Moehrle](https://globalfocusmagazine.com/author/martin-moehrle/)
* [No Comments](https://globalfocusmagazine.com/embracing-ai-to-unleash-growth-and-innovation-an-opportunity-for-corporate-learning/#respond)

![Embracing AI to Unleash Growth and Innovation: An Opportunity for Corporate Learning?](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20720'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

* [AI](https://globalfocusmagazine.com/tag/ai/), [case study](https://globalfocusmagazine.com/tag/cases-study/), [corporate learning](https://globalfocusmagazine.com/tag/corporate-learning/), [innovation](https://globalfocusmagazine.com/tag/innovation/), [soft skills](https://globalfocusmagazine.com/tag/soft-skills/)

[Download PDF](https://globalfocusmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/2026-Global-Focus-Vol20-Issue01-embracing-ai-to-unleash-growth-and-innovation.pdf)

**Executive summary.** Artificial intelligence is transforming organisations foremost through how people learn, judge, and collaborate with machines. Drawing on insights from the [2025 EFMD CLO Roundtable](https://blog.efmdglobal.org/2025/10/21/efmd-roundtable-corporate-learning/) and the cases of UBS and Siemens, the paper argues that AI elevates—not replaces—human judgment and creativity. Predictive AI sharpens decisions, while generative AI expands creative capacity, increasing the importance of context, ethics, and critical thinking. Corporate Learning therefore moves to the organisational core, evolving from content provision to strategic orchestration of human–machine collaboration and continuous learning and adaptation.

 Key takeaways

* Learning becomes strategic infrastructure: Corporate learning shifts from a support function to a central engine, shaping AI-enabled transformation, innovation, and growth.
* Human judgment gets amplified: As AI improves prediction and generation, critical thinking, contextual understanding, and ethical awareness become decisive capabilities.
* L&D must be reinvented: Learning functions evolve into ecosystem orchestrators and translators between technological, organisational, and human domains.

---

## From Hype to Responsible Use

Few technologies have captured the imagination as quickly as Artificial Intelligence. In less than three years, AI has evolved from a niche tool to a strategic imperative — cutting across industries, functions, and geographies. Yet as the pressure to adopt intensifies, the gap between technological potential and organisational readiness continues to be wide.

Against this backdrop, senior learning and development executives from over 20 global companies from four continents gathered in late September at London Business School for the 2025 EFMD CLO Roundtable. Under the title “Embracing AI to Unleash Growth and Innovation: An Opportunity for Corporate Learning?” they explored a pivotal question:

How can corporate learning not merely respond to AI-driven change — but become a driving force behind it?

At the heart of the discussion was a shared conviction: innovation through AI is less a technological challenge than an organisational one. It demands structures, skills, and mindsets that enable people to use AI responsibly and productively.

The event opened with a masterclass by Professor Keyvan Vakili (London Business School) on Identifying and Exploiting AI Opportunities. As EFMD’s Director of Corporate Services, I had the pleasure of facilitating a session to explore the role of corporate learning in accelerating AI transformation, showcasing two corporate use cases — UBS and Siemens, presented by Katarina Rosen (UBS) and Jenny Lin (Siemens), respectively.

This article synthesises the key insights from this Roundtable. It combines academic perspective and corporate practice into a single narrative: AI does not end the need for learning – it redefines it.

## Identifying and Exploiting AI Opportunities

Professor Vakili argued that productive engagement with AI requires a deep understanding of its internal logic. His central thesis: AI is not one technology, but a spectrum of cognitive systems built on two fundamental capabilities: prediction and generation.

Predictive AI enhances decision-making by improving the prediction part of it, e.g., detecting patterns, estimating probabilities, and recommending solutions in routine contexts, from credit risk models to medical diagnostics or dynamic pricing. Frequent, low-visibility decisions are prime targets for Predictive AI, and these are the hidden levers of efficiency. As prediction becomes more commoditised by using AI, judgment becomes more important.

![Identifying and exploiting ai opportunities](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20709%20240'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Generative AI, by contrast, produces new content — text, code, imagery, and ideas — reshaping the boundaries of human creativity. Creative and communication-intensive tasks offer fertile ground for Generative AI as a main source of productivity and innovation gains.

Yet both forms of AI create a new tension — *the precision–persuasion trade-off.* Predictive AI provides precision but lacks persuasion; Generative AI excels at persuasion but might lack accuracy. The implication is profound: the use of AI makes human judgment more valuable than ever.

![Precision and persuasion matrix](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20483%20355'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

AI allows the automation of tasks that require less judgment; humans can augment themselves with AI for tasks that require more judgment. As research shows, lower-skilled employees gain most from working with GenAI and therefore they are more likely to delegate tasks to it. However, they are also the most likely to overlook errors due to their lower level of expertise.

This proposes a conundrum for strategic workforce planning and talent pipelining: the tasks that junior talent usually get assigned are the ones that increasingly get automated, but given their limited context knowledge, juniors lack the judgment to properly augment AI. How and where can they then develop expertise? We can already observe a drop in job openings for career starters, whether this is only a temporary phenomenon remains to be seen. However, the development of critical thinking and judgment that normally comes with experience must become a main goal of education and traineeships. Incidentally, in his *Critique of Pure Reason*, Kant defines stupidity not as ignorance but as the absence of judgment.

For corporate learning, this broadens the mission. Learning functions must not only equip employees with the knowledge of AI tool potential, but also to critically reflect and interpret their outputs responsibly.

## The Role of Corporate Learning in AI Transformations

The deployment of AI will lead to a reconfiguration of human work. Learning, therefore, becomes the critical mechanism through which this reconfiguration takes place. Corporate learning must become an architect of human–machine collaboration and enable organisations to reinvent how they learn, decide, and create value. I introduced a framework describing four complementary arenas where corporate learning can and should accelerate AI transformation:

![Corporate learning in ai transformations](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20566%20334'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

* **Arena 1***— Learning and Development itself*: AI allows significant productivity gains along the entire learning value chain, from automated needs anticipation, rapid design of learning programmes, personalised learning journeys and tutoring at scale, through to assessing impact by monitoring vast sets of data. AI will allow a better integration of learning and work. The coming human-machine collaboration may require a fresh look at leadership and competency models. The skill sets in L&D must also evolve.
* **Arena 2** *— The Workforce:* AI and robots will automate tasks, with some jobs being more affected than others. Strategic workforce planning must identify skills (and jobs) that will erode, endure, and emerge, for L&D to offer a rich array of systematic upskilling, reskilling, and redeployment opportunities — not as one-off campaigns but as a permanent operating model. Innovations like talent marketplaces will become instrumental, as will a focus on essential human skills. This will allow staff to remain employable, provided they are willing to learn and adapt, and to regard AI as a friend, not an enemy.
* **Arena 3** *— The Business:* Businesses and enabling functions must learn to leverage data and algorithms in their own domain, e.g., pricing, logistics, R&D, or customer engagement. In addition to providing staff with basic AI literacy, L&D must orchestrate a segmented approach to capability building up to expert level by aligning learning agendas with business priorities and performance metrics. Cultural readiness may vary across businesses, and a few might require change management support throughout AI deployment.
* **Arena 4** *— The Enterprise Ecosystem and Society:* AI impacts also the corporation’s supply chain, customers, and entire business ecosystem. Corporate learning functions may be well advised to take a broader view on enablement, beyond the enterprise. In addition, it should contribute to the discourse on ethical AI and mitigating AI risks, within the organisation and beyond, and promote the responsible use of AI.

UBS and Siemens both presented a use case on AI adoption. The two companies are global leaders in their markets and have approached AI transformation in an exemplary manner, playing fully across all four arenas. However, the following use cases zoom in on UBS’ engagement in Arena 3 and Siemens’ coverage of Arena 1.

## Case Study: UBS – AI People Enablement for an AI-powered Company

UBS has approached AI not as a technology programme but as an enterprise-wide capability-building effort. The firm’s AI People Enablement initiative, jointly led by HR and Technology, illustrates how corporate learning can effectively anchor large-scale transformation.

The initiative supports the UBS ambition to become an AI-enabled institution. It focuses on both the technical and human dimensions of change—building understanding, skills, and mindset for responsible AI use across all divisions and functions.

At its core are seven workstreams, designed to reach across the entire workforce:

![Ai people enablement - 7 workstreams addressing the entire workforce](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20654%20336'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

* AI People Enablement – 7 workstreams addressing the entire workforce
* AI awareness and foundational knowledge – establishing a baseline understanding for all employees of AI concepts, risks, and opportunities.
* Leadership development – helping leaders and line managers champion AI adoption.
* Organisational transformation – helping UBS’ senior leaders design the right structures, processes, client engagement and talent strategies to enable the successful adoption of AI.
* GenAI tool proficiency – training employees to use tools effectively, including M365 Copilot and the UBS in-house AI assistant, Red.
* Expert learning – deep technical development for data and AI specialists.
* Reskilling – bridging emerging skill gaps.
* Embedding AI – into HR employee lifecycle processes such as hiring, employee listening and performance management.

A central pillar of leadership engagement is the Oxford Saïd AI Senior Leadership Journey, a multi-cohort programme for over 250 of the firm’s senior leaders. Delivered through immersive on-campus sessions, case studies, and simulations, it enables leaders to create an *AI Blueprint*, a strategic roadmap identifying where AI can deliver measurable business impact while maintaining ethical and regulatory integrity. In addition, UBS has built an AI Expert Network with industry leaders from select AI companies and academic institutions, providing strategic advisory support to the firm’s senior leaders.

Complementing this top-down engagement, UBS has an AI Champions programme, mobilising more than 1,000 employees across 20 countries so far. These champions function as internal ambassadors, sharing use cases, facilitating peer learning, and creating momentum for responsible adoption. And colleagues are benefiting from comprehensive learning offerings catered to all levels of expertise and experience, with over 170,000 trainings completed to date.

The impact of the enablement programme gets monitored at three levels: (1) the quantity and quality of AI-related learning, (2) the capabilities built regarding AI, and (3) the number of AI users and prompts, as well as surveyed AI sentiment. The internal enablement programme is accompanied by a global employer branding campaign, positioning UBS as an AI-enabled employer of choice, aiming at attracting AI-savvy talent to the bank.

The key insight from this case is clear: UBS is on an ambitious and comprehensive AI transformation journey, with corporate learning being the central mechanism to accelerate responsible and productive AI adoption.

## Case Study: Siemens – Harnessing AI for Learning and Growth

For more than 178 years, the guiding purpose of Siemens—*We create technology to transform the everyday,* *for everyone*—has shaped the company’s evolution. Today, this transformation extends to how its people learn, collaborate, and grow within a platform-based learning ecosystem.

At the heart of Siemens are its people. Supporting their ongoing development, My Learning World (MLW) serves as a global learning experience platform for over 300,000 active users, offering access to over 180,000 learning resources. MLW integrates learning paths, channels, and knowledge boards, curated by Siemens’ learning experts, into a coherent architecture that is infused with AI.

AI is not a peripheral feature; it is embedded throughout the learner and curator experience. AI Assistant Zoiee provides conversational search, guidance, and knowledge retrieval for 300,000 learners, and authoring tools, including video creation via the *SynthAIze* *Studio*, for the hundreds of content curators at Siemens.

![Ai assistant](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20725%20325'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

These tools create an environment where learning becomes both adaptive and agentic — able to interact with users in natural language, anticipate needs, and suggest next learning steps in the flow of work.

In addition, Siemens is currently introducing its *Growth Talks Bot*, an AI companion that supports people and leaders in preparing and conducting performance and development conversations.

Siemens’ long-term vision, described as the *Smart P&O Companion*, goes further: an agentic AI framework that connects the company’s people and organisational (P&O) ecosystem, linking HR systems, learning platforms, and vendor tools into one intelligent infrastructure.

The lesson from Siemens is about reframing learning as a platform for organisational intelligence. AI enables Siemens to scale personalisation and autonomy while maintaining alignment with corporate purpose. By empowering its people to invest ample time in learning, Siemens ensures they gain not just the skills for today, but the skills for life. In doing so, the company turns its learning and growth ecosystem into a strategic asset, one capable of continuously sensing, adapting, and evolving, alongside the business.

## Synthesis: What We Can Learn from the UBS and Siemens cases

Despite operating in very different industries, the UBS and Siemens cases converge on three critical principles.

*First, learning is strategic in nature.* At UBS, L&D operates at the intersection of HR, technology, and business, shaping how the firm becomes AI-powered. At Siemens, learning platforms are embedded into the company’s digital backbone. In both cases, learning is not reactive but constitutive.

*Second, leadership and culture are the multipliers of adoption.* UBS invests heavily in leadership journeys that translate AI strategy into behavioural change. Siemens fosters community-based learning to sustain experimentation.

*Third, new roles are emerging for Learning and Development.* L&D professionals must evolve from content creators to content curators, and to ecosystem orchestrators, integrating data, platforms, and partnerships. They also function as translators between technological and human domains, ensuring that ethical, legal, and cultural dimensions remain visible.

## Conclusion: From Technology to Transformation

Artificial Intelligence’s most profound impact will be in how people think, decide, and create differently. AI does not diminish the human role, it redefines it. Predictive systems enhance decisions but elevate the value of judgment. Generative systems accelerate creativity but heighten the need for context knowledge.

Corporate Learning moves to the very centre of the organisation. It becomes an engine for adaptation. As seen at UBS and Siemens, when learning functions operate as strategic orchestrators, they not only enable technology adoption; they also shape the very trajectory of innovation and growth.

Eventually, this means that Corporate Learning must reinvent itself. It is no longer about providing learning but about enabling learning. The age of artificial intelligence is, at heart, an age of amplified learning. Organisations that cultivate curiosity, critical inquiry, and ethical awareness will lead it.

args.summary:
This article from EFMD Global Focus Magazine, written by Martin Moehrle (EFMD's Director of Corporate Services), explores how corporate learning can embrace AI to drive growth and innovation. It synthesizes insights from the 2025 EFMD CLO Roundtable held at London Business School, where senior L&D executives from over 20 global companies across four continents gathered in late September to discuss how corporate learning can become a driving force behind AI-driven change rather than merely responding to it.

The article presents a framework for AI transformation across four arenas: (1) Learning and Development itself, (2) The Workforce, (3) The Business, and (4) The Enterprise Ecosystem and Society. It features two corporate case studies. UBS's AI People Enablement initiative, jointly led by HR and Technology, uses seven workstreams including AI awareness, leadership development, GenAI tool proficiency, and reskilling. Key elements include the Oxford Saïd AI Senior Leadership Journey (for 250+ senior leaders), an AI Champions programme with 1,000+ employees across 20 countries, and over 170,000 trainings completed. Siemens' My Learning World (MLW) platform serves 300,000+ active users with 180,000+ learning resources, featuring the AI Assistant Zoiee and video creation tool SynthAIze Studio, plus a planned Growth Talks Bot and Smart P&O Companion framework.

Key takeaways include: learning becomes strategic infrastructure; human judgment gets amplified by AI; and L&D must be reinvented as ecosystem orchestrators and translators. The article concludes that AI elevates rather than replaces human judgment and creativity — predictive AI sharpens decisions while generative AI expands creative capacity, making context, ethics, and critical thinking increasingly important. Corporate learning must evolve from content provision to strategic orchestration of human-machine collaboration.

## Abstract

Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications streamline workflows, automate tasks, and require adaptive strategies for effective integration into business processes. This research explores the transformative influence of AI on various industries, such as software engineering, automation, education, accounting, mining, legal services, and media. We investigate the relationship between technological advancements and the job market to identify relevant skills for individuals and organizations for implementing and managing AI systems and human–machine interactions necessary for actual and future jobs. We focus on the essential adaptations for individuals and organizations to flourish in this era. To bridge the gap between AI-driven demands and the existing capabilities of the workforce, we employ the Rapid Review methodology to explore the integration of AI in businesses, identify crucial skill sets, analyze challenges, and propose solutions in this dynamic age. We searched the Scopus database, screening a total of 39 articles, of which we selected 20 articles for this systematic review. The inclusion criteria focused on conference papers and journal articles from 2020 or later and written in English. The selected articles offer valuable insights into the impact of AI on education, business, healthcare, robotics, manufacturing, and automation across diverse sectors, as well as providing perspectives on the evolving landscape of expertise. The findings underscore the importance of crucial skill sets, such as technical proficiency and adaptability, to successfully adopt AI. Businesses respond strategically by implementing continuous skill adaptation and ethical technology to address challenges. The paper concludes by emphasizing the imperative of balanced skill development, proactive education, and strategic integration to navigate the profound impact of AI on the workforce effectively.

## 1. Introduction

In the ever-evolving landscape of technology, Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a powerful force transforming industries worldwide [Wamba-Taguimdje et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B39-admsci-14-00127) ([2020](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B39-admsci-14-00127)). To truly comprehend the ground-breaking impact of AI, we need to explore its fundamental building blocks, including neural networks, which are like the digital counterparts of brains, enabling computers to learn and make decisions, much like humans. Machine learning is another crucial aspect where computers improve their abilities and adaptability without explicit programming ([Kumar et al. 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B27-admsci-14-00127)). At the same time, Big Data analytics involves navigating vast amounts of data to uncover insights. Deep learning, a form of machine learning, uses neural networks to tackle complex problems. These elements collectively indicate AI’s multifaceted nature, redefining traditional notions of software engineering and execution ([Kumar et al. 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B27-admsci-14-00127)). This transformation extends beyond machines; it is about reshaping how we work and what we work on. AI applications are used in various sectors to optimize workflow, automate routine tasks, and improve decision-making ([Anagnoste et al. 2021](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B2-admsci-14-00127); [Brown and Berzin 2021](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B7-admsci-14-00127)). In the robotics industry, the emergence of chatbots enables natural interaction between humans and digital systems, highlighting the shifting dynamics of human-to-robot and robot-to-robot collaboration in the workplace ([Anagnoste et al. 2021](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B2-admsci-14-00127)). The educational sector is also going through a paradigm shift, focusing on expediting skill growth through AI-driven learning possibilities ([Faraj 2022](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B15-admsci-14-00127)), impacting the teaching and learning process. As universities struggle to fulfill their role in the digital age, preparing students for a dynamically changing job market becomes critical ([Dos Santos et al. 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B14-admsci-14-00127); [Faraj 2022](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B15-admsci-14-00127)).

AI technologies—such as ChatGPT—already significantly impact various sectors. AI enhances diagnostics, personalized medicine, and patient care in healthcare through advanced algorithms and conversational agents. The finance sector benefits from AI in automating fraud detection, risk analysis, and providing personalized investment advice. Retail and e-commerce are leveraging AI to optimize supply chains, personalize customer experiences and create targeted marketing content. AI improves efficiency and quality control in manufacturing through automation and predictive analytics. Education is being reshaped by AI through personalized learning and intelligent tutoring systems, with ChatGPT assisting in student guidance and material customization. Human Resources is seeing improvements in candidate screening and employee engagement with AI-driven solutions. Lastly, customer service is being revolutionized by AI-driven chatbots and virtual assistants, which handle complex inquiries and reduce the burden on human representatives. These sector-specific applications underscore AI’s broad and transformative impact across different industries ([George et al. 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B20-admsci-14-00127)). [Usman et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B38-admsci-14-00127) ([2024](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B38-admsci-14-00127)) highlight that the widespread adoption of AI brings about notable ethical, social, and economic issues, including job displacement, privacy risks, and algorithm biases.

In this context, businesses are increasingly turning to AI for development and cost reduction, leading to organizational reforms ([Kumar et al. 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B27-admsci-14-00127)). However, there is still much to be understood about the impact of AI adoption on employees’ work outcomes. In this dynamic AI-driven work environment, job crafting—the process by which employees personalize their job roles to better fit their interests, skills, and values, enhancing job satisfaction and engagement—appears as a critical adaptability mechanism ([Cheng et al. 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B11-admsci-14-00127); [He et al. 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B22-admsci-14-00127)). In the post-pandemic period, we have witnessed the increased adoption of Robotic Process Automation (RPA) in accounting, highlighting AI’s transformational potential ([Lui and Shum 2022](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B30-admsci-14-00127)). Industries such as services ([He et al. 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B22-admsci-14-00127)) and mining ([Chirgwin 2021](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B12-admsci-14-00127)) are also undergoing significant shifts toward automation, improving productivity while raising concerns about job security and skill development ([Chirgwin 2021](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B12-admsci-14-00127); [He et al. 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B22-admsci-14-00127)). Professional services companies are utilizing digital technology and AI for skill-based planning, stressing innovation and service quality ([Baral et al. 2022](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B5-admsci-14-00127)).

Robots and automation are transforming operations in the manufacturing industry, creating a demand for skilled workers ([Bal 2021](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B4-admsci-14-00127)). The impact of these automation technologies on jobs is a concern in various industries and deserves careful consideration ([Filippi et al. 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B17-admsci-14-00127)). The advance of AI is bringing new changes in the job market, with almost all occupations being somehow impacted by AI adoption ([Frey and Osborne 2017](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B19-admsci-14-00127)). The increase in technological unemployment ([Lima et al. 2021](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B29-admsci-14-00127)) and changes in the skills demanded from workers ([Lima et al. 2021](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B29-admsci-14-00127)) emphasizes the role of robots and autonomous systems in enhancing human capacity in different types of occupations ([O’Donovan et al. 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B32-admsci-14-00127)). The World Economic Forum has identified the shortage of digital skills as a substantial obstacle, given the digitalization and integration of robotics across industries ([Jurczuk and Florea 2022](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B25-admsci-14-00127)).

In this work, we investigate the relationship between technological advancements and the evolving demand of the job market, focusing on the essential adaptations and developments necessary for individuals and organizations to adopt, manage, and interact with AI systems. Our research is focused on the growing gap between the demands of the job market, which are increasingly shaped by AI technologies, and the current capabilities of the workforce. As industries continue to adopt AI, there is a risk of a mismatch between the skills that employers require and the skills that employees possess ([Dos Santos et al. 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B14-admsci-14-00127)). This can lead to inefficiencies in the workforce and job displacement ([Bukartaite and Hooper 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B8-admsci-14-00127); [Lui and Shum 2022](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B30-admsci-14-00127)), making it difficult to integrate AI into various sectors fully. Our investigation aims to explore the skills demanded for implementing AI in organizations.

This work employs the Rapid Review methodology ([Cartaxo et al. 2018](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B9-admsci-14-00127)) to address this critical issue, offering a comprehensive analysis of integrating AI technologies into business operations and workforces across various industries, such as software engineering, automation, education, accounting, mining, legal services, and media. We analyzed the Scopus database, retrieving 20 articles for in-depth analysis. The choice of RR as the methodology is justified by its ability to synthesize existing research, providing timely and relevant insights quickly. Unlike Systematic Literature Reviews, which can take six months to two years, RRs typically take about five weeks, allowing for a faster response to rapidly evolving technological trends. This expedited process is crucial for understanding the swift advancements and their implications in AI technology, ensuring that businesses and stakeholders can make informed decisions based on the latest evidence. By defining broader research questions a priori, RR enables a more targeted search and efficient extraction of precise information from selected studies, maintaining academic rigor while significantly reducing the time required for comprehensive analysis [Khangura et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B26-admsci-14-00127) ([2012](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B26-admsci-14-00127)).

The expected results of our research include a detailed understanding of how businesses integrate AI into their workforce, the specific skill sets crucial to successful AI adoption, the challenges that hinder this integration, and a diverse set of strategies businesses employ to address these challenges. We expect to identify patterns, trends, and variations across different industries, offering a comprehensive picture of the current landscape of AI integration and its impact on workforce dynamics. We aim to contribute to the literature by providing significant insights, identifying challenges, and proposing potential solutions in AI and the future of skills. This contribution includes informing strategies for enhancing workforce readiness in the AI era and facilitating a smoother integration of AI into the workplace.

The structure of this work is organized as follows: [Section 2](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#sec2-admsci-14-00127) explores the existing literature to examine the intersection of artificial intelligence and future skills. [Section 3](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#sec3-admsci-14-00127) describes the application of the Rapid Review methodology in detail. [Section 4](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#sec4-admsci-14-00127) presents the study’s findings. [Section 5](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#sec5-admsci-14-00127) addresses the research questions, providing comprehensive responses. Finally, [Section 6](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#sec6-admsci-14-00127) presents the final remarks and summarizes our study’s conclusions.

## 2. Literature

AI is no longer a future concept but is actively utilized in various domains. [Soni et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B37-admsci-14-00127) ([2020](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B37-admsci-14-00127)) assert that nearly every industry employs AI technologies, encompassing healthcare, finance, gaming, and more. The adoption of AI is attributed to factors such as advancements in computer technology, enhanced transparency through code sharing, and the availability of open-source software. They propose a global trend where companies proudly identify themselves as “AI companies”, underscoring AI’s significant role in today’s society. Progressing further, [Soni et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B37-admsci-14-00127) ([2020](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B37-admsci-14-00127)) identify multiple ways AI positively influences businesses. They emphasize the quick identification of patterns in big data, rapid visualization and analytics, improved product design, and the provision of accurate insights. These advantages are anticipated to introduce novel service levels, increase profits, expand businesses, and enhance efficiency and cost structures. The study also establishes a connection between the success of AI and the broader concept of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, or Industry 4.0, highlighting AI’s pivotal role in advancing other technologies. The discourse subsequently transitions to AI startups, acknowledging the United States as a prominent player in AI development and the growing interest from investors. [Soni et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B37-admsci-14-00127) ([2020](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B37-admsci-14-00127)) recognize that AI heavily relies on software that is susceptible to vulnerabilities. They identify obstacles concerning systemic failure modes, repeatability, transparency, and explainability in AI systems. Despite progress, there are instances where deep learning algorithms yield unreliable outcomes. Additionally, [Soni et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B37-admsci-14-00127) ([2020](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B37-admsci-14-00127)) briefly touches upon ethical challenges in AI, encompassing trust, bias, and ethics issues. These aspects deserve attention for the commercial utilization of AI applications. Lastly, the research indirectly indicates the challenge of a shortage of skilled professionals in AI. As the adoption of AI grows, so does the demand for talent in this domain.

[Rožman et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B35-admsci-14-00127) ([2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B35-admsci-14-00127)) present a comprehensive analysis of the transformative impact that artificial intelligence has on education. They strongly advocate for educational institutions to adapt to these changes. Specifically, they investigate students’ perspectives regarding the emerging job opportunities in the Data and AI Cluster, underscoring the essential role of analytical thinking, problem-solving skills, and collaborative work in preparing students for a rapidly evolving job market. AI is a valuable asset in education, simplifying tasks and customizing learning experiences. [Rožman et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B35-admsci-14-00127) ([2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B35-admsci-14-00127)) emphasize the importance of grasping numerical concepts and understanding data to enable students to thrive in an information-driven world. However, challenges loom, including concerns about privacy and potential biases. Failure to address these issues can hinder the seamless integration of AI into daily work routines. To overcome these obstacles and promote the effective adoption of AI, practical strategies are recommended by [Rožman et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B35-admsci-14-00127) ([2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B35-admsci-14-00127)). Educational institutions should provide students with a solid foundation in AI knowledge, integrate AI concepts into regular coursework, and ensure that students possess proficiency in handling quantitative information. In addition, it is crucial to cultivate adaptable and AI-ready skills to build a versatile workforce. Addressing privacy concerns and promoting fairness are vital components of this endeavor. [Rožman et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B35-admsci-14-00127) ([2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B35-admsci-14-00127)) propose that by implementing these strategies, educational institutions can fully exploit the potential of AI, leading to a more streamlined and efficient learning experience for educators and students. The study acts as a guiding compass, navigating the education path in a world where AI is integral to the educational journey.

[Franken and Wattenberg](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B18-admsci-14-00127) ([2019](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B18-admsci-14-00127)) explore the profound impact of Artificial Intelligence on the industrial workforce. They explore how AI applications, such as robotics and automation, drive transformative changes. The authors emphasize that AI affects algorithms and significantly influences people and organizational structures in various tasks, ranging from production work to management. [de Lima](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B13-admsci-14-00127) ([2021](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B13-admsci-14-00127)) proposes the development of a model designed to enable the collaborative assessment of the impact of AI and automation technologies on employment. Employing the Soft Design Science Research methodology, he introduced two innovative models. The first model uses crowd computing to gather comprehensive insights into the effects of automation technologies across various occupations. The second model utilizes groupware to facilitate a collaborative evaluation of the impact of specific technologies within an organization. [Franken and Wattenberg](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B18-admsci-14-00127) ([2019](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B18-admsci-14-00127)) envision AI to act independently, support human tasks, optimize resource usage, and introduce novel working models. They anticipate AI’s autonomy. Regarding skills, the research underscores that success in the era of digitalization depends more on the adaptability of employees and executives than on technology or investment. The authors highlight the need for skills such as understanding AI applications, ensuring secure and transparent AI solutions, and grasping data-driven business models. Strategies are suggested to address concerns about job displacement and the possible societal consequences of AI, including reorganizing management, fostering cooperation, and prioritizing ongoing qualifications. The complexities of the digitalized working world call for flexible organizational structures, less hierarchical settings, and participative leadership. [Franken and Wattenberg](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B18-admsci-14-00127) ([2019](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127#B18-admsci-14-00127)) provide practical examples of AI applications, such as predictive maintenance and chatbots, to illustrate efficiency gains and improved customer experiences. However, they cautiously discuss potential risks related to data security and privacy. In conclusion, the authors stress the necessity of reimagining the role of people, work design, and organizational structures in the face of rapid digitization. They view AI not as a threat, but as a tool to enhance human work.

These works make it clear that while adopting AI brings numerous benefits across various sectors, it also presents several challenges that must be addressed. The subsequent section will outline the methodology used in this research to review the literature and provide a comprehensive understanding of these challenges and strategies to overcome them.

This is an academic article from MDPI's journal "Administrative Sciences" (Adm. Sci.) 2024, Vol. 14, Issue 6, Article 127, titled "AI in the Workplace: A Systematic Review of Skill Transformation in the Industry." Published on June 16, 2024 (submitted May 8, 2024; revised and accepted June 12, 2024), the open-access review article is authored by Leili Babashahi, Carlos Eduardo Barbosa, Yuri Lima, Alan Lyra, Herbert Salazar, Matheus Argôlo, Marcos Antonio de Almeida, and Jano Moreira de Souza, all affiliated with the Program of Systems and Computer Engineering at Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro, Brazil (with Barbosa also at the Centro de Análises de Sistemas Navais, Brazilian Navy). DOI: 10.3390/admsci14060127. The article has 94,927 views and 131 citations and belongs to the Special Issue "Innovations, Projects, Challenges and Changes in A Digital World."

The research explores AI's transformative influence on industries (software engineering, automation, education, accounting, mining, legal services, and media), investigating the relationship between technological advancements and the job market to identify skills needed for implementing and managing AI systems and human-machine interactions. Using the Rapid Review (RR) methodology—which takes about five weeks versus six months to two years for systematic reviews—the authors searched the Scopus database, screening 39 articles and selecting 20 for in-depth analysis (inclusion criteria: conference papers and journal articles from 2020 or later, written in English).

Key findings include: critical skill sets for AI adoption include technical proficiency and adaptability; businesses respond to AI adoption challenges through continuous skill adaptation and ethical technology implementation; AI applications span healthcare (diagnostics, personalized medicine), finance (fraud detection, risk analysis), retail/e-commerce (supply chain optimization), manufacturing (automation, predictive analytics), education (personalized learning), HR (candidate screening, engagement), and customer service (chatbots). The paper highlights concerns about job displacement, privacy risks, and algorithm biases from widespread AI adoption, and emphasizes the need for balanced skill development, proactive education, and strategic integration. Keywords: automation, skill development, workforce dynamics, artificial intelligence, technological advancements.

The literature review covers works by Soni et al. (2020) on AI adoption across industries and the Fourth Industrial Revolution/Industry 4.0; Rožman et al. (2023) on AI's impact on education emphasizing analytical thinking, problem-solving, and collaborative work; Franken and Wattenberg (2019) on AI's impact on industrial workforce emphasizing adaptability of employees and executives over technology or investment; and de Lima (2021) on models for assessing AI and automation's impact on employment using Soft Design Science Research methodology.
args.key_excerpts: "The findings underscore the importance of crucial skill sets, such as technical proficiency and adaptability, to successfully adopt AI. Businesses respond strategically by implementing continuous skill adaptation and ethical technology to address challenges."

# Explaining Job Polarization: Routine-Biased Technological Change and Offshoring

* [Maarten Goos](https://research.tilburguniversity.edu/en/persons/maarten-goos/)
* , Alan Manning
* , [Anna Salomons](https://research.tilburguniversity.edu/en/persons/anna-salomons/)

Research output: Contribution to journal › Article › Scientific › peer-review

## Abstract

This paper documents the pervasiveness of job polarization in 16 Western European countries over the period 1993-2010. It then develops and estimates a framework to explain job polarization using routine-biased technological change and offshoring. This model can explain much of both total job polarization and the split into within-industry and between-industry components.

args.summary:
This is a Semantic Scholar record for the academic paper "Explaining Job Polarization: Routine-Biased Technological Change and Offshoring" by Maarten Goos, Alan Manning, and Anna Salomons, published in 2014 in The American Economic Review (Volume 104, pages 2509-2526). DOI: 10.1257/AER.104.8.2509.

The paper documents the pervasiveness of job polarization across 16 Western European countries over the period 1993-2010. It develops and estimates a framework to explain job polarization using routine-biased technological change (RBTC) and offshoring. The model explains much of both total job polarization and the split into within-industry and between-industry components.

The paper has 1,977 citations and includes 6 figures/tables (tables 1-4 and two figures). Key citing works include studies on job polarization in the UK, Sweden, Greece, developing economies, Korea, and the US. Important references include earlier work by the same authors (Goos & Manning 2004 on rising polarization of work in Britain; Goos, Manning & Salomons 2009 and 2010 on job polarization in Europe), work by Michaels, Natraj & Van Reenen (2014) on ICT and skill demand polarization across 11 countries, Autor & Dorn (2013) on low-skill service job growth and US labor market polarization, and Acemoglu & Autor (2011) on the skill-biased technological change hypothesis. Related citing research examines the links between ICT, offshoring, firm-level dynamics, and job polarization across various national and regional contexts.

# The Growth of Low Skill Service Jobs and the Polarization of the U.S. Labor Market

We offer an integrated explanation and empirical analysis of the polarization of U.S. employment and wages between 1980 and 2005, and the concurrent growth of low skill service occupations. We attribute polarization to the interaction between consumer preferences, which favor variety over specialization, and the falling cost of automating routine, codifiable job tasks. Applying a spatial equilibrium model, we derive, test, and confirm four implications of this hypothesis. Local labor markets that were specialized in routine activities differentially adopted information technology, reallocated low skill labor into service occupations (employment polarization), experienced earnings growth at the tails of the distribution (wage polarization), and received inflows of skilled labor.

URL: https://ideas.repec.org/a/ucp/jpolec/doi10.1086-705716.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a RePEc/IDEAS bibliographic record for the academic paper "Robots and Jobs: Evidence from US Labor Markets" by Daron Acemoglu (MIT) and Pascual Restrepo, published in the Journal of Political Economy, vol. 128(6), pages 2188-2244, in 2020 (DOI: 10.1086/705716; Handle: RePEc:ucp:jpolec:doi:10.1086/705716). The paper has received 1,571 citations.

Key findings of the study: The authors study the effects of industrial robots on US labor markets. Theoretically, robots may reduce employment and wages, and their local impacts can be estimated using variation in exposure to robots (defined from industry-level robotics advances and local industry employment). They find robust negative effects of robots on employment and wages across commuting zones. Areas most exposed to robots after 1990 showed no differential trends before then, and robots' impact is distinct from other capital and technologies. Specifically, one more robot per thousand workers reduces the employment-to-population ratio by 0.2 percentage points and wages by 0.42%.

The page also lists two earlier working paper versions (NBER Working Paper 23285, 2017, and Boston University Institute for Economic Development Working Paper dp-297, 2017). The paper is classified under JEL codes J23 (Labor Demand) and J24 (Human Capital; Skills; Occupational Choice; Labor Productivity), and is featured on ReplicationWiki.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents the NBER working paper "Robots and Jobs: Evidence from US Labor Markets" by Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo, which analyzes the effect of increased industrial robot usage between 1990 and 2007 on US local labor markets. The study uses a model in which robots compete against human labor in production tasks, showing that robots may reduce employment and wages. The local labor market effects are estimated by regressing changes in employment and wages on robot exposure, defined from national robot penetration into industries and local employment distribution across industries. Key findings include: (1) large and robust negative effects of robots on employment and wages across commuting zones; (2) commuting zones most exposed to robots post-1990 show no differential trends before 1990; (3) robot effects are distinct from imports from China and Mexico, decline of routine jobs, offshoring, other IT capital, and total capital stock. Specifically, one more robot per thousand workers reduces the employment-to-population ratio by approximately 0.18-0.34 percentage points and wages by 0.25-0.5 percent. The paper was later published in the Journal of Political Economy, vol 128(6), pages 2188-2244 (2020), DOI: 10.1086/705716. --- SOURCE 5: Robots and jobs: Evidence from the US | CEPR ---
URL: https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/robots-and-jobs-evidence-us

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a VoxEU column by Pascual Restrepo (Postdoctoral Fellow, Cowles Foundation, Yale University) and Daron Acemoglu (MIT Institute Professor) published on April 10, 2017, discussing their research (Acemoglu and Restrepo 2017, NBER Working Paper No. 23285) on the impact of industrial robots on employment and wages in US local labour markets between 1990 and 2007.

The article addresses the growing concern about technological unemployment, referencing Keynes' 1930 prediction of "technological unemployment." It notes various estimates of automation risk: Frey and Osborne (2013) estimated 47% of US workers at risk of automation, McKinsey claimed 45%, the World Bank estimated 57% for OECD, while Arntz et al. (2016) argued only 9% of OECD jobs are at risk.

Key findings from the research:
- Industrial robots are defined by the International Federation of Robotics as "an automatically controlled, reprogrammable, and multipurpose machine," excluding software and single-function machines.
- Industrial robots in the US and Western Europe quadrupled between 1993 and 2007. The IFR estimates 1.5-1.75 million robots in operation currently, potentially rising to 4-6 million by 2025.
- Robot usage is concentrated: automotive industry (39% of robots), electronics (19%), metal products (9%), and plastic/chemicals (9%).
- The study uses commuting zones as local labour markets and measures exposure to robots based on national industry penetration weighted by local employment shares.
- To address endogeneity concerns, the researchers used the spread of robots in other advanced economies as an instrument, similar to how Autor et al. (2013) and Bloom et al. (2016) treated Chinese import increases.
- Baseline estimates: one extra robot per 1,000 workers reduced the local employment-to-population ratio by 0.37 percentage points and wages by 0.73%, equivalent to 6.2 workers losing jobs per robot.
- Allowing for trade between commuting zones reduces estimates to 0.34 percentage points lower employment-to-population ratio and 0.5% lower wages.
- Accounting for spillovers to non-tradable industries further reduces estimates to 0.18 percentage points and 0.25% respectively (about three workers losing jobs per robot).
- Results are robust to controlling for capital intensity, IT capital, Chinese and Mexican import exposure, routine job decline, and offshoring.
- Employment effects are strongest for routine manual, blue-collar, assembly occupations, and workers with less than college education, but no group showed positive impacts.
- The researchers estimate robots caused 360,000 to 670,000 job losses in the US between 1990 and 2007.
- Under BCG's aggressive scenario (robots quadrupling by 2025), this would imply a 0.94-1.76 percentage point lower employment-to-population ratio and 1.3-2.6% lower wage growth between 2015 and 2025.
- The authors conclude that while effects are significant, the findings do not support the view that robots will make most jobs disappear or humans largely redundant.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We are being afflicted with a new disease of which some readers may not have heard the name, but of which they will hear a great deal in the years to come, namely, technological unemployment." (Keynes 1930)
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Tasks, Automation, and the Rise in U.S. Wage Inequality ---
URL: https://ideas.repec.org/a/wly/emetrp/v90y2022i5p1973-2016.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an IDEAS/RePEc bibliography page for the academic paper "Tasks, Automation, and the Rise in U.S. Wage Inequality" by Daron Acemoglu (MIT) and Pascual Restrepo (Boston University), published in Econometrica, Vol. 90(5), pages 1973-2016, September 2022 (DOI: 10.3982/ECTA19815; Handle: RePEc:wly:emetrp:v:90:y:2022:i:5:p:1973-2016).

KEY FINDINGS FROM THE ABSTRACT:
- Between 50% and 70% of changes in the U.S. wage structure over the last four decades are accounted for by relative wage declines of worker groups specialized in routine tasks in industries experiencing rapid automation.
- The authors develop a conceptual framework where tasks across industries are allocated to different types of labor and capital; automation expands the set of tasks performed by capital, displacing worker groups from jobs where they have comparative advantage.

--- SOURCE 13: Reading Companion: Acemoglu & Restrepo, The Task Model of the Labor Share ---
URL: https://www.mikekonczal.com/blogs_2026_07_AI_uses/reading_companion_AR_labor_share.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## The Task Model of the Labor Share: A Comprehensive Guide

This webpage is a detailed "Reading Companion" that reconstructs, from first principles, the labor-share formula at the heart of Acemoglu & Restrepo's influential 2018 and 2019 papers on automation and labor ("The Race between Man and Machine" in the *American Economic Review* (2018) and "Automation and New Tasks" in the *Journal of Economic Perspectives* (2019)).

### Core Formula and Framework
The central equation for the labor share of value added is:
s_L = 1 / [1 + (1-Γ(I,N))/Γ(I,N) × ((R/A_K)/(W/A_L))^(1-σ)]

The framework models a final good assembled from a continuum of tasks indexed over interval [N-1, N], each produced by either labor or capital. The single structural assumption is monotone comparative advantage (γ_L(z)/γ_K(z) increasing in z), which yields a clean sorting of tasks into capital and labor regions separated by a threshold. Key variables:
- **I** = automation frontier (tasks capital can technically perform)
- **N** = new-task frontier (high-index tasks where labor has advantage)
- **σ** = elasticity of substitution (estimated below 1, ~0.8)
- **Γ(I,N)** = labor task content (share of comparative advantage in labor region)
- **W/A_L** and **R/A_K** = effective factor prices

### Key Derivation Steps
The ten steps move from production technology through competitive pricing, threshold determination, CES demand, revenue shares, and price substitution to arrive at the final formula. A critical distinction separates the *technology* frontier I from the *cost* cutoff Ĩ (where effective costs equalize); the papers assume automation is cost-effective wherever feasible (I < Ĩ). Two technology shifts move labor's region: **automation** (rise in I, shrinks labor share via displacement effect) and **new tasks** (rise in N, grows it via reinstatement effect). The full CES representation shows Γ is a technology-determined share parameter and Π = (B_L + B_K)^(1/(σ-1)) is total factor productivity.

### Key Results
- **Displacement effect**: Automation always cuts the labor share of value added, even when productivity rises
- **Reinstatement effect**: New tasks raise the labor share; history kept shares stable because reinstatement offset displacement (0.48%/yr displacement vs 0.47% reinstatement in 1947–1987)
- **Substitution effect is weak** because σ<1, so the labor-share story runs through task content, not prices
- **So-so technologies**: automation that displaces while delivering small productivity gains (self-checkout, phone menus) is unambiguously bad for labor

### Application to AI Debate
The page applies the framework to current AI debates, analyzing what AI does to each variable:
- **I**: AI expands the automation frontier into cognitive tasks (unlike routine-task robots), with exposure rising with wages/education. Feasible ≠ adopted; Acemoglu's 2024 accounting takes only ~quarter of ~20% exposed US tasks as cost-effective within a decade
- **N**: Unknown and exogenous in the model—this is where forecasts live. Candidate channels include direct new tasks (model trainers, evaluators), cheaper complements (ATM story), and Autor's expertise channel (AI extending expertise down skill ladder)
- **σ**: Possibly rising above 1 as AI output becomes interchangeable, which would flip the sign of the price channel
- **R/A_K**: Collapsing for cognitive tasks at unprecedented speed, dragging adoption cutoff toward the frontier
- **W/A_L**: Augmentation (Copilot-style) evidence shows 14–15% productivity gains concentrated among novices (Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond customer-support study; Noy & Zhang writing; Peng et al. coding), raising wages but barely moving the share

### Four Scenarios for s_L Evolution
A) **So-so automation** (Acemoglu's modal case): modest labor share decline, stagnant wages, disappointing TFP
B) **Rapid displacement**: sharp share decline, income concentrates on capital, wages fall for exposed groups even amid GDP growth
C) **Augmentation & reinstatement** (Autor/Brynjolfsson): stable or rising share, wage inequality compresses, middle class rebuilt around AI-extended expertise
D) **Overshoot & self-correction**: labor share falls then recovers via endogenous innovation dynamics; fails if innovation frontier shifts toward automation or policy blunts price signals (US tax code tilt toward capital being the standing example)

### Historical Context
The papers answered three stylized facts: falling US labor share (mid-60s to high-50s percent), productivity-pay gap since ~1980, and wage polarization (Autor-Levy-Murnane routine-task automation). The framework reframed labor-share debate from price-driven to task-content-driven, gave reinstatement a formal home, made stagnant wages a prediction, and resolved a growth-theory puzzle (how automation coexists with Kaldor facts—equal I and N growth is equivalent to labor-augmenting change). The lineage runs from Ricardo's 1821 "On Machinery" recantation through Keynes's "technological unemployment" (1930) to Leontief's horses, with the papers directly answering Leontief: humans, unlike horses, acquire comparative advantage in new tasks. Within labor economics, the papers completed a handoff from the Katz-Murphy skills/SBTC canonical model to a task framework with general equilibrium, and the follow-on 2022 *Econometrica* paper attributed 50–70% of US wage-structure change since 1980 to task displacement. The framework is explicitly competitive/demand-side, omitting monopsony, bargaining, and rent-sharing institutions.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The labor share is now literally the fraction of task revenue that falls in the labor region. Every result in both papers is a statement about how technology moves that region and reprices what is inside it.", "Automation always cuts the labor share of value added. This is the displacement effect, and it holds even though Π rises.", "Every claim anyone makes about AI and the labor share is, whether they know it or not, a claim about which of these AI moves, in which direction, and how fast.", "The difference between workers and horses is that humans acquire comparative advantage in new tasks, and horses did not.", "Whether we get C instead of B is, on the Brynjolfsson 'Turing Trap' reading, a design and policy choice about the direction of innovation, not a fact about the technology."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:

This webpage is from Scientific Research Publishing (SCIRP), an academic publishing platform, and displays a citation record for the influential work by Autor, D.H., Levy, F. and Murnane, R.J. (2003) "The Skill Content of Recent Technological Change: An Empirical Investigation," published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics, 118, 1279-1333. The page shows that this seminal article has been cited by a paper by Francisco Parro titled "Private Incentives for Specialization in a Changing and Unpredictable Labor Market," published in Theoretical Economics Letters (Vol.5 No.2, March 25, 2015).

The citing paper's abstract examines how labor market uncertainty arising from technological change influences private incentives for specialization. Key findings: in a world of risk-averse agents, technologies generating a positive covariance of wages across sectors or tasks strengthen incentives for specialization, whereas technological progress generating negative covariance of wages creates strong private incentives for agents to become generalists. The paper concludes there is no unique relationship between technological progress and specialization—the nature of new technologies introduced in the labor market is what matters. Keywords include Specialization, Human Capital, and Technological Change.

The page also includes SCIRP contact information (customer@scirp.org, WhatsApp +86 18163351462, QQ 1655362766, WeChat) and social media links (Twitter, Facebook, LinkedIn, Weibo), along with standard SCIRP navigation links for journals, publishing, services, and policies.

<key_excerpts>
"Technological change is a distinctive characteristic of modern labor markets. New technologies change the demand for different skills in the labor market and thus introduce uncertainty in the wage structure that agents will face in the future." This is an NBER Working Paper (No. 8706, June 2002) titled "The Skill Content of Recent Technological Change: An Empirical Exploration" by David H. Autor (MIT), Frank Levy (MIT), and Richard J. Murnane (Harvard University). The paper applies an understanding of what computers do—the execution of procedural or rules-based logic—to study how computer technology alters job skill demands.

**Core Framework:** The authors contend that computer capital (1) substitutes for a limited set of human activities involving routine (repetitive) cognitive and manual tasks, and (2) complements activities involving non-routine problem solving and interactive tasks. Tasks can only be computerized if they can be proceduralized (expressed in "If-Then-Do" logical commands). Non-routine tasks requiring visual/manual skills (like truck driving) or complex reasoning (like writing persuasive legal briefs) are difficult to computerize.

**Theoretical Model:** Using a Cobb-Douglas production function with routine (R) and non-routine (N) tasks, the model shows that a decline in the price of computer capital lowers the wage per efficiency unit of routine tasks, increases the relative intensity of routine task input (via computer substitution), and raises the wage per efficiency unit of non-routine labor. Workers choose occupations based on comparative advantage (a Roy model), and a fall in computer prices reduces labor supply to routine occupations while raising supply to non-routine occupations.

**Empirical Methodology:** The authors use data from the Dictionary of Occupational Titles (DOT) 4th and Revised 4th editions (1977, 1991), matched to Census IPUMS (1960, 1970, 1980, 1990) and CPS MORG (1980, 1990, 1998) files, aggregated to 140 industries and ~450 Census Occupation Codes. They select five DOT measures: DCP (Direction/Control/Planning—non-routine cognitive/interactive), GED-MATH (non-routine cognitive/analytic), STS (routine cognitive), FINGDEX (routine manual), and EYEHAND (non-routine manual).

**Key Findings:**
1. From 1960-1998, employment shifted strongly toward non-routine cognitive tasks (both interactive and analytic) and away from routine cognitive, routine manual, and non-routine manual tasks.
2. Four of five 1959 industry task measures significantly predicted subsequent computer adoption (1977-1997), validating the task measures.
3. Computerization is associated with declining industry demand for routine manual and cognitive tasks and increased demand for non-routine cognitive tasks.
4. The sum of within-industry and within-occupation task changes explains 30-40% of the observed relative demand shift favoring college versus non-college labor during 1970-1998, with the largest impact after 1980.
5. Changes in task content within nominally identical occupations explain more than half of the overall demand shift induced by computerization.
6. Task changes were primarily a within-industry phenomenon (especially for non-routine cognitive/interactive tasks), accelerating after the 1970s.
</summary>
