## 1 Introduction

The role of AI in change management in the context of public administrations is of great importance, not only in terms of the impact of emergent technologies on the policy-making but also in view of the increasing role of algorithms in the management of organizations.

The scope of the research has been broadened to cover all public organizations, including academic institutions and not only the EU administrations as this has allowed to align the research to the local context of the host country, i.e., the United States, and gain insights from local authorities. As an EU Fellow, reaching out to private industry representatives was also considered beneficial as it enabled a holistic approach. The ultimate goal was to adapt the findings to the European context, namely EU institutions.

How to lead the people side of change effectively and where are the boundaries to the data-driven decision-making? What are the correlations between AI as a tool and change process in public administrations? Ultimately, will AI change management? These questions form the focus of the present research.

### 1.1 The select approach

A possibility to apply a multi-disciplinary approach to the research has been of particular value. The topic of the research project is multi-faceted as it comprises sociological, organizational, and technological paradigms. As such, it necessitates a multitude of sources as well, considering a spill-over effect on the emergence of new technologies linking private and public sectors. Research on the way this change is managed in public administrations is not cemented yet.

We cannot talk about change management and AI without reflecting on management theories, without providing at least a concise overview of the AI evolution and its impactful relationship with working methods in organizations. We cannot leave aside the main aspects of change management either. Despite plentiful academic resources on change management as a distinct discipline, linking it to AI narrows the subject matter. It thus allows to concentrate on more targeted questions, such as: how will the alleged efficiency gained due to AI take-up inside the organizations impact working methods and management? How to estimate resistance to change and how it might be managed? How to balance different organizational structures to allow for both execution and innovation (assess the alignment between the vision and structure to motivate for change)?

Thus, the study also includes the socio-economic element—evolutionary role of AI in Change Management in organizations so far, as well as the legal and political element—the regulatory steps taken by the EU to put forward legislation for a coordinated European approach on the human and ethical implications of AI. It also focuses on the EU institutions’ perspective in embracing the need for change as a response to technological developments. This ties with a need to look deeper into the impact of AI on the profession of public servants at large. How will the alleged efficiency gained due to AI take-up inside the organizations impact working methods and management?

### 1.2 The rationale of this study

Taken as such, the research in the domain of emergent technologies and public administrations facilitates the discourse on decision-making, broadens the outlook on AI uptake by public organizations, and fits in the increasingly relevant discussion as to how AI will change relations between employees and managers, job profiles and management at large, including public administrations’ ability to manage change.

AI technology has brought the promise of productivity, engagement, and especially next-level efficiency. However, as with any type of workflow change, stakeholders ought to have a complete understanding of the changes in order to continue being productive, but foremost—engaged.The hype surrounding AI is driven not only by the premise of increased efficiency and innovation, but also by some concerns as to its eventual impact on the workforce of organizations.

While AI’s potential is widely seen to significantly transform organizations by making them more productive, it is also acknowledged that implementing AI will also trigger changes in the ways organizations are managed. For organizations to reap the benefits of AI, they will need to introduce changes in workplace structures, technology strategies, and technology governance.

In the context of organizations, the concerns expressed in relation to AI have to be looked at holistically. One part of the equation is certainly technological implications, both for the organization and its people. Organizations have to make decisions on their AI strategy with any underlying concrete questions of AI design, deployment, investment and intensity of readiness to face AI-fueled future. For people, it would mean confronting new horizons of innovation facing new technologies and the resulting ever-increasing need to update their current skillset. The other part would relate to the people’s perception of AI. This aspect is not tangible and thus seems difficult to measure. But it is crucial both for the introduction of AI within the organizations and for the sake of the change management process itself. For this reason, as part of the research project, a survey on the way people perceive AI has been carried out the results of which will be presented later in the paper.

## 2 Literature review

### 2.1 Perceptions and introduction of AI

The hype surrounding AI has been powerful since its first mention in the 1950s. The Dartmouth Summer Research Project of 1956 is often taken as the event that initiated AI as a research discipline. It was a catalyzer of the next 20 years of AI exploration. The initial flourish was followed by quite a few obstacles. One of them was a clear lack of computational power to do anything substantial. Funding and consequently research slowed down for a decade. In the 1980s, AI was reignited by two sources: an expansion of the algorithmic toolkit and a boost of funds.

The 1990s and 2000s marked the milestone since many of the goals of AI had been achieved: in 1997, reigning world chess champion Gary Kasparov was defeated by IBM’s _Deep Blue_, a chess playing computer program. In the same year, speech recognition software, developed by _Dragon Systems_, was implemented on _Windows_ and Google’s _Alpha Go_ was able to defeat Chinese Go champion, Ke Jie. Even human emotion was fair game as evidenced by Kismet, a robot developed by Cynthia Breazeal that could recognize and display emotions.

The recent years have been characteristic of high-profile developments in machine learning which proved once again how rapidly AI is progressing. Big Tech companies have been infusing AI deeply into their products at an exponential pace, and this has been happening even before the initial release of ChatGPT in November 2022. The roll-out by OpenAI of DALL-E (which creates original images to match text prompts and is seen as a crucial step towards general intelligence) and GPT-3.5, followed by GPT-4 in 2023, has been outmatched by Google DeepMind’s next-generation AI model Gemini (adding to the current list of the most recognized models Midjourney, Bard AI/LaMDA, Aleph Alpha, Bloom, Llama v1-2 and Stable Diffusion). With the latest Google’s quantum computing breakthrough, this race is not set to slow down bringing a huge potential for the stakeholders, especially considering the evolution of Natural Language Processing (NLP) with generative AI models, which leverage computer programs to generate content that closely mirrors human-produced content. New large language models showing impressive contextual understanding are now laying down new records on technical benchmarks. All these technical developments have inherent implications on humans, way of working and society at large.

Since its inception in the 1950s, AI has become a significant research discipline with major commercial applications. These applications have increasingly had a tangible effect on many aspects of social life including organizations. We can surely talk about this process as a digital transformation. The COVID crisis has had a landmark role—it accelerated the adoption of analytics and AI, boosted companies’ AI strategies and led some to state that AI was becoming their mainstream technology. A study by PwC found that 52% of companies accelerated their AI adoption plans because of the COVID crisis.

The definition of AI is an act subject to massive variations and interpretations. Although the domain has been discussed and researched for over seven decades, there is still no commonly accepted definition of AI. Depending on the sector, AI can mean different things to different people.

According to the 2019 OECD Recommendation on artificial intelligence, AI is referred to as machine-based systems that can, for a given set of human-defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations or decisions influencing real or virtual environments.

The definition from _Britannica_ states that AI is “the ability of a digital computer or computer-controlled robot to perform tasks commonly associated with intelligent beings.”

In broad terms, it is a collection of technologies that can solve problems and carry out tasks to achieve defined objectives not involving human guidance. Automation and machine learning are central to AI. Defined from a user’s perspective, AI includes algorithmic systems that provide enhanced or completely new capabilities that have normally been assigned to the domain of human decision-making and action such as visual and speech recognition, reasoning, problem-solving, creative expression, navigation, and interaction (De Freitas et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR8 "De Freitas J, Agarwal S, Schmitt B, Haslam N (2023) Psychological factors underlying attitudes toward AI tools. Nat Hum Behav 7(11):1845–1854. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-023-01734-2
                  
                ")).

From the technical point of view, although AI takes a range of forms, all AI nowadays can be classified as narrow AI (or weak AI), in the sense that it is designed to perform a specific task (e.g., facial recognition, natural language processing or NLP, internet searches, driving a car, prediction and pattern recognition, detection and classification of objects through computer/machine vision and speech recognition). However, the long-term goal of many researchers is to create general AI (AGI or strong AI).

The discourse concerning AI varies. For some, it is neither artificial, nor intelligent. Applying a political approach and a material perspective, Kate Crawford argues, that “AI systems are built to see and intervene in the world in ways that primarily benefit the states, institutions, and corporations that they serve. In this sense, AI systems are expressions of power that emerge from wider economic and political forces, created to increase profits and centralize control for those who wield them” (Crawford [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR6 "Crawford K (2021) The atlas of AI: power, politics, and the planetary costs of artificial intelligence. Yale University Press, New Haven")).

For Prof. John W. Murphy, there is nothing artificial about AI.[Footnote 1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#Fn1) He argues that it is crucial to expose the human core of algorithms as they only appear to be artificial and thus autonomous. This calls for politicization of AI to reveal the vested interests of those who control how AI will likely be employed. Shoshana Zuboff defines surveillance capitalism as a “new economic order” and “an expropriation of critical human rights that is best understood as a coup from above” (Zuboff [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR36 "Zuboff S (2019) The age of surveillance capitalism: the fight for a human future at the new frontier of power. Profile Books, London")).

For others, AI is a revolutionary positive enabler. This “enthusiastic” part of the equation reflects the inevitable reality of AI already being part of people’s lives. From healthcare, education, transport, security, and more recently emotion recognition or sentiment analysis, this technology is rapidly transforming the world we know it. With the premise of calls for human-centered AI being taken into consideration, the question of whether AI is changing many aspects of our lives for the better could be answered in the affirmative. Undoubtedly, AI has many advantages: (if coded correctly), it is available 24/7, it reduces human error, can replace repetitive jobs, take risks in place of humans, enhance digital, and decision-making processes.

We can certainly look at AI from different angles, depending on which perspective we choose. For organizations, it is useful to look at it through the lens of business capabilities rather than technologies. Thomas H. Davenport and Rajeev Ronanki suggest that AI can support three important business needs: automating business processes, gaining insight through data analysis and engaging with customers and employees (Davenport and Ronanki [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR7 "Davenport, Thomas H, and Rajeev Ronanki. Artificial Intelligence For The Real World: Don’t Start With Moon Shots. N.p., 2018.")). It is a rational classification of AI, which allows to look not only at the benefits but also at the challenges related to AI. By the same token, a special attention needs to be paid to the challenges of AI, especially in the domain of its uptake in organizations.

Coming back to the implementation of AI within organizations, an organizational assessment is of paramount importance in the process of defining its AI planning strategy. How is it seen internally, considering that every organization has its specific context, organizational culture and management and operational practices? Is it a generic organization where AI is just presented as a new working tool? Thus, AI has to be properly contextualized. It is important to look at the social context where this technology would be deployed. Prof. J. Murphy argues that planning with a generic organization in mind is a serious mistake.[Footnote 2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#Fn2) To reach levels of AI smoothly aligned with the organizational structure and culture, it might necessitate more than a technical fix or employee training. In the quest towards human-centric AI, which strives to align the development of this technology to human values and goals, and thus better engagement, we may need to address the problem of alienation, i.e., theories and perceptions that incremental advancements in AI technologies continue to alienate mankind from the existential human nature. Marx’s theory of alienation, according to which a man is alienated from his creative capacities under capitalism, perfectly reflects a predictive analysis of digital culture. But most importantly, we might need to apply a new outlook on organizations.

### 2.2 Outlook on AI adoption

The optics of AI adoption can be manifold. First, it is essential to understand the dynamics of AI in human contexts. The interaction between humans and AI and in particular the way AI is shaping human understanding of themselves and the societies at large come to the fore. The correlation between humans and AI manifests itself _inter alia_ in the rise of misinformation, algorithmic bias, and amplified disinformation (Shin [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR24 "Shin D (2024) Artificial misinformation: exploring human-algorithm interaction online. Springer Nature, Switzerland. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-52569-8
                  
                ")).

This leads to an important discourse about the future of AI-based society, especially considering that the development of AI is currently “algorithm-driven” and technically-oriented rather than human-centered (Shin [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR23 "Shin DD (2023). Algorithms, humans, and interactions: how do algorithms interact with people? Designing meaningful AI experiences (1st ed.). Routledge. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1201/b23083
                  
                ")). Social implications of algorithmic systems, means to counter misinformation (e.g., through algorithmic nudging) are important elements in any discussion about a “buy-in” of AI and its adoption (Shin [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR24 "Shin D (2024) Artificial misinformation: exploring human-algorithm interaction online. Springer Nature, Switzerland. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-52569-8
                  
                ")).

Any AI adoption strategy depends on the existence of the conditions for meaningful AI experiences. This entails designing AI systems that would be legitimate, beneficial, usable by humans, and respectful of human values. Meaningful control of AI is the sought-after scenario in which ethical considerations would be balanced with real-world practical solutions and humans would be able to control their choices (Shin [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR23 "Shin DD (2023). Algorithms, humans, and interactions: how do algorithms interact with people? Designing meaningful AI experiences (1st ed.). Routledge. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1201/b23083
                  
                ")).

Thus, any reflection about individual perceptions of AI readiness or adoption needs to integrate the social dimension of algorithms.

Second, discussion about AI adoption at organizational level calls for an integrated approach involving sociotechnical dimensions and jointly conceptualizing technology, organizations, and employees (Tursunbayeva and Gal [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR32 "Tursunbayeva A, Chalutz-Ben Gal H (2024) Adoption of artificial intelligence: a TOP framework-based checklist for digital leaders. Bus Horiz 67(4):357–368. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bushor.2024.04.006
                  
                ")). The TOP framework having its origins in a sociotechnical perspective introduced by Stevens ([1989](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR27 "Stevens GC (1989) Integrating the Supply Chain. Int J Phys Distrib Mater Manag 19(8):3–8. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1108/EUM0000000000329
                  
                ")) puts a special focus on the importance of addressing technological, organizational, and people-related aspects in order to take up AI within organizations. Organizational culture is one of the main challenges for organizations when adopting AI but equally important are individual skills, training, and motivation (Tursunbayeva and Gal [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR32 "Tursunbayeva A, Chalutz-Ben Gal H (2024) Adoption of artificial intelligence: a TOP framework-based checklist for digital leaders. Bus Horiz 67(4):357–368. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bushor.2024.04.006
                  
                ")).

One of the biggest challenges in the adoption of new technologies is the availability of workforce with the necessary skills. Next to the organizations’ data science capabilities, which are in the development phase for the major part of organizations, having training in place to address any shortages of the pertinent skills is the _sine qua non_. At the same time, development of the relevant skills in the existing pool of employees is seen as a viable part of AI implementation initiatives. This requires a proactive identification of the skills already present within an organization.

Conceptualizing technology, cloud services are an indispensable asset for AI. Compared with traditional technologies, the implementation of AI differs significantly: its deployment process is dynamic and requires continuous monitoring. Moreover, with the AI already present in an organization, data have to be managed in a proactive and comprehensive manner, which requires an increased and earlier business and IT collaboration.

Looking at Europe, it is unclear what the current level of AI adoption by European firms actually is. Estimates vary widely because of uneven data collection and lack of a standard definition and taxonomy of AI.

In the AI adoption path, the public sector has been falling behind the private sector. Nevertheless, governments are taking measures to close this gap as soon as possible. Not being immune to AI transformation, they showcase their commitment to AI releasing national AI strategies or guiding principles that demonstrate their strategic vision and approach to AI. Such strategies can facilitate states to streamline their AI practices and position relevant AI actors within their technological systems. They also enable AI to become an integral part of the whole policy-making. The OECD 2019 report on Artificial Intelligence and its use in the public sector notes that one of the tangible outcomes of the AI use for the public sector is defined as enhancement of civil service capacity through training, tools and recruitment.

Speaking about technology adoption at organizational level, it is important to look at its drivers. Technology adoption decisions at the company level are influenced by technological, organizational, and environmental factors. Overall, it is technological readiness that is without any reasonable doubt important for AI.

As far as organizational aspects are concerned, these are connected to leadership, structure and networks. If management has positive attitudes towards change, it facilitates adoption. Decentralized power structures and lower levels of formality stimulate innovation, in the same way as high levels of knowledge and staff expertise.

#### 2.2.1 Obstacles to AI adoption

We may address the question of obstacles to AI adoption from a multitude of angles. First, basing ourselves on industry reports and practical realities at organizational level, we get a general overview of the macro-factors such as regulatory and financial constraints, lack of IT resources, shortage of skills among existing workforce. Skills and financial constraints are the leading barriers across adopters and non-adopters (2020 European enterprise survey on the use of technologies based on AI).

For non-AI adopters, the obstacles are mainly of internal nature: a higher degree of insufficient IT resources, lack of internal data and lack of skills among existing staff. While small- and medium-sized enterprises report higher internal barriers, large companies indicate higher external barriers in terms of skills and data.

Another obstacle is related to legal uncertainty. Regulatory certainty is also crucial, not only in terms of liability for damages caused by AI. Predictable regulatory environment is essential for the organizations to be able to start assessing potential risks and returns on investment in AI technology. The EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has been a landmark success, providing one set of data protection rules for all companies operating in the EU, wherever they are based. It has forced big tech companies to make changes to their privacy and data-handling policies and, even more importantly, through its global regulatory reach, has incited other world actors to start considering regulatory actions in the domain.

Since 2017, at least 60 countries have adopted some form of AI policy. The US is on the way to propose regulations on AI and China is also embracing efforts leading to something that could be comparable to GDPR (in March 2022, China was set to outlaw specific cases of algorithmic discrimination in relation to setting prices, controlling search results, recommending videos, and filtering content as part of what may be the world’s most ambitious effort to regulate AI). In November 2021 UNESCO Member States adopted the first ever global agreement on the Ethics of AI. Thus, claims that strict regulation may hinder any technological advancement seem not grounded. Instead, there seems to be a global consensus that some regulatory certainty in the field of AI is needed, not least because it would benefit businesses.

Even if a clear regulatory foundation in terms of data privacy exists, the lack of legal certainty in the EU with respect to the use of AI is delaying the absorption of existing technologies in the private sector. For this reason, and to address the issue of a more comprehensive regulatory uncertainty, a clear and future-proof regulatory framework for the use of AI in business is needed. Talking about regulation at large in the digital world, it is projected that the EU’s Digital Markets Act (DMA) and Digital Services Act (DSA) regulatory tools will help to create a safer digital space in which the fundamental rights of users would be protected and that they will facilitate the establishment of a level playing field for businesses. The landmark DSA deal reached by the European regulators obliges Big Tech companies to meet new EU requirements to curb illegal content and disinformation on their platforms. Whereas, once in force, the proposed EU AI Act would set a new global standard for AI oversight worldwide.

Second, apart from the macro-factors of obstacles, it may be important to note how individual users see, perceive and make sense of AI. Psychologically induced resistance to AI adoption can be a powerful factor limiting the process. Inevitably, it is essential to determine the psychological factors, which drive attitudes toward AI tools. Such attitudes are rooted in five fundamental AI-related and user-related factors such as opacity or AI as “black box”, emotionlessness or AI as “unfeeling”, rigidity or AI as “inflexible”, autonomy or AI as “in control”, and group membership or AI as “non-human” (De Freitas et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR8 "De Freitas J, Agarwal S, Schmitt B, Haslam N (2023) Psychological factors underlying attitudes toward AI tools. Nat Hum Behav 7(11):1845–1854. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-023-01734-2
                  
                ")). Certainly, attitudes across domains also matter. The five mentioned factors could impact attitudes across different domains (for example, AI use is known to be high for data analysis, medium for driving and low for painting) (Morewedge [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR19 "Morewedge CK (2022) Preference for human, not algorithm aversion. Trends Cogn Sci 26(10):824–826. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tics.2022.07.007
                  
                ")). Cultural variation is to be factored in as well. There is still limited understanding of whether and how attitudes towards AI systems are affected by culture. Another important aspect is temporal evolution, since attitudes toward new technology often evolve over time. Starting with resistance, moving on to curiosity and exploration, followed by rapid adoption, normalization, and integration and evolution (Rogers [1962](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR21 "Rogers EM (1962) Diffusion of innovations. Free Press of Glencoe, New York")). Types of AI systems can also be a separate element to take into account. AI systems have evolved from performing specific tasks in a limited domain (narrow AI) to performance at human levels across multiple domains (general AI), and may eventually consistently outdo humans (super-intelligence) (Bostrom [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR4 "Bostrom N (2014) Superintelligence: paths, dangers, strategies. Oxford University Press, Oxford")). OpenAI’s conversational chatbot, ChatGPT, has brought a new push in the direction of the artificial general intelligence (AGI), performing different tasks at levels that have been likened to general intelligence (Zhang et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR35 "Zhang C et al (2023) One small step for generative AI, one giant leap for AGI: a complete survey on ChatGPT in AIGC era. Preprint at 
                  https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.06488
                  
                ")).

The above factors are inter-related, but at the same time conceptually distinct, and each of them encompasses distinguishable perceptions and attitudes that affect whether the technology is actually uptaken. Resistance to AI tools can be eased by targeted interventions that address these concerns at both AI-related and user-related levels. However, understanding these five factors, we can know when to not implement an intervention, adjust the degree to which an intervention is implemented to limit negative side-effects, and implement an intervention also taking further actions to mitigate new risks arising from the intervention (De Freitas et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR8 "De Freitas J, Agarwal S, Schmitt B, Haslam N (2023) Psychological factors underlying attitudes toward AI tools. Nat Hum Behav 7(11):1845–1854. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-023-01734-2
                  
                ")).

Consequently, it is not only engineering factors that really matter for AI adoption. The rise of algorithmic systems has led to the need for the users to make sense of fairness and transparency. The research has also come with a composite concept of transparent fairness around user sense-making processes and their inherent perception of quality and credibility of AI systems (Lim et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR18 "Lim J, Ahmad N, Ibarahim M (2024) Understanding user sensemaking in fairness and transparency in algorithms: algorithmic sensemaking in over-the-top platform. AI Soc 39:447–490. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s00146-022-01525-9
                  
                ")). When people believe the algorithm is fair and transparent, they trust and accept it. The way users perceive fairness goes beyond purely mathematical fairness. It transcends into contextual equality for users with AI systems being impartial, indiscriminate and accurate and transparency being identified (or equaled to) as observable, explainable, verifiable and ultimately visible (Lim et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR18 "Lim J, Ahmad N, Ibarahim M (2024) Understanding user sensemaking in fairness and transparency in algorithms: algorithmic sensemaking in over-the-top platform. AI Soc 39:447–490. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s00146-022-01525-9
                  
                ")).

Another important aspect to consider in the discourse on the adoption of AI is the impact of AI on the ways in which users actually process and respond to misinformation, especially in the contexts of generative AI (Koerber and Lim [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR16 "Koerber A, Lim J (2024) Impact of misinformation from generative AI on user information processing: how people understand misinformation on generative AI. New Media Soc. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/14614448241234040
                  
                ")). The industry practice and user experiences have shown that although AI-generated text has gained huge popularity, there is a lot of concern that its unverified use could result in widespread dissemination of misinformation. Moreover, generative AI has also an inherent tendency to generate plausible-sounding misinformation, not being able to discern between likelihood and fact. Misinformation is defined as false or objectively incorrect information, which is not sustained by expert opinion or evident proof (Vraga and Bode [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR33 "Vraga E, Bode L (2020) Defining misinformation and understanding its bounded nature. Polit Commun 37(1):136–144")).

As such, misinformation can have impact on the AI adoption, also in view of the above-mentioned concept of transparent fairness on behalf of the users. To predict whether users will be inclined to adopt AI, it is important to understand how they might perceive potential misinformation in AI systems and the inherent challenges in verification thereof. Verifying the accuracy of AI-generated content is a substantial challenge due to intrinsic limitations in AI models, their black-box nature, opaqueness of their underlying algorithms, and the potential for contamination in their data sources (Shin and Valente [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR25 "Shin J, Valente T (2020) Algorithms and health misinformation. J Health Commun 25(5):394–401"); UK National Cyber Security Center, 2023). This leads to the need to focus on the way in which users perceive potential misinformation in AI systems. Modeling such perceptual and cognitive processes behind the spread of misinformation is essential in order to comprehend users’ reasoning or their cognitive heuristics for diagnosing misinformation, especially in the contexts of generative AI-generated contents, which is still under-researched, due to the early stages of the technology (Koerber and Lim [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR16 "Koerber A, Lim J (2024) Impact of misinformation from generative AI on user information processing: how people understand misinformation on generative AI. New Media Soc. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/14614448241234040
                  
                ")).

To address this, research has put forward insights from two theoretical accounts—the heuristic–systematic (HS) processing framework and the concept of information diagnosticity. The HS model of information processing is geared at the analysis of the attitude formation and cognitive processing of users, in accordance to two types of response to information: heuristic and systematic (Chaiken et al. [1996](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR5 "Chaiken S, Giner-Sorolla R, Chen S (1996) Beyond accuracy. In: Gollwitzer PM, Bargh JA (eds) The psychology of action: linking cognition and motivation to behavior. Guilford Press, New York, pp 553–578")). If in heuristic responses, information is processed intuitively and autonomously, with little reflection on the content of the message, in systematic responses, users thoroughly evaluate the information to check its validity, and reflect on the content of the message (Todorov et al. [2002](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR30 "Todorov A, Chaiken S, Henderson MD (2002) The heuristic-systematic model of social information processing. In: Dillard JP, Pfau M (eds) The persuasion handbook: developments in theory and practice. Sage, Thousand Oaks, pp 195–211")). Heuristic assessment of misinformation by users entails evaluation of the intrinsic nature of algorithmic features such as fairness, transparency, and accountability. These are the essential elements, which commonly form the discourse around AI development, and overall users’ trust. Since users are unable to assess AI systematically, they rely on heuristic cues (such as fairness, trustworthiness and transparency) in order to process large amounts of generated information.

The theoretical approach of heuristic–systematic (HS) information processing has been reinforced further by the concept of diagnosticity, which is defined by the extent to which users interpret information as relevant and useful, in accordance with their decision-making and judgment (Ahluwalia et al. [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR1 "Ahluwalia R, Unnava H, Burnkrant R (2001) The moderating role of commitment on the spillover effect of marketing communications. J Mark Res 38(4):458–470")). In the context of algorithmic systems, information that is perceived to be highly diagnostic is automatically given more weight in users’ evaluations and judgments (Shin [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR23 "Shin DD (2023). Algorithms, humans, and interactions: how do algorithms interact with people? Designing meaningful AI experiences (1st ed.). Routledge. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1201/b23083
                  
                ")). Thus, diagnosticity can determine the extent to which users believe that information is true while evaluating an AI-generated content. Explainability, as diagnosticity, is integral to user trust and comprehension as it relates to the AI system’s capability to enable AI system users to understand how specific information is generated. When a piece of information is generated by algorithmic systems in transparent, fair, and accountable ways, users perceive it with a high level of diagnosticity. This, in turn, improves their intention to systematically analyze that information. Thus, explainability is pivotal to establishing faith, credibility, and rapport between an AI agent and users, especially when it comes to assessing fake news and misinformation (Helberger [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR37 "Helberger N (2019) On the democratic role of news recommenders. Digital Journalism 7: 993–1012")). Trust in a platform and consequently to AI adoption in general is generated when diagnosticity and established information credibility are high (Koerber and Lim [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR16 "Koerber A, Lim J (2024) Impact of misinformation from generative AI on user information processing: how people understand misinformation on generative AI. New Media Soc. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/14614448241234040
                  
                ")). Literacy of users also plays a role, especially when countering misinformation, and it is essential to cater to it. If diagnosticity may depend on the technological features of an AI system, it can also be contextual, and the perceived diagnosticity of users can significantly depend on how they view the system’s fairness, accountability and transparency. Future studies should explore the correlation among algorithm literacy, trust, and diagnosticity in order to further clarify what may determine the efficacy and capacity of users when exposed to misinformation through algorithms (Koerber and Lim [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR16 "Koerber A, Lim J (2024) Impact of misinformation from generative AI on user information processing: how people understand misinformation on generative AI. New Media Soc. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/14614448241234040
                  
                ")).

#### 2.2.2 AI as the driver for organizational transformation

Articles and blogs on AI-driven organizational transformation abound. There is an omnipresent agreement that AI is already driving change within organizations and the question to ask is no longer when but how it is transforming organizations.

Organizations that lag behind in AI capability development will eventually find themselves in a less competitive position than AI-fueled organizations. In its survey on the _State of AI in the Enterprise_ carried out in 2021, Deloitte distinguishes four areas where AI has an impact from the organizational point of view: strategy, operations, culture and change management, and ecosystems. One of the conclusions is that the mere existence of a strategy, however clear, well communicated and tightly aligned with the overall business strategy, is not enough. It has to be accompanied by operations and culture as well as change management.

Operations are seen as new operating processes that steer innovation, continued and robust quality, and value formation. Some organizations have even created new roles of chief automation officers as bilingual talent of the organizational entity: being knowledgeable in both business and data analysis, they act as translators between business stakeholders and AI and machine learning (ML) development teams.

When it comes to culture, AI-savvy organizations foster culture that is agile, data-fluent, but most of all displaying trust. Such organizations also invest in change management to support new ways of working (In fact, the survey shows that organizations that invest heavily in change management are 1.6 times as likely to indicate that AI initiatives exceed expectations and more than 1.5 times as likely to achieve their goals, compared to other organizations).

The biggest challenge in AI-transformation efforts is culture change. You cultivate trust by setting a clear direction and giving people what they need to see it through, i.e., by supporting them. It might raise eyebrows but the 2021 Deloitte study indicates that “fear can be an indicator of positive change if paired with supportive culture and change management”. If we talk about fear related to AI, the general concern is that it will lead to job losses and machines replacing humans. However, if an organization shows its focus on training, collaboration, and relationship building efforts, it creates trust. Trust in the organization’s competence to manage change and to use the new technologies in the ways that would be beneficial to workers.

Beyond all the mentioned aspects that can facilitate AI-driven organizational transformation, research emphasizes the importance of a people-focused approach and human-centered AI, which is there if there is a real focus on augmenting human capabilities (Human-centered AI: The power of putting people first). Industry and academic reporting increasingly mentions humanness in AI, but how actually do we understand humanness? How can we define humanness in AI?

In the context of conversational journalism, and more specifically chatbots, perceived humanness is defined as the degree to which users believe that chatbots might be human (Shin [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-024-02136-2#ref-CR22 "Shin D (2022) The perception of humanness in conversational journalism: an algorithmic information-processing perspective. New Media Soc 24(12):2680–2704. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/1461444821993801
                  
                ")). These days, conversational AI is able to use natural language to communicate with users. Such an enhanced interactive modality can lead to user trust since it shows that AI is becoming more powerful. Nonetheless, the absence of user trust has become a major concern for AI developers and many questions arise as to how lack of trust actually occurs. Some research studies suggest focusing on the unique features of conversational AI (namely, speaking and listening) which discern conversational AI from other forms of AI systems.

There is an increasingly proven link between trust and the perceived humannes

## Article Overview

This is an open-access research article published in the journal **AI & SOCIETY** (Volume 40, pages 3953-3981, 2025), titled "Change management: artificial intelligence (AI) at the service of public administrations." It was published on December 30, 2024, and authored by **Ieva Mainardi** (ORCID: orcid.org/0009-0005-7773-412X, affiliated with two institutions). The article has received 17k accesses and 30 citations.

## Core Thesis

The research examines the role of AI in change management within public administrations, including national government agencies and EU institutions. The study emphasizes that AI adoption requires not only technological advancement but also human "soft components" such as institutional culture, inter-cultural awareness, and organizational needs to facilitate the "mental shift" and buy-in. The author argues that AI-driven change in public organizations must move away from "silo mentality" toward matrix-based structures with advanced reporting relationships.

## Key Research Questions

1. How to lead the "people side of change" effectively and where are the boundaries of data-driven decision-making?
2. What are the correlations between AI as a tool and the change process in public administrations?
3. Will AI change management?

## Methodology and Scope

- Applied a **multi-disciplinary approach** covering sociological, organizational, and technological paradigms
- Research was broadened to cover all public organizations, including academic institutions, and aligned to the US local context (host country of the EU Fellow author) while aiming to adapt findings to the European/EU context
- Included interviews with private industry representatives for a holistic approach
- Conducted a **survey on how people perceive AI** (results presented later in the paper)

## Historical Context of AI

- AI initiated as a research discipline at the **Dartmouth Summer Research Project of 1956**
- 1980s: AI reignited by algorithmic toolkit expansion and funding boost
- 1997: IBM's **Deep Blue** defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov; Dragon Systems speech recognition implemented on Windows
- Recent developments: OpenAI's DALL-E, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 (2023), Google DeepMind's Gemini, plus Midjourney, Bard AI/LaMDA, Aleph Alpha, Bloom, Llama v1-2, Stable Diffusion
- ChatGPT released November 2022
- COVID crisis accelerated AI adoption: a PwC study found **52% of companies accelerated their AI adoption plans** because of the pandemic

## Definitions of AI

- **OECD 2019 Recommendation**: "machine-based systems that can, for a given set of human-defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations or decisions influencing real or virtual environments"
- **Britannica**: "the ability of a digital computer or computer-controlled robot to perform tasks commonly associated with intelligent beings"
- No commonly accepted definition exists despite seven decades of research
- Current AI classified as **narrow AI**; long-term goal is artificial general intelligence (AGI/strong AI)

## Critical Perspectives on AI

- **Kate Crawford** (2021): AI systems are "expressions of power that emerge from wider economic and political forces, created to increase profits and centralize control"
- **Prof. John W. Murphy**: There is "nothing artificial about AI" — human core of algorithms must be exposed; planning with a "generic organization" in mind is a serious mistake
- **Shoshana Zuboff** (2019): Surveillance capitalism is "an expropriation of critical human rights that is best understood as a coup from above"
- **Marx's theory of alienation** referenced for analyzing AI's effect on digital culture

## Business Applications (Davenport and Ronanki, 2018)

AI supports three business needs: (1) automating business processes, (2) gaining insight through data analysis, (3) engaging with customers and employees

## Obstacles to AI Adoption

- **Internal barriers** (non-adopters): insufficient IT resources, lack of internal data, lack of skills among staff
- **External barriers** (large companies): skills and data gaps
- **Regulatory/legal uncertainty**: GDPR cited as landmark success; since 2017 at least **60 countries** have adopted some form of AI policy
- China (March 2022): set to outlaw algorithmic discrimination in pricing, search results, video recommendations, content filtering
- **UNESCO** (November 2021): first global agreement on Ethics of AI
- Upcoming EU regulations: Digital Markets Act (DMA), Digital Services Act (DSA), and the proposed **EU AI Act** (would set a new global standard for AI oversight)

## Psychological Factors in AI Resistance (De Freitas et al., 2023)

Five fundamental factors driving attitudes toward AI:
1. **Opacity** (AI as "black box")
2. **Emotionlessness** (AI as "unfeeling")
3. **Rigidity** (AI as "inflexible")
4. **Autonomy** (AI as "in control")
5. **Group membership** (AI as "non-human")

## Misinformation and User Trust

- Generative AI has an inherent tendency to generate plausible-sounding misinformation
- **Heuristic-systematic (HS) processing framework** and **information diagnosticity** theory applied to understand how users process AI-generated misinformation
- Users rely on **heuristic cues** (fairness, trustworthiness, transparency) since they cannot systematically assess AI
- **Explainability** is pivotal to establishing faith, credibility, and rapport between AI agents and users

## AI-Driven Organizational Transformation

**Deloitte's 2021 "State of AI in the Enterprise" survey** identifies four areas of AI impact: strategy, operations, culture and change management, and ecosystems. Key findings:
- Organizations investing heavily in change management are **1.6 times more likely** to have AI initiatives exceed expectations and **more than 1.5 times more likely** to achieve their goals
- Culture change is the biggest challenge in AI transformation
- "Fear can be an indicator of positive change if paired with supportive culture and change management"
- New roles like **chief automation officers** emerging as bilingual talent (business + data analysis)

## Additional Frameworks

- **TOP framework** (Tursunbayeva and Gal, 2024): technological, organizational, and people-related aspects needed for AI adoption
- Public sector has been **falling behind the private sector** in AI adoption
- Organizational culture, individual skills, training, and motivation are key challenges
- AI-savvy organizations foster agile, data-fluent cultures displaying trust
args.key_excerpts: "Public administrations, including national government agencies as well as the EU institutions, face not only structural changes, but are increasingly talking about the need to transform management, foster innovation, and share responsibilities. The role of AI is the key composite element of this process."

# The Race between Man and Machine: Implications of Technology for Growth, Factor Shares, and Employment

*    Daron Acemoglu 
*    Pascual Restrepo 

American Economic Review 

[vol. 108, no. 6, June 2018](https://pubs.aeaweb.org/issues/510)

(pp. 1488–1542)

[Download Full Text PDF (Complimentary)](https://pubs.aeaweb.org/articles/pdf/doi/10.1257/aer.20160696)

*   [Article Information](https://pubs.aeaweb.org/doi/10.1257/aer.20160696#article-information)

#### Abstract

 We examine the concerns that new technologies will render labor redundant in a framework in which tasks previously performed by labor can be automated and new versions of existing tasks, in which labor has a comparative advantage, can be created. In a static version where capital is fixed and technology is exogenous, automation reduces employment and the labor share, and may even reduce wages, while the creation of new tasks has the opposite effects. Our full model endogenizes capital accumulation and the direction of research toward automation and the creation of new tasks. If the long-run rental rate of capital relative to the wage is sufficiently low, the long-run equilibrium involves automation of all tasks. Otherwise, there exists a stable balanced growth path in which the two types of innovations go hand-in-hand. Stability is a consequence of the fact that automation reduces the cost of producing using labor, and thus discourages further automation and encourages the creation of new tasks. In an extension with heterogeneous skills, we show that inequality increases during transitions driven both by faster automation and the introduction of new tasks, and characterize the conditions under which inequality stabilizes in the long run.

# The Race Between Machine and Man: Implications of Technology for Growth, Factor Shares and Employment

We examine the concerns that new technologies will render labor redundant in a framework in which tasks previously performed by labor can be automated and new versions of existing tasks, in which labor has a comparative advantage, can be created. In a static version where capital is fixed and technology is exogenous, automation reduces employment and the labor share, and may even reduce wages, while the creation of new tasks has the opposite effects. Our full model endogenizes capital accumulation and the direction of research towards automation and the creation of new tasks. If the long-run rental rate of capital relative to the wage is sufficiently low, the long-run equilibrium involves automation of all tasks. Otherwise, there exists a stable balanced growth path in which the two types of innovations go hand-in-hand. Stability is a consequence of the fact that automation reduces the cost of producing using labor, and thus discourages further automation and encourages the creation of new tasks. In an extension with heterogeneous skills, we show that inequality increases during transitions driven both by faster automation and introduction of new tasks, and characterize the conditions under which inequality is increasing or stable in the long run.

<webpage_content>
NBER WORKING PAPER SERIES THE "TASK APPROACH" TO LABOR MARKETS: AN OVERVIEW David H. Autor Working Paper 18711 http://www.nber.org/papers/w18711 NATIONAL BUREAU OF ECONOMIC RESEARCH 1050 Massachusetts Avenue Cambridge, MA 02138 January 2013 Autor acknowledges funding from the National Science Foundation (grant SES-1227334). I thank Joachim Möller and Brendan Price for valuable comments that improved this essay. The views expressed herein are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of the National Bureau of Economic Research.
NBER working papers are circulated for discussion and comment purposes. They have not been peer-reviewed or been subject to the review by the NBER Board of Directors that accompanies official NBER publications.
© 2013 by David H. Autor. All rights reserved. Short sections of text, not to exceed two paragraphs, may be quoted without explicit permission provided that full credit, including © notice, is given to the source.
The "Task Approach" to Labor Markets: An Overview David H. Autor NBER Working Paper No. 18711 January 2013 JEL No. J23,J24,J31 ABSTRACT An emerging literature argues that changes in the allocation of workplace “tasks” between capital and labor, and between domestic and foreign workers, has altered the structure of labor demand in industrialized countries and fostered employment polarization—that is, rising employment in the highest and lowest paid occupations. Analyzing this phenomenon within the canonical production function framework is challenging, however, because the assignment of tasks to labor and capital in the canonical model is essentially static. This essay sketches an alternative model of the assignment of skills to tasks based upon comparative advantage, reviews key conceptual and practical challenges that researchers face in bringing the “task approach” to the data, and cautions against two common pitfalls that pervade the growing task literature. I conclude with a cautiously optimistic forecast for the potential of the task approach to illuminate the interactions among skill supplies, technological capabilities, and trade and offshoring opportunities, in shaping the aggregate demand for skills, the assignment of skills to tasks, and the evolution of wages.
David H. Autor Department of Economics MIT, E52-371 50 Memorial Drive Cambridge, MA 02142-1347 and NBER dautor@mit.edu Introduction The canonical production function found in economic models is anthropomorphic—it’s built to resemble humans. It features a role for labor and a role for machinery (capital), and, in general, these roles are distinct. This is not illogical—after all, these are separate inputs. But what precisely is distinctive about the role of each input is left opaque, and the nature of the interactions among them is highly constrained. In particular, capital is either a complement or a substitute for labor, diﬀerent types of labor are either complements or substitutes for one another, and these roles are essentially ﬁxed. Changes in the supply of each input can of course aﬀect marginal products, but each factor’s “purpose” in the production function is both distinct and static.
These restrictions stem from the fact that the canonical production function implicitly equates two distinct aspects of production. One aspect is which factors are used as inputs, e.g., capital, high skill labor, low skill labor. The other is what services these factors provide. In the canonical setup, a factor’s identity and its role in the production function are synonymous. In reality, however, the boundary between “labor tasks” and “capital tasks” in production is permeable and shifting. We observe numerous instances in which technological advances allow machinery to substitute for labor in performing a speciﬁc set of tasks—for example, dispensing boarding passes and assigning seats at airport check-in counters in lieu of gate agents—while simultaneously complementing labor in other tasks, for example, allowing gate agents to rapidly identify alternate ﬂights and issue new tickets. This evolving division of labor has a clear economic logic: novel tasks—those demanded by new products, techniques, or services—are often assigned ﬁrst to workers because workers are ﬂexible and adaptive. As these tasks are formalized and codiﬁed, they become fallow for automation since machinery typically has a cost advantage over human labor in rote execution of repetitive tasks.
A growing body of literature argues that the shifting allocation of tasks between capital and labor—and between domestic and foreign labor—has played a key role in reshaping the structure of labor demand in industrialized countries in recent decades. Analyzing this phenomenon is diﬃcult within the canonical production function framework, however, be-2 cause the assignment of tasks to labor and capital is, for most conceptual purposes, static.
To overcome this conceptual hurdle, it is valuable to consider a setting where the equilib-rium mapping between production tasks and productive factors responds dynamically to shifting economic and technological forces. The “task approach” to labor markets oﬀers one promising, though far from complete, set of conceptual tools for studying these forces.
In this brief essay, I ﬁrst sketch a formal model, developed by Acemoglu and Autor (2011), that oﬀers a ﬂexible and tractable approach for analyzing the interactions among skill supplies, technological capabilities, and potential trade and oﬀshoring opportunities in shaping the demand for factors, the assignment of factors to tasks, and the productivity and hence the wage of each factor. This model removes what we view as an artiﬁcial set of distinctions typically made between labor, capital, and trade (or oﬀshoring) in the canonical production model, where diﬀerent factors of production play distinct and often incommensurate roles.
In the this alternative model, the fundamental units of production are job tasks, which are combined to produce output. Tasks can be supplied by domestic labor, foreign labor, or capital, the capabilities of which may change over time. Consequently, the assignment of factors to tasks in this model is determined by comparative advantage; in equilibrium, only the least-cost factor is assigned to any given task.
The second part of the essay brieﬂy discusses some of the key conceptual and practical challenges that researchers face in bringing the “task approach” to the data. The literature is already grappling with these issues, as I note below, and I’m cautiously optimistic that progress will be rapid.
I end by highlighting some of the pitfalls that researchers may encounter in applying the task approach, most prominently, loose and inconsistent task deﬁnitions that tend to sow confusion, and the beguiling temptation for researchers to conﬁdently forecast the “future of work” based only on the very modest understanding that we have developed to date.
3 1 Tasks in production1 For the purposes of this discussion, it is essential to draw a distinction between skills and tasks. A task is a unit of work activity that produces output. A skill is a worker’s stock of capabilities for performing various tasks.
Workers apply their skills to tasks in exchange for wages.
Canonical production functions draw an implicit equivalence between workers’ skills and their job tasks, as noted above. Here, we emphasize instead that skills are applied to tasks to produce output—skills do not directly produce output.
This distinction is of course inconsequential if workers of a given skill always perform the same set of tasks. It is relevant, however, when the assignment of skills to tasks is subject to change, either because shifts in market prices mandate reallocation of skills to tasks or because the set of tasks demanded in the economy is altered by technological developments, trade, or oﬀshoring. In my view, we are currently in such an era.
If the boundary between “labor tasks” and “capital tasks” is ﬂuid, what determines the division of labor—or, more precisely, the allocation of tasks—between these factors? At least two forces are central, one technological, the other economic. On the technological front, the boundary between labor and capital shifts primarily in one direction: capital typically takes over tasks formerly performed by labor; simultaneously, workers are typ-ically assigned novel tasks before they are automated. This sequence of task allocation makes intuitive sense: when a task is unfamiliar or poses unexpected obstacles, workers can often draw on outside knowledge and problem-solving skills to devise work-arounds.
By contrast, few machines can improvise. Consequently, automating a task requires at-taining a level of mastery beyond what is required for a worker to simply perform the task; it must be codiﬁed to the point where a relatively inﬂexible machine can perform the work semi-autonomously.
Even when a task is fully codiﬁed, however, this does not mean it will be automated.
When Nissan Motor Company builds cars in Japan, it makes extensive use of industrial robots to reduce labor costs. When it assembles cars in India, it uses robots far more 1 This section draws extensively on Acemoglu and Autor (2011), and some sections of text are directly reproduced from that article.
4 sparingly.2 The key diﬀerence between production in India and Japan is not technology but cost: labor is comparatively cheap in India.
At the intersection of these two forces—technological feasibility and economic cost— lies the principle of comparative advantage. Comparative advantage in production means that the factor with the lowest economic cost of performing a task is assigned that task.
Economic cost in turn reﬂects both a factor’s technological capability and its opportunity cost. It’s likely that the technological capabilities and economic costs of robots in Japan and India are quite similar. The opportunity cost of labor in India is far lower, however, and hence Nissan hires Indian workers to perform assembly tasks that are roboticized in Japan.
Though I’ve drawn examples from the information age so far—electronic check-in coun-ters, industrial robots—the ongoing reallocation of tasks between labor and capital is in no sense unique to the current era. One could argue broadly, for example, that the Indus-trial Revolution was an era in which artisanal tasks were rapidly reallocated from labor to capital while, simultaneously, new cognitive engineering and repair tasks were demanded of labor.3 The era in which we currently live also oﬀers a particularly salient and econom-ically important source of task reallocation: the rapid diﬀusion of computer technology, spurred by precipitous real price declines, has likely altered the tasks performed by work-ers at their jobs and ultimately the demand for human skills. In a 2003 paper, Frank Levy, Richard Murnane and I argued that: “...(1) computer capital substitutes for workers in carrying out a limited and well-deﬁned set of cognitive and manual activities, those that can be accom-plished by following explicit rules (what we term “routine tasks”); and (2) that computer capital complements workers in carrying out problem-solving and complex communication activities (“nonroutine” tasks). Provided that 2 Fackler (2008). Fackler writes, “With Indian wages only about a tenth of wages in Japan, the Chennai [India] factory will rely more on human labor than Oppama [Japan], where robots staﬀmany assembly lines.” 3 See Goldin and Katz (1998); Katz and Goldin (2008) and Bessen (2011). Katz and Margo (2012) present evidence that the occupational distribution of U.S. manufacturing (though not the broader economy) “hollowed out” between 1850 and 1910 as new manufacturing capital replaced skilled ar-tisans, thus increasing the occupational shares of both high skill professional, technical, managerial, clerical and sales workers, and, simultaneously, low skill operatives and laborers.
5 routine and nonroutine tasks are imperfect substitutes, these observations im-ply measurable changes in the task composition of jobs” (Autor, Levy and Murnane, 2003).
The 2003 paper also oﬀered a simple production function framework that showed in barebones terms how information technology might simultaneously displace labor from routine tasks while complementing labor in non-routine tasks.4 Subsequent work has greatly enriched this framework.
In this section, I lay out a simple task-based framework proposed in Acemoglu and Autor (2011), which in turns builds on Autor, Levy and Murnane (2003), Acemoglu and Zilbotti (2001), Autor, Katz and Kearney (2006, 2008) and Costinot and Vogel (2010), among others.5 Distinct from the canonical model, this framework explicitly incorporates the potential for technological change or international trade and oﬀshoring to cause tasks that were previously performed by domestic workers to either be replaced by capital or substituted by workers abroad. This provides a natural mechanism through which tech-nological advances can lead to real non-monotone changes in the structure of employment by occupation as well as declines in the wages for certain groups of workers.
A task assignment model Consider a static environment with a unique ﬁnal good. For now, assume that the economy is closed and there is no trade in tasks (a possibility we allow for later). The unique ﬁnal good is produced by combining a continuum of tasks represented by the unit interval, [0, 1]. Suppose, to simplify the analysis, that the technology combining the services of tasks is a constant elasticity of substitution aggregator, so that the ﬁnal good is produced as Y = "ˆ 1 0 y(i) η−1 η di # η η−1 , (1) 4 In The New Division of Labor, Levy and Murnane (2004) provide a rich and nuanced discussion of the interaction between information technology and human labor in accomplishing workplace tasks.
5 Goldin and Katz also explore related ideas in many recent writings. See, for example, Katz and Goldin (2008).
6 where Y denotes the output of a unique ﬁnal good, y (i) is the “service” or production level of task i, and η is the elasticity of substitution between tasks.6 Suppose that there are three types of labor, high, medium and low skill workers, who inelastically supply H, M and L units of labor respectively. At any given point in time, a subset I ⊂[0, 1] of the potentially feasible tasks is available (the remaining tasks cannot be produced). In particular, αL (i) is the productivity of low skill workers in task i, and l (i) is the number of low skill workers allocated to task i. The remaining terms are deﬁned analogously. Similarly, αK (i) is the task productivity schedule of cap-ital and k (i) is the amount of capital allocated to task i.
