## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231)Abstract

Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) has transformative potential in healthcare to enhance patient care, personalize treatment options, train healthcare professionals, and advance medical research. This paper examines various clinical and non-clinical applications of Gen AI. In clinical settings, Gen AI supports the creation of customized treatment plans, generation of synthetic data, analysis of medical images, nursing workflow management, risk prediction, pandemic preparedness, and population health management. By automating administrative tasks such as medical documentations, Gen AI has the potential to reduce clinician burnout, freeing more time for direct patient care. Furthermore, application of Gen AI may enhance surgical outcomes by providing real-time feedback and automation of certain tasks in operating rooms. The generation of synthetic data opens new avenues for model training for diseases and simulation, enhancing research capabilities and improving predictive accuracy. In non-clinical contexts, Gen AI improves medical education, public relations, revenue cycle management, healthcare marketing etc. Its capacity for continuous learning and adaptation enables it to drive ongoing improvements in clinical and operational efficiencies, making healthcare delivery more proactive, predictive, and precise.

**Keywords:**Generative AI, Artificial intelligence, Healthcare, Large language models, Clinical excellence, Ethics, Health information technology, AI applications, ChatGPT, Medicine

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231)Introduction

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly utilized across various fields, including healthcare, where it has the potential to revolutionize clinical decision-making and enhance operational efficiencies. A significant branch within AI, Generative AI (Gen AI), has recently attracted attention for its ability to create precise data through machine learning algorithms, such as text, images, and music [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR1), [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR2), [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR5)]. AI has been defined as “a set of technologies that mimic the functions and expressions of human intelligence, specifically cognition, logic, learning, adaptivity, and creativity” [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR3)]. Gen AI is characterized by its specialized capabilities to produce new content, data, or solutions based on patterns and information learned from existing datasets [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR4)]. This capability arises from powerful foundation models that utilize advanced machine learning and deep learning techniques [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR6)]. Foundation models are “large, complex models trained on vast quantities of digital general information that can later be adapted for more specific uses” [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR7)]. These models feature two important characteristics: “emergence,” the propensity to develop new and often unexpected capabilities as they scale, and “homogenization,” the tendency to serve as a common intelligence base for varied specialized functions and AI applications [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR7)]. The generative pre-trained transformer (GPT) model, particularly GPT-3 as a large language model (LLM) and GPT-4 as a large multi-modal model (LMM), exemplifies a foundation model [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR11), [12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR12)]. Other essential AI methods, such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) and variational autoencoders (VAEs), also play a critical role.

GANs involve a pair of neural networks—the generator and the discriminator—that work against each other. The generator strives to create data as realistically as possible. At the same time, the discriminator evaluates this data against real-world examples, iterating until the generated data is indistinguishable from actual data, at least to the discriminator [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR9), [10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR10)]. According to the market research firm Market.us, the global net value of Gen AI in healthcare was approximately $800 million in 2022, with projections to grow to $17.2 billion by 2032 [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR8)]. The healthcare industry has embraced AI-powered solutions, allocating substantial funding to explore their practical benefits. A recent survey from the Deloitte Center for Health Solutions reveals that approximately 75% of large healthcare organizations are currently using or planning to scale up generative AI in their operations [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR13)]. In 2023, Gen AI technologies made substantial advancements, as evidenced by a recent study in which ChatGPT surpassed physicians in both quality and empathy metrics [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR14)], and Google’s MedPaLM-2 LLM achieved expert-level scores on the United States Medical Licensing Examination [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR15)]. Furthermore, the first drug entirely designed with Gen AI entered clinical trials [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR15)], while new GPUs are expected to reduce LLM costs in 2024 [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR16)].

The healthcare industry is grappling with numerous systemic challenges, many of which have been intensified by the COVID-19 pandemic, affecting both workforce stability and patient care delivery. The pandemic has exacerbated labor shortages in healthcare, making workforce challenges a top concern for hospital CEOs [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR17)]. The Association of American Medical Colleges predicts a shortfall of 124,000 physicians by 2034 in the US [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR18)]. The industry also faces a shortage of 1.1 million nurses [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR19)], resulting in longer waiting times to see a clinician. In 2019, the average wait time to see a physician was 26 days, with patients often making numerous phone calls to schedule visits [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR13)]. Provider burnout is another significant concern, with 81% of the clinicians reporting high-stress levels primarily due to increased workloads and administrative burdens [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR20)]. Clinicians have low trust in leadership, with fewer than 45% trusting their organization’s leadership to prioritize patient care [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR20)]. Financially, the healthcare sector struggles with rising operational costs, shrinking reimbursement rates, and low profitability margins [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR21)]. Despite increasing national healthcare expenditures, US life expectancy has declined recently, and healthcare accessibility remains a significant issue, especially in underserved communities [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR13)]. Gen AI has the potential to address some of these challenges by improving healthcare efficiency, reducing administrative burdens, and enhancing patient care [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR22)]. Given that Gen AI is a relatively new technology, literature is scarce on its clinical and non-clinical uses. This review article aims to explore the potential applications of Gen AI for clinical and non-clinical uses.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231)Clinical Applications

### Tailored Treatment Plans

Generative AI has the potential to improve personalized medicine by analyzing extensive health datasets and identifying patterns for tailored treatment plans, thereby significantly enhancing patient outcomes. For instance, a research study demonstrated that deep learning models can predict cardiovascular risk factors from retinal images and pinpoint biomarkers for complex diseases, thus formulating precise, personalized treatment plans [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR25)]. Using GANs to simulate virtual patient populations also helps predict treatment outcomes across diverse demographic and genetic backgrounds. Scientists have successfully utilized GANs to generate synthetic patient data, facilitating the creation of personalized treatment plans, especially for rare diseases where data is scarce or non-existent [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR26)].

The Generative Tensorial Reinforcement Learning (GENTRL) model is particularly adept at designing drugs tailored to specific biological mechanisms, ensuring that drugs interact optimally with biological targets relevant to an individual patient’s condition [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR27)]. This level of specificity significantly supports the development of personalized treatment plans. It also optimizes resources in genetic testing by streamlining workflows and automating tasks, making personalized medicine more accessible. Additionally, Gen AI enhances pharmacogenomic optimization by analyzing data to predict individual medication responses, leading to customized prescriptions and improved treatment outcomes [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR28)]. Gen AI also processes wearable device data in real-time to monitor vital health indicators, facilitating early intervention and personalized treatment strategies [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR23)].

In mental health, Gen AI creates interactive tools for cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) [[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR24)]. The TP-GAN (treatment planning with GAN) framework, a cGANs-based model, represents a significant advancement in the automation of prostate brachytherapy planning. By reducing the planning time and potentially the variability associated with manual planning, this approach can lead to more standardized treatment plans and improve overall treatment efficacy [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR29)]. AI algorithms also assist in diagnosing dental health conditions such as caries and periodontal diseases through image analysis and data interpretation, leading to timely interventions, personalized treatment plans, and enhanced treatment outcomes [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR30)]. The implications of Gen AI for personalized medicine are vast, as evidenced by recent studies exploring its role in improving the diagnosis and management of rare genetic disorders. These technologies analyze large datasets for accurate classification and employ facial recognition to aid in diagnosing genetic conditions [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR31)].

### Surgical Care

Surgical teams are increasingly leveraging AI to enhance surgical procedures. Before surgery, surgeons must synthesize medical literature with comprehensive patient data, including imaging, medical history, and relevant laboratory results, while adhering to the most recent treatment guidelines and protocols [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR32)]. Gen AI models can integrate, analyze, and interpret these complex datasets, expediting surgical decision-making and improving the timeliness of treatment [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR33)]. Since patients’ understanding of surgical procedures is crucial, Gen AI can play a vital role in educating patients about surgical procedures and associated risks, both pre- and post-surgery [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR34)]. Additionally, Gen AI can be used for quality assurance, to detect errors and suggest new policies to improve patient care and ultimately improve health outcomes [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR35)].

A notable collaboration between Johnson & Johnson’s MedTech unit and Nvidia has been established to enhance surgical processes by integrating AI from pre- to post-operative stages. This initiative uses AI to analyze surgical videos and automate the extensive documentation required after surgery [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR36)]. Other surgical applications include the introduction of real-time AI annotation in urologic robotic surgeries to enhance surgical training and quality metrics. This technology aims to automatically annotate surgical videos, providing real-time feedback and support to surgeons and trainees, thereby increasing the safety, efficiency, and educational value of surgical procedures [[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR37)]. AI also has the potential to augment surgical decision-making through personalized risk assessments [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR38)]. In recent years, minimally invasive surgical techniques such as laparoscopic surgery (LS) and robotic surgery (RS) have become increasingly prevalent. The ultimate goal of RS development is the creation of fully autonomous AI-powered surgical instruments. Although current systems require human supervision, their success in procedures like prostatectomies (Da Vinci system) and bowel suturing (STAR robot) showcases the potential of AI in enhancing surgical outcomes [[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR39)].

### Provider Burnout

Provider burnout is one of the major challenges for healthcare systems worldwide. The Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC) declared physician burnout a public health crisis [[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR40)]. According to a 2019 study, more than half of US physicians have experienced at least one common burnout symptom, such as a reduced sense of personal accomplishment, emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and the inability to connect with family members. As the same study reports, burnouts substantially negatively impact the US economy, costing approximately $4.6 billion annually [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR41)]. Gen AI tools have shown promise in reducing physician burnout and enhancing efficiency. Large language models, such as generative pre-trained transformer 4 (GPT-4; OpenAI), have shown the ability to draft empathetic responses to online patient questions [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR42)].

A recent study found that using GPT-4 to generate draft replies to patient inbox messages improved mental task load and work exhaustion, reducing burnout scores for medical professionals. However, no improvements in overall response time were noted [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR42)]. The study also showed that gastroenterology and hepatology nurses had higher draft utilization, a trend towards time saved, and positive net promoter scores, suggesting that future Gen AI tools may vary according to specific practice patterns and workflows [[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR43)]. These findings underscore the potential positive impact of Gen AI in healthcare settings to enhance efficiency and reduce burnout among physicians and other healthcare professionals.

Another study found that lower satisfaction and higher frustration with Electronic Health Records (EHRs) were significantly associated with physician burnout [[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR44)]. Gen AI has the potential to not only reduce the documentation burden but also remove the computer from the physician-patient interaction and bring the “care” back to healthcare [[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR45)]. This allows the physician to assess the patient’s situation quickly while the AI summarizes and surfaces the relevant data. Companies like Axtria are using Gen AI to improve patient and physician care and advance core information management capabilities such as master data and multi-modal data [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR46)].

### Nursing

Gen AI demonstrates the potential to enhance patient care, optimize workflows, and advance nursing education and training. AI-enhanced simulations are increasingly integrated into nursing education, utilizing AI technologies to create realistic scenarios that replicate complex medical situations. This enables nursing students to acquire practical skills in a controlled environment, mitigating the risks associated with real-world scenarios. A recent review underscores the potential of AI in medical education, highlighting its ability to tailor learning experiences and refine clinical decision-making skills for healthcare professionals [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR47)]. Other applications of AI systems include predicting patient fall risks, generating personalized treatment plans, and automating routine tasks such as medical documentation, allowing nurses more time for direct patient care [[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR48)].

AI-powered tools like voice-to-text transcription, automated charting, and intelligent data entry could reduce the time spent on documentation by 21–30%, saving nurses 95–134 h per year. Streamlining administrative processes like patient admissions, transfers, and discharges with AI could save nurses 37–46% of the time spent on these tasks, equating to 32–40 h per year [[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR48)]. This workflow optimization ensures efficient utilization of human resources, alleviating the burden on overburdened staff and potentially enhancing job satisfaction and retention [[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR49)].

Studies have revealed that AI chatbots can provide social support to patients, serving as a practical and accessible means of improving patient well-being, particularly in situations where traditional interventions are limited, such as during pandemics [[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR50)]. A recent study explores the transformative potential of Gen AI in nursing practices in Taiwan, focusing on the capabilities of the A + Nurse system, a digital assistant designed to automate routine nursing tasks, enhance communication within healthcare teams, and integrate current medical information into nursing workflows [[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR51)]. Prompt engineering is critical to effectively interact with AI, as precise prompts yield desired outputs [[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR52)]. Educators can leverage Gen AI-based models like ChatGPT to enrich teaching and learning experiences, including creating virtual simulation scenarios, developing lesson plans, and designing assessments [[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR53)].

### Synthetic Data Generation

Synthetic data, as defined by the Royal Society and The Alan Turing Institute, is data that has been generated using a purpose-built mathematical model or algorithm to address a data science task [[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR54)]. GANs and VAEs, among other technologies, can be used to generate synthetic data that safely replaces sensitive patient information while complying with strict privacy regulations such as GDPR and HIPAA [[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR55)–[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR57)]. Generated through generative models, synthetic data has numerous applications, including AI model training, validation, realistic simulations for medical training, and decision support systems, and enables researchers to conduct large-scale studies and analyses without real patient data [[58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR58)]. Synthetic EHR and imaging data, developed using GANs, aid research and enhance diagnostic algorithms without compromising patient privacy [[59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR59)].

A recent study describes how synthetic healthcare records can be generated using convolutional GANs and convolutional autoencoders (CorGAN). This architecture captures correlations between adjacent medical features and addresses the challenge of generating discrete data outputs [[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR60)]. Synthetic data, when produced using techniques like Gaussian Copulas (GC), Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (CGAN), VAEs, and Copula-GAN, can supplement real datasets, enhancing the performance and robustness of non-invasive diabetes prediction models [[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR61)]. While synthetic data generation is useful in medical tasks, data is often scarce to train robust predictive models. For instance, a 2023 study demonstrated that augmenting real datasets with synthetic chest radiograph images generated by latent diffusion models can improve classification performance [[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR62)].

Additionally, another recent study showed that tailored prompts provided to ChatGPT can produce task-specific synthetic data, substantially improving performance in tasks such as biological named entity recognition and relation extraction [[63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR63)]. Synthetic data is invaluable for training models and analysis and in scenarios where data is missing from healthcare databases, potentially skewing clinical decisions [[64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR64)]. MDClone, a startup in this field, offers a platform that provides synthetic health data, eliminating the need for direct access to patient records while ensuring regulatory compliance [[65](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR65)].

### Medical Image Analysis

Medical image analysis can be defined as the process of examining medical images for diagnosis, improved treatment planning, and disease monitoring. This analysis plays a pivotal role in fields such as radiology, neurology, and oncology, where examining large volumes of images and data is crucial for extracting significant information [[66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR66)]. Gen AI synthesizes, augments, and interprets heterogeneous complex images across various modalities, such as X-rays, MRIs, and CT scans. AI models such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), among several others, facilitate the synthesis of anatomically precise images for training and education, addressing the shortage of certain types of images and the subtleties of ethical and privacy issues [[67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR67)]. GANs can synthesize MRI brain images specifically to enhance the detection accuracy of neurological disorders using machine-learning models without violating patient privacy regulations [[67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR67)].

Furthermore, studies have shown that GANs can be used for data augmentation in liver lesion detection, where synthetic images improve the diagnostic accuracy of the convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that utilize these images [[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR68)]. The CGAN model, enhanced with a 3D discriminator and adaptive identity loss, significantly improves synthetic MRI generation, especially in studying Alzheimer’s disease progression. This addresses the limitations of previous models that primarily operate in 2D and suffer from spatial artifacts [[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR69)]. Gen AI is also highly effective for anomaly detection and segmentation, which are crucial for early disease detection and intervention. For instance, developing the AnoGAN model for segmenting anomalies in retinal images aids in early diabetic retinopathy diagnosis [[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR71)].

A study investigating the use of GAN to segment MRI images of the brain showed that the GAN technique outperformed traditional methods, achieving an average Dice coefficient of 0.89 [[70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR70)]. Another study utilizing GAN to generate synthetic images of the retina found that these images were as effective as real images in training deep-learning models for diabetic retinopathy detection [[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR71)]. GANs are also employed in image enhancement and reconstruction, such as enhancing low-dose CT images to promote safer imaging practices with reduced radiation exposure [[72](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR72)]. Gen AI has the potential to not only reduce healthcare disparities through improved diagnostic accuracy but also to usher in a new era of personalized medicine, where patient-specific models will aid in surgical planning and make treatments more individualized [[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR73)].

### Population Health Management

Gen AI can play a crucial role in predicting health trends, personalizing medicine, and optimizing healthcare services by analyzing vast datasets and tailoring health interventions to meet service demands. A promising application of deep learning is to interpret biological data and make predictions of disease within populations, such as using neural networks to analyze genetic information for early disease detection. AI considerably brings value-based care for individual patients into practice by personalizing treatment plans and improving patient outcomes, contributing to improved population health [[74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR74), [75](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR75)].

By Integrating individual-level health data with socio-markers(quantifiable social conditions)— AI enhances disease surveillance and predicts health risks more accurately [[76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR76)]. Using mobile technologies and the Internet of Things (IoT) allows for real-time health monitoring. It enhances the ability of health systems to deliver care remotely, which is crucial during events like the Ebola outbreak [[77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR77)]. For example, AI algorithms can analyze individual health data alongside socioeconomic factors to predict which populations are mostly at risk for certain diseases, allowing for targeted interventions and resources. In addition, IoT devices like wearable fitness trackers can provide continuous health monitoring for individuals in remote areas, enabling healthcare providers to remotely monitor and treat patients during emergencies such as disease outbreaks [[78](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR78)].

Gen AI can streamline service delivery and operations for public health and community health workers by reducing administrative burdens, optimizing supply chain processes, and fostering tailored interactions with diverse communities [[79](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR79)]. AI models excel at analyzing extensive and varied datasets to forecast outcomes like hospital readmissions and recommend proactive measures for patient well-being [[80](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR80)]. Further, by categorizing populations based on risk factors, AI models enhance the effectiveness of interventions by targeting high-risk groups. In addition, AI can help predict the population’s health needs, optimizing resource allocation. Health Catalyst and ClosedLoop.ai also focus on using the potential of AI for predictive analytics and population health management, thereby personalizing individual care plans for members [[81](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR81)]. As Gen AI continues to evolve, it is poised to pioneer a new population health era by harnessing a wide range of data sources, including real-time health data from wearable technology, to deliver increasingly precise interventions and drive enhanced health outcomes for entire populations.

### Risk Prediction of Pandemic Preparedness

The outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic, coupled with rapid advancements in AI and ML algorithms, has paved the way for significant investments and developments in AI and ML for pandemic management and surveillance [[82](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR82), [83](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR83)]. Examples of AI use during the pandemic include disease forecasting, enhancing outbreak detection, and monitoring disease progression [[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR84)]. Gen AI processes real-time data from diverse sources, including social media, health reports, and environmental data, to identify early signs of emerging infectious diseases. Detecting unusual patterns or clusters can contribute to early warning systems [[85](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR85)]. AI has also supported public health initiatives through public policy efforts [[86](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR86)].

Additionally, socioeconomic factors have been modeled to gain improved insights into pandemic management [[87](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR87)]. A recent application of AI during the COVID-19 pandemic, spanning from 2020 to as recent as 2023, involves NERVTAG, a UK Government Advisory Group. They developed the QCOVID3 risk prediction algorithm to anticipate potential hospitalizations and deaths among those infected with COVID-19. Since this algorithm was implemented in Wales, UK, and its results were based on that area’s demographics, it can only be considered successful within that region [[88](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR88)]. Similarly, the Australian government developed a COVID-19 Pandemic Vulnerability Index (CPVI) to assess vulnerability across different areas in Australia, thereby helping to delay the pandemic’s exponential growth and mitigate its impact on communities and the healthcare system. This widespread experiment covered 563 zones, each with an average population of 45,000, encompassing the entire country. Australia’s CPVI evaluates vulnerability across four subsections: socio-demographics, medical conditions, public works, and land use patterns. By analyzing these factors, the index provides a more robust understanding of areas at risk during a pandemic [[89](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR89)]. Both NERVTAG’s algorithm and Australia’s CPVI have been successful in their respective regions. However, both relied on ample data and specific factors differentiating them from other COVID-19 tools. Researchers have also explored whether solely comorbidity data, socioeconomic status, age and race could predict COVID-19 death rates.

To determine how these factors relate to hospitalization, ICU admission, ventilator use, and mortality, researchers analyzed a dataset of 1.4 million diagnosed COVID-19 cases [[90](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR90)]. During the QCOVID3 risk prediction experiments, scientists found that the predictions closely matched actual numbers for deaths and admissions up to the fifteenth predicted risk level, beyond which the predictions for deaths were higher and lower for admissions [[88](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR88)]. In the CPVI experiment, the index indicated that vulnerability to COVID-19 is highest in more populated areas, whereas it is much lower in rural areas [[89](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR89)]. However, graphs based solely on comorbidity proved insignificant, as the comorbidity-predicted death rates were far from actual outcomes in the experiment in the US and other selected countries.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231)Non-Clinical Applications

### Medical Education and Training

Gen AI has the potential to enhance medical education by producing realistic medical images and simulating patient interactions. [[91](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR91)] It allows students to explore a variety of medical conditions, including rare diseases and complex clinical cases, through detailed images. Advanced frameworks such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) facilitate synthesizing these educational tools, thereby expanding the range of learning materials available to students. GANs, for example, can generate synthetic medical images for educational purposes, enriching the pool of diverse and essential learning materials [[92](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR92)]. Another critical benefit of Gen AI in medical education is its potential to improve machine translation, fostering knowledge exchange and global collaboration. The advent of Gen AI technology has enhanced the accuracy and sophistication of machine translation. For instance, eBay’s Machine Translation service demonstrates a 7% increase in translation accuracy over its previous iterations, highlighting the potential of AI to overcome language barriers [[93](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR93)].

Additionally, Gen AI models have been utilized in medical education and surgical training to create dynamic, interactive models of patient anatomy, allowing students to gain theoretical and practical experience without relying on real patients [[94](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR94)]. Large Language Models (LLMs) are invaluable in medical research, literature review, and writing because they can quickly extract accurate data with appropriate usage of terminologies and language [[95](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR95)]. LLMs like GPT-4 can provide personalized learning experiences through adaptive educational content tailored to learners’ needs. The increase in dermatological datasets with synthetic images has improved the accuracy of AI model classifications of skin diseases, making them effective and valuable tools in medical education [[96](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR96)]. Gen AI has the potential to personalize education by adapting content according to students’ performance and preferences, showcasing AI’s ability to cater to diverse learning needs [[97](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR97)]. Western Michigan University has enhanced its medical curriculum with over 100 h of simulation training, providing realistic patient scenarios and feedback from professors to prepare students for real-world medical situations [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR23)]. As Gen AI technology continues to evolve, its application in medical education is expected to facilitate more advanced simulations and personalized learning pathways, preparing professionals for the dynamically changing field of medicine.

### Revenue Cycle Management

Gen AI integrated with Health Revenue Cycle Management (RCM) automates and enhances various sectors in healthcare financial operations, including automated data entry, patient communication, documentation of lab procedures, compliance, procurement, contracting, and fraud detection [[98](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR98)]. Utilizing AI for patient scrutiny and treatment records facilitates the automatic generation of accurate billing codes with fewer errors, ensuring compliance with frequently changing regulations [[99](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR99)]. Moreover, Gen AI can predict personalized patient communication strategies, offer predictive analytics for financial planning, and provide insights into preventive measures to reduce claim denials. Automating administrative tasks like coding and billing significantly reduces the workload for healthcare staff, allowing them to focus more on patient care [[100](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR100)]. Leveraging AI-generated insights to identify and address the root causes of claim denials can lead to more efficient and accurate RCM processes [[101](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR101)].

According to a study by the Deloitte Center for Health Solutions, Gen AI can save between 41% and 50% of the time spent by revenue cycle professionals across all revenue cycle stages, including patient access, clinical revenue cycle, and patient financial services [[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR48)]. For example, Codametrix and Adonis.io exemplify the application of advanced technologies in healthcare RCM. Codametrix Inc. uses Natural Language Processing (NLP) to extract data from unstructured medical texts. It transforms it into structured data for medical language interpretation, thus facilitating analysis, billing, and population health management [[102](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR102)]. Adonis.io integrates revenue intelligence and automation throughout the process, enhancing efficiency and effectiveness in healthcare RCM [[103](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR103)].

### Healthcare Marketing and Public Relations

Gen AI can assist healthcare organizations with marketing and public relations (PR) by personalizing content, automating customer support, and identifying areas for optimization in marketing campaigns [[104](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR104)]. By analyzing large datasets, Gen AI can create customized content, such as health tips and articles, that promote engagement between patients and healthcare providers [[105](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR105)]. It enhances personalized patient service by fine-tuning responses based on individual needs, supporting live agents, and providing real-time feedback, leading to higher customer satisfaction, faster issue resolution, and lower costs. Additionally, Gen AI can optimize supply chains by predicting disruptions, enabling scenario analysis, and assisting in supplier evaluations, allowing quicker adaptation to market changes and improved operational efficiency [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR13)]. Evidence indicates that one-third of individuals in the United States first search online for health information before seeking professional medical advice [[106](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR106)].

Research shows a rising trend in individuals investigating mental health symptoms online, with mental health queries increasing significantly [[107](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR107)]. The development of digital mental health tools, such as AI-driven chatbots, has escalated to meet this growing demand. This highlights the critical importance of enhanced emotional intelligence in general AI systems, especially in providing empathetic and personalized user interactions. Generative AI revolutionizes strategic content analysis in marketing by identifying high-performing content types and messaging strategies [[108](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR108)]. The integrative Gen AI-equipped tools add competitive advantages to health organizations in patient engagements and public interactions, underlining its transformational potential for health marketing and PR [[109](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11739231#CR109)].

args.summary:
This peer-reviewed review article, published in the Journal of Medical Systems (J Med Syst, 2025 Jan 16;49(1):10, DOI: 10.1007/s10916-024-02136-1), examines the clinical and non-clinical applications of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) in healthcare. The article, authored by Soumitra S. Bhuyan and colleagues from Rutgers University, Rice University, and other institutions, was received June 27, 2024 and accepted December 19, 2024, under an open-access Creative Commons license (PMCID: PMC11739231, PMID: 39820845).

Key findings on the transformative potential of Gen AI in healthcare include:

**Market Context:** The global net value of Gen AI in healthcare was approximately $800 million in 2022, projected to grow to $17.2 billion by 2032. About 75% of large healthcare organizations are currently using or planning to scale up generative AI. In 2023, ChatGPT surpassed physicians in both quality and empathy metrics, and Google's MedPaLM-2 achieved expert-level scores on the US Medical Licensing Examination.

**Clinical Applications:**
1. **Tailored Treatment Plans:** Gen AI improves personalized medicine through deep learning models that predict cardiovascular risk factors from retinal images, GANs for simulating virtual patient populations, the GENTRL model for drug design, pharmacogenomic optimization, and real-time wearable device data processing. TP-GAN automates prostate brachytherapy planning, and AI assists in dental and rare genetic disorder diagnostics.

2. **Surgical Care:** Gen AI expedites surgical decision-making, educates patients, provides real-time AI annotation in urologic robotic surgeries, and supports quality assurance. Johnson & Johnson's MedTech unit partnered with Nvidia to integrate AI from pre- to post-operative stages. AI-powered surgical systems like the Da Vinci system and STAR robot showcase autonomous surgical potential.

3. **Provider Burnout:** Physician burnout costs the US economy approximately $4.6 billion annually. GPT-4 draft replies to patient inbox messages improved mental task load and reduced burnout scores, though response times did not improve. Gen AI can reduce documentation burden and remove the computer from physician-patient interactions.

4. **Nursing:** AI-powered voice-to-text transcription and automated charting could reduce documentation time by 21-30% (saving nurses 95-134 hours per year), and streamlining admissions/transfers/discharges could save 37-46% of time (32-40 hours per year). The A+Nurse system in Taiwan demonstrates these applications.

5. **Synthetic Data Generation:** GANs and VAEs generate synthetic data that complies with privacy regulations (GDPR, HIPAA), enabling model training, validation, and research without real patient data. Techniques include CorGAN, Gaussian Copulas, CGAN, VAEs, and Copula-GAN. MDClone provides a commercial synthetic health data platform.

6. **Medical Image Analysis:** GANs synthesize MRI brain images for neurological disorder detection, enhance liver lesion detection, and improve diabetic retinopathy diagnosis. A GAN-based MRI segmentation achieved an average Dice coefficient of 0.89. Gen AI also enhances low-dose CT images, promoting safer imaging with reduced radiation exposure.

7. **Population Health Management:** AI integrates individual-level health data with socio-markers for disease surveillance and health risk prediction, uses IoT/wearable devices for real-time monitoring, and forecasts hospital readmissions. Companies like Health Catalyst and ClosedLoop.ai focus on AI for predictive analytics.

8. **Pandemic Risk Prediction:** AI was used extensively during COVID-19, including the UK's NERVTAG QCOVID3 risk prediction algorithm and Australia's COVID-19 Pandemic Vulnerability Index (CPVI), which covered 563 zones with average populations of 45,000.

**Non-Clinical Applications:**
1. **Medical Education and Training:** GANs and VAEs generate synthetic medical images for education, enhance machine translation (eBay's service showed 7% improvement), and enable dynamic interactive models of patient anatomy. Western Michigan University enhanced its curriculum with over 100 hours of simulation training.

2. **Revenue Cycle Management:** Gen AI automates data entry, billing codes, compliance, and fraud detection. Deloitte found Gen AI can save 41-50% of time for revenue cycle professionals. Codametrix uses NLP to extract data from unstructured medical texts, and Adonis.io integrates revenue intelligence and automation.

3. **Healthcare Marketing and Public Relations:** Gen AI personalizes content, automates customer support, and optimizes marketing campaigns. One-third of US individuals search online for health information before seeking professional advice, and mental health queries are increasing significantly.

The article concludes that Gen AI's capacity for continuous learning and adaptation enables ongoing improvements in clinical and operational efficiencies, making healthcare delivery more proactive, predictive, and precise. It addresses systemic challenges including labor shortages (124,000 physician shortfall predicted by 2034, 1.1 million nurse shortage), 81% clinician high-stress levels, and declining US life expectancy despite increasing healthcare expenditures.

## Abstract

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has had a profound impact on biomedicine and health, both in professional work and in education. Based on large language models (LLMs), generative AI has been found to perform as well as humans in simulated situations taking medical board exams, answering clinical questions, solving clinical cases, applying clinical reasoning, and summarizing information. Generative AI is also being used widely in education, performing well in academic courses and their assessments. This review summarizes the successes of LLMs and highlights some of their challenges in the context of education, most notably aspects that may undermine the acquisition of knowledge and skills for professional work. It then provides recommendations for best practices to overcome the shortcomings of LLM use in education. Although there are challenges for the use of generative AI in education, all students and faculty, in biomedicine and health and beyond, must have understanding of it and be competent in its use.

The overall goal of this review is to present the key issues for generative artificial intelligence (AI) in the context of biomedical and health professions education. Biomedical and health professions students are defined broadly as any individuals who work professionally in healthcare, individual health, public health, and research. These include clinicians such as physician, nurses, pharmacists, etc., as well as those who do not provide clinical care, such as administrators, project managers, researchers, educators, and more. Also among these are those who work in biomedical and health informatics, data science, and related fields. Although the review is focused on AI in biomedicine and health, it draws on areas outside this broad domain where additional perspectives may be insightful.

AI has been defined in many ways, and this author prefers the notion that it consists of information systems and algorithms that are capable of performing tasks that are associated with human intelligence ([1](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B1)). AI is sometimes classified into two broad categories ([2](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B2)):

*   ▪ Predictive AI uses data and algorithms to predict some output, e.g., diagnosis, treatment recommendation, prognosis, etc. 
*   ▪ Generative AI generates new output based on prompts, e.g., text, images, etc. 

A large part of the modern success of AI is due to machine learning (ML), whose origins have been attributed to Arthur Samuel in the 1950s and which has been defined as computer programs that learn without being explicitly programmed ([3](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B3)). The most success in applying ML to AI has come from so-called deep learning, which is based on many-layered neural networks ([4](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B4)). Predictive AI has typically used supervised ML, where models are trained with labeled or annotated data split into training and test data. On the other hand, generative AI systems are mostly trained with unsupervised ML due to the much larger sizes of training data and their generative, i.e., non-predictive, uses, although some supervised ML takes place to avoid inappropriate generation, e.g., racist or sexist language ([5](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B5)).

Generative AI had been around for a number of years but came to the fore with the release of ChatGPT by OpenAI on November 30, 2022. Based on large language models (LLMs) trained using deep learning with massive amounts of digital text, generative AI systems have had a profound impact in biomedicine and health, including in education. A number of reviews describe LLMs generally ([6](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B6), [7](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B7)) as well as their applications in biomedicine ([8](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B8%20B9)–[10](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B10)).

This review focuses on generative AI, with a particular perspective on its implications for biomedical and health education. Some of the discussion may go beyond education, but only if there is some relevance to education. The review begins by describing the use of generative AI. It then discusses the successes and limitations of generative AI, especially those that apply to education. The review then covers issues specific to education, describing challenges and accomplishments, and then wraps up with future directions.

Since the introduction of ChatGPT and other systems, generative AI has been rapidly taken up by a large proportion of people around the world, including biomedical and health professionals, students, consumers, and others. A survey from mid-2023 found that 56% of college students stated they had used AI on assignments or exams, with 54% agreeing that the use of AI tools on college coursework counts could, in some instances, constitute cheating or plagiarism ([11](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B11)). A survey from mid-2024 of teachers, students, and parents found 49–52% of each group using generative AI frequently, 18–33% using it occasionally, and less than a quarter of each group stating they had never used it ([12](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B12)). Both of these surveys noted positive views of AI but also a lack of consistent or comprehensive policies by educational institutions and faculty within them.

Other surveys have looked at larger populations and noted similar large-scale uptake of generative AI. One analysis from August 2024 found that 39% of working-age adults use generative AI ([13](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B13)). It also found that more than 24% of such individuals used it in their work at least once in the week, and approximately 10% used it every day at work. The authors of the survey noted that the adoption of generative AI has been faster than even adoption of personal computers or the Internet. Another survey, this one of over 1,000 physicians from the United Kingdom, found that 20% reported using generative AI tools in clinical practice ([14](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B14)). Among those who used such tools, 29% reported using them to generate documentation after patient appointments and 28% to develop a differential diagnosis.

A survey of 2,428 US adults of varying age, geographic location, and race/ethnicity carried out by the Kaiser Family Foundation found that approximately two-thirds of respondents reported some use or interaction with AI ([15](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B15)). However, use of AI chatbots for health information and advice was much lower than for social media or Internet search ([Table 1](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#t1)).

An avalanche of research has been published on the results of generative AI applied to biomedical and health tasks. Many of these studies have focused on answering questions, especially those on examinations, including medical board tests. Others have expanded to solving clinical cases or carrying out other clinical tasks, although few involve actual users and almost none have been implemented in real-world settings. Nonetheless, the activities considered in these studies impact education in that they are related to tasks used in educational activities, including student practice and assessments. The following categories of research are described in this section: medical board examinations, other medical examinations, answering clinical questions, solving clinical cases, assessing clinical reasoning, summarization tasks, predictive tasks, performance in graduation courses in biomedicine and health, and performance in academic courses beyond biomedicine and health.

3.1. Medical Board Examinations
One of the most widely used datasets for LLM evaluation comes from a set of sample questions from the US Medical Licensing Exam (USMLE) ([16](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B16)). This multiple-choice question (MCQ) exam is taken in three steps during the second and fourth years of medical school and then in the first year out of medical school. The dataset, called MedQA, includes 12,723 questions in English (and others in Chinese). An early and highly publicized success of the original ChatGPT using the GPT-3.5 LLM on the MedQA dataset was to achieve a score of over 60%, which would equate to a passing grade ([17](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B17)). This level was surpassed by other LLMs, including GPT-4 ([18](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B18)) and Google's Med-Gemini ([19](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B19)). The most recent leader in the USMLE arms race is OpenAI's o1 model, which scored 96.0% ([20](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B20), [21](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B21)) ([Figure 1](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#f1)). LLMs have even been found to perform well on portions of the USMLE exam covering soft skills, e.g., communication skills, ethics, empathy, and professionalism ([22](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B22)).

Figure 1 Incremental progress of large language models on the US Medical Licensing Exam's MedQA dataset over time ([20](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B20), [21](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B21)). Figure adapted with permission from Reference [20](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B20).

This has led to the assessment of LLMs on other US-based medical board exams, with similar success being found, among others, in the fields of radiology ([23](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B23), [24](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B24)), neurosurgery ([25](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B25)), and clinical informatics ([26](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B26)). LLM success on board exams is not limited to the United States. In Israel, the scores of all resident physicians who completed board exams in the specialties of pediatrics, internal medicine, psychiatry, obstetrics/gynecology, and general surgery in 2022 were compared to those of GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 ([27](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B27)). As seen in [Figure 2](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#f2), GPT-4 passed the exams in all of the specialties, scoring comparably in internal medicine and general surgery, better in psychiatry, and inferiorly in pediatrics and obstetrics/gynecology.

Figure 2 LLM success versus physicians completing residency training in five specialties in Israel. The range is shown for all test takers, human and LLM. The dotted line is the passing level for the exam for each specialty. Abbreviation: LLM, large language model. Figure adapted with permission from Reference [27](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B27).

3.2. Other Medical Examinations
Success with generative AI has been shown with other kinds of physician examinations. On an objective structured clinical examination, which provides a series of questions simulating a clinical encounter, ChatGPT-3.5 scored better than a group of physicians in Singapore in a simulation of assessment for membership in the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists ([28](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B28)). Likewise, ChatGPT-4 achieved 81% correct on the Ophthalmology Knowledge Assessment Program ([29](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B29)) and 73.3% on the Nephrology Self-Assessment Program ([30](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B30)).

Many medical specialties give in-training exams to residents and fellows in training. On a family medicine in-training exam, ChatGPT-4 scored 86.5% and outperformed third-year resident national averages in one study ([31](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B31)) and scored 84% on another ([32](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B32)). The latter study also found that GPT-4 was able to integrate new information and carry out self-correction when needed. Likewise, on a radiology in-training exam, GPT-4 achieved results comparable to between second-year and third-year radiology residents ([33](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B33)). On this exam, performance on image-based questions was significantly poorer at 45.4% compared to text-only questions at 80.0%. As has been seen in some other studies, when questions were given again, GPT-4 chose a different answer approximately 25% of the time. Fine-tuning the LLM did not improve accuracy in this study.

3.3. Answering Clinical Questions
The success of generative AI is not limited to exams. Other research has assessed its ability to answer clinical questions in a variety of medical disciplines. One of the most studied applications areas has been cancer. One study assessed ChatGPT output for concordance with National Comprehensive Cancer Network treatment guidelines for breast, prostate, and lung cancer. The study found an overall concordance 61.9% of the time, with 34.3% of outputs recommending one or more nonconcordant treatments. The study also found that responses were hallucinated, i.e., were not part of any recommended treatment, in 12.5% of outputs ([34](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B34)). Another study assessed several different LLMs and found varying performance on different categories of oncology questions, with ChatGPT-4 the only LLM to score higher than 50% ([35](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B35)).

An additional study assessed the ability of GPT-4 to answer clinically relevant questions regarding the management of patients with pancreatic cancer, metastatic colorectal cancer, and hepatocellular carcinoma from clinical practice guidelines ([36](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756#right-ref-B36)). ## Publication: Generative Artificial Intelligence: Implications for Biomedical and Health Professions Education

**Source:** Annual Review of Biomedical Data Science, Volume 8 (2025), pages 355-380. Review article (Open Access).

**Author:** William Hersh, Division of Informatics, Clinical Epidemiology and Translational Science, Department of Medicine, School of Medicine, Oregon Health & Science University, Portland, Oregon (email: hersh@ohsu.edu).

**Citation:** William Hersh. 2025. Generative Artificial Intelligence: Implications for Biomedical and Health Professions Education. Annual Review of Biomedical Data Science 8:355-380. DOI: 10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-103123-094756.

**Publication Details:** First published as a Review in Advance on April 09, 2025; Volume publication date August 2025. Licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. Online ISSN: 2574-3414.

**Abstract/Overview:** This review examines the impact of generative AI (based on large language models, LLMs) on biomedicine and health, with particular focus on implications for biomedical and health professions education. Generative AI has been shown to perform as well as humans in simulated medical board exams, answering clinical questions, solving clinical cases, applying clinical reasoning, and summarizing information. The review summarizes LLM successes, highlights challenges that may undermine knowledge and skill acquisition for professional work, and provides recommendations for best practices to overcome shortcomings of LLM use in education. A key conclusion is that all students and faculty in biomedicine and health (and beyond) must understand and be competent in generative AI use.

**Key Sections and Findings:**

1. **Introduction:** Defines biomedical and health professions students broadly (clinicians plus administrators, project managers, researchers, educators, and those in informatics/data science). Distinguishes predictive AI (predicts outputs from data) from generative AI (generates new output from prompts). Notes generative AI gained prominence with ChatGPT's release by OpenAI on November 30, 2022. Machine learning origins attributed to Arthur Samuel in the 1950s; deep learning based on many-layered neural networks.

2. **Usage of Generative AI:**
   - A mid-2023 survey found 56% of college students had used AI on assignments or exams, with 54% agreeing AI use on coursework could sometimes constitute cheating/plagiarism.
   - A mid-2024 survey found 49-52% of teachers, students, and parents using generative AI frequently, 18-33% occasionally, and less than a quarter never having used it. Both surveys noted positive views but a lack of consistent institutional policies.
   - An August 2024 analysis found 39% of working-age adults use generative AI; over 24% used it at work at least once in the week; ~10% used it daily. Adoption has been faster than personal computers or the Internet.
   - A UK survey of over 1,000 physicians found 20% reported using generative AI tools in clinical practice; among users, 29% used them to generate documentation after patient appointments and 28% to develop differential diagnoses.
   - A Kaiser Family Foundation survey of 2,428 US adults found ~two-thirds reported some use/interaction with AI, but AI chatbot use for health information was much lower than social media (46% daily) or Internet search (42% daily); only 6% used AI chatbots daily for health info, with 63% never using them.

3. **Results in Biomedicine and Health:**
   - **Medical Board Examinations:** On the USMLE MedQA dataset (12,723 English questions), original ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) scored over 60% (passing). GPT-4 and Google's Med-Gemini surpassed this. OpenAI's o1 model scored 96.0%, the current leader. LLMs also performed well on USMLE soft-skill portions (communication, ethics, empathy, professionalism). Similar success found on radiology, neurosurgery, and clinical informatics board exams. In Israel, GPT-4 passed board exams in all five tested specialties (pediatrics, internal medicine, psychiatry, obstetrics/gynecology, general surgery), scoring comparably in internal medicine and general surgery, better in psychiatry, and inferiorly in pediatrics and obstetrics/gynecology.
   - **Other Medical Examinations:** ChatGPT-3.5 beat physicians in Singapore on an objective structured clinical examination for Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists membership simulation. ChatGPT-4 achieved 81% on the Ophthalmology Knowledge Assessment Program and 73.3% on the Nephrology Self-Assessment Program. On a family medicine in-training exam, ChatGPT-4 scored 86.5% (outperforming third-year resident national averages) and 84% in another study (able to integrate new info and self-correct). On a radiology in-training exam, GPT-4 performed comparably to second-to-third-year residents; image-based questions scored much poorer (45.4%) vs. text-only (80.0%); GPT-4 changed answers ~25% of the time on repeated questions; fine-tuning did not improve accuracy.
   - **Answering Clinical Questions:** Cancer was a heavily studied area. ChatGPT output showed 61.9% concordance with NCCN treatment guidelines for breast, prostate, and lung cancer; 34.3% of outputs recommended nonconcordant treatments; 12.5% contained hallucinations (non-recommended treatments). ChatGPT-4 was the only LLM to score above 50% on oncology questions. For pancreatic cancer, metastatic colorectal cancer, and hepatocellular carcinoma management questions, adding retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) information resulted in 84% correct responses vs. only 57% without it.

4. **Keywords:** artificial intelligence, education, educational assessment, generative artificial intelligence, large language models, professional.

5. **Article Structure:** Sections include Introduction; Usage of Generative AI; Results of Generative AI in Biomedicine and Health; Limitations of Generative AI; Impact of Generative AI on Education; Conclusions; Future Issues; Disclosure Statement; Literature Cited (155 references). The page includes figures showing LLM incremental progress on the USMLE MedQA dataset over time and LLM success versus physicians in five Israeli specialties.

## Abstract

### Aim

To examine the challenges and opportunities presented by generative artificial intelligence in healthcare education and explore how it can be used ethically to enhance rather than compromise future healthcare workforce competence.

### Background

Generative artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing healthcare education, yet many universities and healthcare educators have failed to keep pace with its rapid development.

### Design

A discussion paper.

### Methods

Discussion and analysis of the challenges and opportunities presented by students' increasing use of generative artificial intelligence in healthcare education, with particular focus on assessment approaches, critical thinking development and artificial intelligence literacy.

### Results

Students' widespread use of generative artificial intelligence threatens assessment integrity and may inhibit critical thinking, problem-solving skills and knowledge acquisition. Without adequate artificial intelligence literacy there is a risk of eroding future healthcare workforce competence and compromising patient safety and professional integrity.

### Conclusion

While generative artificial intelligence presents significant challenges to healthcare education, it offers great promise if used carefully with awareness of its limitations. The development of artificial intelligence literacy is crucial for maintaining professional standards and ensuring patient safety and mitigating its potentially negative impact on the formation of critical thinking skills.

This is a research article published in Nurse Education in Practice (Volume 87, August 2025, Article 104461), part of a special issue on "Exploring the frontiers of Artificial Intelligence in nursing/midwifery education" edited by Dr. Siobhán O'Connor (King's College London), Dr. Jennie De Gagne (Duke University), and Dr. Vivian Hui (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University). The article is open access under a Creative Commons license and has been cited by 39 subsequent works.

TITLE AND AUTHORS: "Generative AI in healthcare education: How AI literacy gaps could compromise learning and patient safety" by Daniel Rodger, Sebastian Porsdam Mann, Brian Earp, Julian Savulescu, Christopher Bobier, and Bruce P. Blackshaw. DOI: 10.1016/j.nepr.2025.104461.

ABSTRACT/KEY FINDINGS:
- Aim: To examine the challenges and opportunities presented by generative AI in healthcare education and how it can be used ethically to enhance rather than compromise future healthcare workforce competence.
- Design: A discussion paper analyzing challenges and opportunities of students' increasing use of generative AI in healthcare education, focusing on assessment approaches, critical thinking development, and AI literacy.
- Results: Students' widespread use of generative AI threatens assessment integrity and may inhibit critical thinking, problem-solving skills, and knowledge acquisition. Without adequate AI literacy, there is a risk of eroding future healthcare workforce competence and compromising patient safety and professional integrity.
- Conclusion: While generative AI presents significant challenges, it offers great promise if used carefully with awareness of its limitations. Developing AI literacy is crucial for maintaining professional standards and ensuring patient safety.

STRUCTURE: The article covers Introduction, Credit for success, Who is accountable?, Implications for critical thinking, Discussion, and Conclusion sections, plus a table on "Opportunities, challenges and mitigation strategies for using GenAI in teaching and assessment."

KEYWORDS: Artificial intelligence, Nursing, Chatbot, ChatGPT, Generative artificial intelligence, Machine learning, Patient safety, Workforce, Literacy, Universities, AI.

## Abstract

We use detailed administrative data to study the adjustment of local labor markets to industrial robots in Germany. Robot exposure, as predicted by a shift-share variable, is associated with displacement effects in manufacturing, but those are fully offset by new jobs in services. The incidence mostly falls on young workers just entering the labor force. Automation is related to more stable employment within firms for incumbents, and this is driven by workers taking over new tasks in their original plants. Several measures indicate that those new jobs are of higher quality than the previous ones. Young workers also adapt their educational choices, and substitute away from vocational training towards colleges and universities. Finally, industrial robots have benefited workers in occupations with complementary tasks, such as managers or technical scientists.
